Recipe: To prepare Alu Bhuna (Chattogram style), also known as roasted potato curry, begin by boiling 3 medium-sized potatoes, then peel and dice them into even chunks. Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a heavy-bottomed pan and fry the diced potatoes until they turn golden brown, then set them aside. In the remaining oil, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds and let them splutter, followed by 1 finely chopped onion and 1 tablespoon each of ginger and garlic paste; sauté until the onion is soft and fragrant. Next, mix in 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, and 1 teaspoon of cumin powder, along with a pinch of salt to taste, and cook the spices with a splash of water until the oil separates. Add 1 chopped tomato and cook until it softens and blends with the masala, then stir in the fried potatoes, ensuring they are well coated with the spice mixture. Pour in about 1 cup of water to create a thick gravy and let it simmer, covered, for about 10 minutes until the gravy thickens and the potatoes are tender and fully cooked. Finish by stirring in 1 teaspoon of garam masala and a handful of fresh coriander leaves, then serve hot with roti, paratha, or rice.

To prepare Alu Bhuna in the Hill Tracts style, a distinctively spicy and often dry potato preparation, first boil 3 medium-sized potatoes until tender, then peel and dice them into cubes. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until it smokes lightly, then lower the heat and add 1 teaspoon of whole cumin seeds and 2 dried red chilies, allowing them to crackle. Next, add 1 large chopped onion, 1 teaspoon each of ginger paste and garlic paste, and sauté until the onion turns golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste, cooking the masala with a splash of water until the raw smell disappears and the oil separates. Add the diced boiled potatoes and 2 slit green chilies, mixing gently so the potatoes are coated completely in the spicy bhuna masala. Cook on medium-low heat, stirring occasionally, for about 10 minutes until the potatoes are well-roasted and the curry is dry, not gravy-like. Finish with a sprinkle of fresh chopped coriander and serve hot.

To prepare Alu Bhuna in the Khulna style, known for its rich and slightly tangy flavor, begin by boiling 3 medium-sized potatoes until they are three-quarters done, then peel and cube them. Heat 3 tablespoons of vegetable oil in a pan and lightly fry the potato cubes until golden on the edges, then remove and set aside. In the same oil, add 1 large finely chopped onion and sauté until it turns light brown, followed by 1 teaspoon each of ginger paste and garlic paste; cook until fragrant. Now, stir in 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of cumin powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste, adding a small amount of water to prevent burning, and cook the spice mix until the oil begins to separate. Add 1 finely chopped or puréed tomato and a dollop of yogurt, cooking until the tomato softens and the masala is well-bhuna or roasted. Return the fried potato cubes to the pan, add 1 cup of water for a semi-dry gravy, and let it simmer for about 10 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender and the gravy has thickened. Garnish with chopped green chilies and fresh coriander leaves before serving hot.

To prepare Alu Bhuna in the Rajshahi style, a rich and aromatic potato dish, begin by boiling and cubing 3 medium-sized potatoes, and then set them aside. Heat 3 to 4 tablespoons of oil in a pan and add 1 teaspoon of whole cumin seeds to splutter; then add 1 large finely chopped onion and sauté until it turns a deep golden brown. Next, add 1 teaspoon each of ginger and garlic paste and cook until fragrant. Reduce the heat and stir in 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste, adding a splash of water to cook the spices until the oil separates. Add 1 chopped tomato and cook until it softens and the masala is well-bhuna or roasted. Return the cubed potatoes to the pan along with 2 to 3 slit green chilies and 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala powder, mixing gently to coat the potatoes in the thick masala. Cover and cook on low heat for about 5 to 7 minutes until the flavors are fully absorbed and the curry is mostly dry. Garnish with fresh chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Alu Bhuna in the Sylhet style, a simple yet spicy version, begin by boiling, peeling, and cubing 3 medium-sized potatoes, then lightly fry them in 3 tablespoons of oil until they are slightly golden and set them aside. In the remaining oil, add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until it turns light brown, followed by 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. Reduce the heat and stir in 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste, mixing with a splash of water to form the bhuna masala. Add 1 half cup of chopped tomatoes and 3 slit green chilies and cook, stirring frequently, until the tomatoes soften and the oil separates. Now, return the fried potato cubes to the pan and gently mix to coat them thoroughly with the spicy masala. Add 1 half cup of water for a semi-dry consistency and simmer for about 5 minutes, or until the gravy thickens and clings to the potatoes. Stir in 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala and finish the dish by garnishing with fresh chopped coriander leaves before serving hot.

To prepare Alu Dry in the Barisal style, a rustic and aromatic dish characterized by its dry texture and mustard flavor, start by washing and peeling 3 medium-sized potatoes, then slicing them into thin wedges. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until it begins to smoke lightly, then reduce the heat. Add 1 teaspoon of black mustard seeds and let them splutter. Next, add 1 large onion sliced thinly and sauté until it turns golden brown. Mix in 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, stirring until the raw aroma disappears. Now, add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste. Sprinkle a few drops of water to help the spices combine and cook the masala until oil begins to separate.

Add the sliced potatoes to the pan and stir well to coat them evenly with the spices. Cover and cook on low heat for about 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. Do not add water—allow the potatoes to cook in their own steam until soft and slightly crisp at the edges. Once done, sprinkle 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala and a handful of chopped fresh coriander leaves. Mix gently and serve hot as a side dish with steamed rice or paratha.

To prepare Alu Dry in the Khulna style, a flavorful and earthy potato dish known for its smoky and slightly tangy taste, begin by peeling and cubing 3 medium-sized potatoes. Heat 3 tablespoons of soybean oil in a pan and lightly fry the potato cubes until they turn golden on the edges, then remove and set aside. In the same oil, add 1 teaspoon of panch phoron (Bengali five-spice mix) and let it splutter to release its aroma. Add 1 large finely chopped onion and sauté until light brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears.

Reduce the heat and add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of roasted coriander powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Mix the spices with a splash of water and fry the masala until oil separates. Add 1 chopped tomato and 2 slit green chilies, cooking until the tomato softens. Return the fried potato cubes to the pan and mix thoroughly so they are evenly coated with the spice mixture. Continue to cook uncovered on low heat for about 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes are well roasted and the dish becomes completely dry with a light caramelized coating.

Finish by adding a squeeze of fresh lemon juice and a few chopped coriander leaves for brightness. Serve hot with plain rice or khichuri.

To prepare Alu Dry in the Rajshahi style, a subtly spiced and slightly sweet potato dish known for its balanced flavor and use of roasted spices, start by peeling and dicing 3 medium-sized potatoes into small cubes. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until lightly smoking, then reduce the heat. Add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds and let them crackle. Follow with 1 large onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until soft and golden. Add 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, stirring until fragrant.

Now, incorporate 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 half teaspoon of roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add a small splash of water to prevent burning and fry the masala until oil separates. Stir in 1 half cup of finely chopped ripe tomatoes and 1 teaspoon of sugar, allowing the mixture to cook until it becomes thick and glossy. Add the potato cubes and mix gently to coat them evenly with the spiced base.

Cover and cook on medium-low heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes become tender and lightly crisp on the edges. Ensure the dish remains dry and aromatic, not saucy. Finish by adding 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala and a few chopped fresh coriander leaves. Serve warm with steamed rice, ruti, or paratha.

To prepare Alu Dry in the Rangpur style, a distinctly rustic and sharp-flavored dish known for its mustard and green chili intensity, start by peeling and slicing 3 medium-sized potatoes into thin rounds or wedges. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a heavy pan until it reaches smoking point, then lower the heat. Add 1 teaspoon of black mustard seeds and let them splutter. Immediately add 1 large onion, finely sliced, and sauté until light golden. Mix in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste and 1 half teaspoon of ginger paste, frying until aromatic.

Next, reduce the heat and add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste. Sprinkle a few drops of water and stir until the spices form a smooth paste and the oil begins to separate. Add 4–5 slit green chilies and 1 tablespoon of freshly ground mustard paste (made from soaked mustard seeds and a pinch of salt), stirring gently to combine.

Now, add the sliced potatoes and toss well to coat them thoroughly with the spicy mustard mixture. Cover and cook on low heat for about 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent burning. Avoid adding water — the potatoes should cook in steam and develop a dry, slightly crisp exterior. Once done, drizzle a few drops of raw mustard oil over the top for extra aroma and mix lightly. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves before serving hot.

To prepare Alu Dry in the Sylhet style, a mildly spiced and aromatic potato dish that emphasizes simplicity and the fragrance of green chilies, begin by peeling and cutting 3 medium-sized potatoes into thin wedges or small cubes. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil or soybean oil in a pan and lightly fry the potatoes until the edges turn golden, then remove and set aside. In the same oil, add 1 large onion, finely sliced, and sauté until translucent. Add 1 teaspoon of garlic paste and 1 half teaspoon of ginger paste, stirring until the raw smell disappears.

Reduce the heat and add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add a splash of water to keep the masala from burning and fry until oil separates. Add 3–4 slit green chilies and stir for a minute to infuse the flavor. Return the fried potatoes to the pan and mix gently so they are well-coated with the spice blend.

Continue to cook uncovered on low flame for about 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes are tender and the mixture becomes completely dry, with a light golden crust forming on some pieces. For an authentic Sylheti touch, sprinkle 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala and a few drops of lemon juice before removing from heat. Garnish with freshly chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice or paratha.

To prepare Alu Fry in the Chattogram style, a crisp, spicy, and coastal-flavored potato dish that reflects the region’s fondness for sharp chili heat and mustard oil, begin by peeling and cutting 3 medium-sized potatoes into thin matchstick-like pieces or small wedges. Wash and pat them dry to remove excess starch. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a heavy pan until it begins to smoke lightly, then reduce the heat.

Add 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds and let them splutter. Immediately add 1 large onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until light golden. Stir in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste and 1 half teaspoon of ginger paste, frying until aromatic. Now, add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste. Mix well with a small splash of water and fry the masala until oil separates.

Add the potato pieces and toss thoroughly so they are evenly coated with the spice mixture. Cook uncovered on medium heat for about 10–12 minutes, stirring occasionally to ensure even frying and slight crisping on the edges. When the potatoes turn deep golden and dry, add 4–5 slit green chilies and 1 teaspoon of lemon juice for a tangy finish. Stir for another minute, then turn off the heat.

Garnish with a few chopped coriander leaves and serve hot — best enjoyed with plain rice, dal, or paratha.

To prepare Alu Fry, a simple yet flavorful Rajshahi-style potato dish, begin by peeling and slicing 3–4 medium potatoes into thin sticks or wedges, then washing them well and patting dry. In a frying pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil until lightly smoking, then add ½ teaspoon nigella seeds and 2–3 slit green chilies, letting them splutter for aroma. Add the potato slices, sprinkle with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, and fry on medium heat, stirring occasionally so they cook evenly without sticking. Continue frying until the potatoes turn golden, crisp on the outside, and soft inside, which usually takes about 12–15 minutes. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil for an extra punch of flavor. Serve hot with plain bhaat and lentils as a homestyle side.

To prepare Alu Fry in the Rangpur style, a bold and rustic dish known for its smoky mustard flavor and fiery spice, start by peeling and slicing 3 medium-sized potatoes into thin strips or small cubes. Rinse them in water and pat dry to remove excess starch. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until it begins to smoke, then lower the flame.

Add 1 teaspoon of black mustard seeds and let them splutter, releasing their aroma. Next, add 1 large onion, finely sliced, and sauté until golden brown. Mix in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste and 1 half teaspoon of ginger paste, stirring until the raw smell fades. Reduce the heat and add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 half teaspoon of roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add a small splash of water to blend the spices, then fry until oil separates and the masala becomes aromatic.

Now, add the potato slices and coat them evenly in the spiced mixture. Cook uncovered on medium heat, stirring frequently, for about 12–15 minutes until the potatoes are crisp and golden brown on the outside but tender inside. Toward the end, add 4 slit green chilies and drizzle a few drops of raw mustard oil for extra sharpness — a signature of Rangpur cuisine.

Finish with a sprinkle of chopped coriander leaves and serve hot as a side dish with rice and lentils or khichuri.

To prepare Alu Fry in the Sylhet style, a light, flavorful, and mildly spicy potato dish known for its simplicity and aromatic touch, begin by peeling and thinly slicing 3 medium-sized potatoes into long strips or small wedges. Wash them thoroughly and pat dry. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil or soybean oil in a frying pan until it begins to shimmer.

Add 1 large onion, finely sliced, and sauté over medium heat until translucent and lightly golden. Stir in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste and 1 half teaspoon of ginger paste, cooking until the raw aroma disappears. Now, reduce the heat and add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste. Sprinkle a few drops of water and fry the spices until oil separates.

Add the sliced potatoes and toss thoroughly to coat them evenly with the masala. Cook uncovered over medium heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes turn golden brown and slightly crisp on the edges. Add 3–4 slit green chilies and a handful of chopped coriander leaves, stirring for another minute to infuse the flavor.

For an authentic Sylheti finish, drizzle a few drops of fresh lemon juice before turning off the heat. Serve hot with plain rice, khichuri, or paratha.

To prepare Alu Fry in the Tribal style, a traditional hill-tracts-inspired dish known for its earthy simplicity and use of natural ingredients, start by peeling and cutting 3 medium-sized potatoes into thin wedges or cubes. Boil them lightly for 3–4 minutes, drain, and set aside. Heat 3 tablespoons of sesame or mustard oil in a thick-bottomed pan over medium flame.

Add 1 teaspoon of crushed dry red chilies and 3–4 cloves of crushed garlic (not paste) and sauté gently until fragrant. Add 1 small onion, coarsely chopped, and cook until it turns soft and translucent. Stir in 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 half teaspoon of salt (adjust to taste), and 1 teaspoon of freshly ground black pepper or roasted chili flakes — typical to hill cuisine. Mix well.

Now, add the half-boiled potato pieces and stir-fry continuously on medium-high heat for about 10–12 minutes until they turn golden brown and develop a slightly crisp surface. Avoid adding water — the texture should remain dry and roasted. Toward the end, add a few sliced green chilies and 1 tablespoon of finely chopped spring onions or wild coriander (if available) for a fresh, herbal aroma.

For an authentic touch, drizzle a few drops of bamboo shoot oil or smoked mustard oil (if available) before removing from heat — this imparts the characteristic tribal smokiness. Serve warm with sticky rice, boiled vegetables, or hill-style chutney.

To prepare Alu Grilled in the Barisal style, a smoky, mildly tangy, and mustard-flavored potato delicacy that reflects the coastal Barisal palate, begin by washing and peeling 3 medium-sized potatoes. Cut them into thick round slices or wedges and boil them halfway (parboil) until slightly tender but not mushy. Drain and let them cool.

In a mixing bowl, prepare the marinade by combining 2 tablespoons of mustard oil, 1 teaspoon of mustard paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, 1 teaspoon of lemon juice, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, and salt to taste. Mix well until smooth. Add the parboiled potatoes to the marinade, tossing gently to coat each piece evenly. Allow the mixture to rest for about 20–30 minutes to absorb the flavors.

Preheat a grill pan or oven to medium-high heat. Brush the surface lightly with oil. Arrange the marinated potato slices in a single layer and grill for 3–4 minutes on each side (or until golden-brown grill marks appear and the edges become crisp). While grilling, brush occasionally with the remaining marinade to retain flavor and moisture.

Once done, sprinkle 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala and garnish with finely chopped coriander leaves and 2–3 slit green chilies for an aromatic finish. Serve hot with puffed rice (muri), dal-bhat, or as a spicy vegetarian appetizer.

To prepare an authentic Dhaka-style Alu Bhuna, a rich and spicy potato curry that achieves a flavor similar to grilling, start by peeling and cutting 2 large potatoes into small cubes. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil and add a few whole spices like cardamom pods and a small cinnamon stick. Now, add 1 large sliced onion and fry until it becomes golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon of ginger-garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of cumin powder, and a pinch of salt. Cook the spices until fragrant, adding a splash of water to prevent them from burning. Now, add the potato cubes and sauté on medium-high heat until they are well-coated with the spices. Pour in about 1 cup of hot water, reduce the heat to low, and cover the pan to let the potatoes simmer for 15-20 minutes, or until they are very tender and the gravy has thickened to a rich, dark brown color. The long cooking process gives the potatoes a deep, savory, and almost roasted flavor that is perfect with rice or roti.

To prepare Alu Grilled in the Hill Tracts style, a smoky and earthy version with a subtle herbal aroma, start by washing and peeling 3 medium-sized potatoes. Cut them into thick wedges or rounds and parboil for 5–6 minutes until slightly tender but firm enough to hold shape. Drain and set aside.

In a bowl, prepare the marinade by mixing 2 tablespoons of sesame or mustard oil, 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of salt (adjust to taste), and 1 teaspoon of crushed local herbs such as coriander stems or wild spinach leaves (optional, for authentic tribal flavor). Toss the parboiled potatoes in the marinade, ensuring all pieces are coated evenly. Allow them to rest for 15–20 minutes to absorb the flavors.

Preheat a grill pan or open flame. Arrange the marinated potato wedges in a single layer and grill for 4–5 minutes on each side until golden-brown grill marks appear and the edges become crisp. While grilling, brush lightly with remaining marinade to retain moisture and flavor.

Once done, sprinkle a few chopped fresh coriander leaves and a few sliced green chilies for aroma. Serve hot as a side dish with sticky rice or boiled vegetables.

Once done, sprinkle 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala and garnish with freshly chopped coriander leaves and a few slit green chilies. Serve hot as a side dish with steamed rice, dal, or flatbreads.

Prepare the marinade by combining 2 tablespoons of mustard or soybean oil, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, 1 teaspoon of yogurt (for slight tanginess), and salt to taste. Prepare the marinade by mixing 2 tablespoons of sesame or mustard oil, 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of salt, and 1 teaspoon of crushed local herbs or wild coriander (optional for authentic tribal flavor). To prepare Alu Jhol in the Barisal style, a light and mildly spiced potato curry, start by peeling and cubing 3 medium-sized potatoes. Set them aside.

In a pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard or soybean oil until hot. Add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, cooking until aromatic.

Add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste. Mix well. Add the potato cubes and sauté for 2–3 minutes to coat them evenly with the spices. Add 1.5 cups of water and 2 slit green chilies, then cover and simmer for 10–12 minutes, or until the potatoes are tender and the gravy has a light consistency.

Finish by sprinkling 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala and garnish with freshly chopped coriander leaves. Serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Alu Khichuri in the Barisal style, a comforting and mildly spiced potato and rice dish, start by washing 1 cup of Basmati or local rice and soaking it for 15–20 minutes. Peel and cube 3 medium-sized potatoes and set them aside.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard or soybean oil until hot. Add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, cooking until fragrant.

Add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste. Mix well. Add the cubed potatoes and sauté for 3–4 minutes to coat them with the spices. Drain the soaked rice and add it to the pot along with 3 cups of water or stock.

Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook for 20–25 minutes, or until the rice and potatoes are tender and the flavors are absorbed. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking. Finish with 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala and garnish with freshly chopped coriander leaves. Serve hot.

To prepare Alu Khichuri in the Hill Tracts style, a hearty and mildly spiced potato and rice dish with an earthy flavor, start by washing 1 cup of Basmati or local rice and soaking it for 15–20 minutes. Peel and cube 3 medium-sized potatoes and set them aside.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons of sesame or mustard oil until hot. Add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, cooking until fragrant.

Add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste. Mix well. Add the cubed potatoes and sauté for 3–4 minutes to coat them with the spices. Drain the soaked rice and add it to the pot along with 3 cups of water or stock.

To prepare an authentic Sylhet-style Alu Khichuri, a flavorful and comforting rice and lentil dish with potatoes, begin by washing 1 cup of aromatic rice (like Chinigura) and ½ cup of moong dal (yellow split lentils) and set them aside. To prepare Barisal-style Alu Korma, peel and cut 500 grams of potatoes into medium cubes, then wash and set aside. Heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 2 bay leaves, 2 cardamoms, and 1 cinnamon stick, and let them release aroma. Add 2 medium onions finely sliced and fry until golden brown, then stir in 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 2 teaspoons chili powder, 1 teaspoon roasted cumin-coriander powder, and salt to taste, cooking until the spices release oil. Add the potato cubes, stir well to coat in the masala, and cook for 5–6 minutes. Stir in ½ cup beaten yogurt and 2 cups warm water, then cover and simmer for 20–25 minutes on low heat until the potatoes are soft and the gravy is rich. Finish with ½ teaspoon garam masala and a handful of fried onions, serving hot with plain rice or paratha.

To prepare Alu Korma in the Chattogram style, a rich and mildly spiced potato curry, start by boiling, peeling, and cubing 3 medium-sized potatoes. Reduce the heat slightly and add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste, mixing with a splash of water to form a smooth masala. Add ½ cup of chopped tomatoes and 3 slit green chilies, cooking until the tomatoes soften and the oil separates. Add the boiled potato cubes and gently stir to coat them with the creamy masala. Finish by sprinkling ½ teaspoon of Garam Masala and garnish with freshly chopped coriander leaves before serving hot.

To prepare Alu Paturi in the Hill Tracts style, a traditional and earthy potato dish, start by boiling, peeling, and lightly mashing 3 medium-sized potatoes. In a bowl, mix the potatoes with 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, salt to taste, and a splash of sesame or mustard oil. Add 2–3 slit green chilies and a handful of chopped fresh coriander leaves, mixing well. Take a banana leaf or foil sheet, place a portion of the potato mixture in the center, fold it securely, and steam or grill for 10–12 minutes until the flavors meld and the potatoes are heated through. Serve hot directly from the leaf for an authentic hill-tract experience.

To prepare Alu Paturi in the Khulna style, begin by peeling and slicing 3 medium-sized potatoes into thin rounds, then marinate them with 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of mustard paste, 1 teaspoon of grated coconut, 1 teaspoon of mustard oil, salt to taste, and 2 chopped green chilies. Mix well and let the mixture rest for 10–15 minutes. Next, take fresh banana leaves, lightly wilt them over a low flame to make them pliable, and place a portion of the potato mixture in the center of each leaf. Fold the leaves securely into small parcels and tie them with thread or toothpicks. Heat a flat pan or tawa and brush it with a few drops of mustard oil; cook the parcels on low heat for about 10–12 minutes on each side, or until the potatoes are tender and infused with the smoky aroma of the banana leaves. Once done, carefully unwrap and serve the fragrant Alu Paturi hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Alu Paturi in the Mymensingh style, begin by boiling 3 medium-sized potatoes until soft, then peel and mash them well. In a mixing bowl, combine the mashed potatoes with 1 tablespoon of mustard paste, 1 tablespoon of finely chopped onions, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili paste, 1 teaspoon of chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon of mustard oil, 1 teaspoon of grated coconut, a pinch of sugar, and salt to taste. Mix everything thoroughly to create a smooth, spicy mixture. Take banana leaves, lightly heat them over a flame to make them flexible, and place a portion of the potato mixture onto each leaf. Fold into small packets and secure them with thread. Heat a tawa or pan, grease it with a little mustard oil, and cook the packets over low flame for 10–12 minutes on each side until the banana leaves slightly char and release a fragrant aroma. Once cooked, carefully unwrap and serve the Alu Paturi (Mymensingh) hot with steamed rice for a rustic, homely taste.

To prepare Alu Paturi in the Rangpur style, start by boiling 3 medium-sized potatoes until just tender, then peel and mash them lightly. Fold the leaves into neat packets and secure with thread or toothpicks. Heat a tawa or flat pan, brush it with a little mustard oil, and cook the packets on low flame for about 8–10 minutes on each side until a rich aroma develops and the leaves are slightly charred. Serve the warm, smoky Alu Paturi (Rangpur) with plain rice or khichuri for an authentic regional flavor.

To prepare traditional Rajshahi-style Alu Stuffed, start by boiling 3 large potatoes (about 400 g) until tender, then peel and mash them smoothly. Mix in ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste, stirring briefly before adding the mashed potatoes. Cook for 3–4 minutes while mixing well, then finish with chopped fresh coriander and let the filling cool. For the outer shell, prepare a dough by mixing 2 cups of wheat flour with 1 teaspoon salt, 1 tablespoon oil, and enough water to make a soft, pliable dough; rest it for 15 minutes. Divide the dough into small balls, roll each into a small disc, place some potato filling in the center, and fold the edges to seal. Roll gently into flat stuffed discs. Heat a tawa or skillet and cook each stuffed piece on medium heat, drizzling with a little ghee or oil, until golden brown on both sides. Cook for 5–6 minutes on low heat until the potatoes are well-flavored and slightly dry. Finish by garnishing with fresh chopped coriander leaves and a few drops of lemon juice before serving hot.

To prepare Barisal-style Beef Bhuna, wash and cut 1 kilogram of beef into medium chunks, then marinate with 3 tablespoons of yogurt, 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 2 teaspoons of chili powder, 1 teaspoon of turmeric, 2 teaspoons of roasted cumin and coriander powder, 1 teaspoon garam masala, 2 tablespoons of mustard oil, and salt, leaving it for at least 1 hour. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat ½ cup of mustard oil, add 3 sliced onions and fry until deep golden, then add the marinated beef and cook on medium heat until the meat releases juices and the masala thickens. Add 2 cups of water, cover, and cook on low for 1.5–2 hours until the beef is tender, then uncover and stir-fry on high heat until the gravy reduces and clings to the meat, leaving it dark, rich, and aromatic. Garnish with green chilies and fried onions, and serve hot with plain rice or parathas.

To prepare Beef Bhuna in the Chattogram style, a rich, spicy, and aromatic dish with deep coastal flavors, start by cutting 500 g of beef into medium-sized cubes. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until it begins to smoke lightly. Add 1 teaspoon of whole cumin seeds and let them splutter.

Add 2 large chopped onions and sauté over medium heat until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, cooking until the raw aroma disappears. Now add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Fry the masala mixture for 2–3 minutes, stirring continuously.

Add the beef cubes to the pan and stir well to coat them with the spice mixture. Cook on medium-high heat for 5–6 minutes until the beef is lightly seared. Reduce the heat, add 1 half cup of water, cover, and simmer for 40–50 minutes, or until the beef becomes tender and the oil begins to separate from the masala. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking.

Finally, sprinkle 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala, garnish with chopped fresh coriander leaves, and serve hot with steamed rice or paratha.

Add 2 large chopped onions and sauté until they turn golden brown. Mix in 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, cooking until the raw aroma disappears. Stir the spices for 2–3 minutes until fragrant.

Add the beef cubes and coat them evenly with the masala. Cook on medium-high heat for 5–6 minutes until the beef is lightly seared. Finish by sprinkling 1 half teaspoon of Garam Masala and garnish with freshly chopped coriander leaves. Serve hot with steamed rice, paratha, or roti.

To prepare Beef Bhuna (Rajshahi), a classic Bangladeshi slow-cooked, rich, and thick beef curry, begin by washing and draining 1 kg of beef, then mix it in a pan with 2 cups of sliced onion, 1.5 tablespoons of ginger and garlic paste, 1 tablespoon of red chili powder, 1 tablespoon of turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon of coriander powder, 1/2 tablespoon of fried cumin powder, 1/4 cup of yogurt, salt to taste, 1/4 teaspoon each of nutmeg and mace powder, and whole spices (2 cinnamon sticks, 4 cardamoms, 3 cloves, 6−7 black peppercorns, and 2 bay leaves), and 1/2 cup of oil; mix thoroughly by hand and let it marinate for 30 minutes. Cook the mixture on high heat for 5 minutes with the lid closed, then reduce the heat to medium and cook for 60 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef releases its water and the spices are well-cooked (bhuna). Add 1 cup of hot water and 5−6 whole green chillies, cooking uncovered for another 10 minutes on medium flame, stirring occasionally. Finish the dish by stirring in 1/3 cup of crushed fried onions and cooking until the gravy is thick and oil separates from the masala, then serve hot with polao or paratha.

To prepare Beef Khichuri in the Chattogram style, a hearty and flavorful one-pot dish, start by washing 1 cup of Basmati or local rice and soaking it for 15–20 minutes. In a separate large pot, heat 1/2 cup of mustard oil, temper with 1/4 cup of sliced onion, ginger and garlic paste, whole spices, and 1 tsp of turmeric powder, then add the drained rice and dal mixture along with 6 cups of hot water and salt; cook for 5 minutes until the water is slightly reduced. Finally, add the fully cooked beef bhuna to the khichuri, mix gently, add 5−6 whole green chilies, cover, and cook on very low heat for 15−20 minutes, followed by a 10-minute rest for the flavors to meld, resulting in a rich, fragrant, and cohesive khichuri.

In the same pan, add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic. Return the fried eggplant to the pan and toss gently to coat with the spices. Cook for another 3–5 minutes to let the flavors blend.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice or roti for an authentic Chattogram-style Begun Fry experience.

To prepare Hill Tracts-style Begun Jhol, wash and cut 2 medium eggplants into medium-sized cubes, then set aside. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 2 slit green chilies, frying until lightly golden. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, and salt to taste, then add the eggplant pieces and sauté for a few minutes until slightly softened. Pour in 2 cups of warm water, cover, and simmer on low heat for 12–15 minutes until the eggplants are tender and the broth takes on a light, soupy consistency. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil for flavor and serve hot with plain rice as a comforting tribal-style dish.

Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add the prepared eggplant pieces and sauté for 5 minutes. Pour in 2 cups of water, cover, and simmer on low heat for 15–20 minutes until the eggplant becomes soft and tender. Optionally, add 2–3 slit green chilies and a handful of chopped coriander leaves before serving.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Rangpur-style Begun Jhol experience.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Begun Khichuri, start with 2 medium-sized eggplants. Wash and cut them into medium cubes or slices. Sprinkle a little salt over the eggplant and set aside for 10 minutes, then pat dry.

Wash and soak 1.5 cups of rice and 0.5 cup of moong dal (yellow lentils) for 20 minutes, then drain.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until lightly smoking. Add 1 medium onion finely chopped and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon garam masala, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add the eggplant cubes and sauté for 5–7 minutes. Then add the drained rice and dal mixture, and 3 cups of water. Mix gently, cover, and cook over medium heat until the water is mostly absorbed. Reduce the heat to low, cover tightly, and steam for another 10–15 minutes until the rice and dal are fully cooked and fluffy.

Serve hot as a wholesome one-pot meal for an authentic Barisal-style Begun Khichuri experience.

In the same pan, add 2 medium onions finely sliced and fry until golden brown, then stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and cook until fragrant. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste, frying the spices with a splash of water until oil separates. Stir in ½ cup of plain yogurt (whisked) slowly on low heat to prevent curdling, then add the fried eggplants and mix gently so they absorb the korma masala. Pour in 1 cup of warm water or milk (for a richer version), cover, and simmer on low until the eggplants are tender and the gravy turns creamy. Finally, finish with 2–3 slit green chilies and a sprinkle of garam masala, letting it rest for a few minutes before serving. Enjoy hot with plain bhaat or paratha for a comforting meal.

Place the marinated eggplant on a banana leaf (or foil if unavailable), fold it securely to seal the flavors, and steam or grill over medium heat for 10–15 minutes until the eggplant is tender and infused with the spices.

Wash and soak 2 cups of basmati or kalijira rice for 20 minutes, then drain.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until lightly smoking. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon garam masala, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add the eggplant pieces and sauté for 5–7 minutes until lightly tender. Then add the drained rice and 3 cups of hot water. Stir gently to mix, cover, and cook over medium heat until the rice absorbs most of the water. Reduce the heat to low, cover tightly, and steam for another 15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and fluffy.

Serve hot, garnished with fried onions or chopped coriander leaves, for an authentic Chattogram-style Begun Polao.

To prepare traditional Dhaka-style Begun Polao, start by washing and soaking 2 cups of basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and set aside.

In a large heavy-bottomed pot, heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil until hot. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon garam masala, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add 2 medium-sized eggplants cut into cubes and sauté for 5–7 minutes until slightly browned. Pour in 2.5 cups of hot water or light stock. Once it starts to boil, gently add the soaked rice and stir carefully. Cover the pot, reduce the heat to low, and let the polao steam for 15–20 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and fluffy.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Begun Stuffed, take 3 medium eggplants, wash them well, and slit each lengthwise without cutting through completely, keeping the stems intact. Heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil in a flat pan, place the stuffed eggplants gently, cover, and cook on low flame for 15–20 minutes, turning occasionally, until the eggplants are soft, aromatic, and the stuffing is cooked through with a slightly charred exterior. To prepare Begun Tok, a tangy and comforting Barisal-style eggplant curry, begin by washing and cutting 2 medium-sized eggplants into medium wedges, then sprinkle lightly with salt and turmeric and set aside. In a pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil until fragrant, then fry the eggplant pieces until lightly golden and half cooked; remove and keep aside. In the same oil, add ½ teaspoon nigella seeds and 3–4 slit green chilies, letting them splutter for aroma. Next, stir in 1 tablespoon of tamarind pulp (soaked from a small lemon-sized tamarind ball in warm water) along with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, salt to taste, and 1–2 cups of water depending on desired consistency. Bring this tangy broth to a gentle boil, then add back the fried eggplants and simmer on low heat until they soften completely and the sour, spicy flavors meld into the gravy. Adjust tanginess with extra tamarind water if needed, and finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil for authenticity. Serve hot with plain bhaat as a light yet flavorful side.

To prepare Begun Tok (Chattogram), start by washing 2 medium-sized eggplants and cutting them into long strips or bite-sized pieces. Sprinkle lightly with salt and let them sit for 10 minutes to draw out excess moisture. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until hot, then fry the eggplant pieces in batches until golden brown and tender; drain on paper towels. In the same pan, add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic, 2–3 slit green chilies, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste, sautéing briefly until fragrant. Return the fried eggplant to the pan, toss gently with the spices, and finish with 1 tablespoon of mustard oil and a squeeze of lemon juice for the characteristic Chattogram-style tangy and slightly smoky flavor. Serve hot or warm as a spicy, flavorful side dish.

To prepare Begun Tok (Dhaka), start by washing 2 medium-sized eggplants and slicing them into long strips or bite-sized pieces. Sprinkle lightly with salt and let them sit for 10 minutes to remove excess moisture. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee in a pan, then fry the eggplant pieces in batches until golden brown and tender; drain on paper towels. In the same pan, add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic, 2–3 chopped green chilies, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste, sautéing briefly until aromatic. Return the fried eggplant to the pan, toss gently with the spices, and finish with a small splash of mustard oil and a few drops of lemon juice for the classic Dhaka-style tangy and spicy flavor. Serve hot or warm as a flavorful side dish.

To prepare Begun Tok (Hill Tracts), start by washing 2 medium-sized eggplants and cutting them into long strips or chunks. Sprinkle lightly with salt and let them rest for 10–15 minutes to remove excess moisture. Heat 3 tablespoons of sesame oil or mustard oil in a pan, then fry the eggplant pieces in batches until golden brown and tender; drain on paper towels. In the same pan, add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic, 2–3 chopped green chilies, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste, sautéing until aromatic. Return the fried eggplant to the pan and toss gently with the spices. Finish by adding a small handful of crushed roasted peanuts or sesame seeds and a splash of lemon juice for the distinct smoky and nutty Hill Tracts flavor. Serve hot or warm as a traditional, spicy side dish.

Serve hot or warm as a flavorful, spicy side dish.

To prepare Begun Tok (Sylhet), start by washing and slicing 2 medium-sized eggplants into long strips. Sprinkle them lightly with salt and set aside for 10 minutes to remove excess moisture. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until smoking slightly, then fry the eggplant slices in batches until they turn golden brown and soft; remove and drain on paper towels. In the same pan, add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic, 2–3 slit green chilies, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste, sautéing briefly until fragrant. Return the fried eggplant to the pan and toss gently with the spices. Finally, add 1 tablespoon of lemon juice and a pinch of sugar, mixing well to achieve the tangy, spicy Sylheti flavor. Serve hot or at room temperature as a flavorful side dish.

To prepare Chal Bhuna (Barisal), start by washing 1 cup of coarse local rice and soaking it for 20–30 minutes, then drain well. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds and sauté until aromatic. Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook until light brown, then stir in 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, ½ teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste. Mix in the drained rice so that each grain is coated with the spice mixture, and add a splash of water to form a semi-thick bhuna masala. Cook on low heat, stirring occasionally, until the rice absorbs the flavors, becomes semi-dry, and slightly golden. Finish by garnishing with freshly chopped coriander leaves and a few slit green chilies for the traditional Barisali-style spicy and aromatic Chal Bhuna.

To prepare Chal Bhuna (Rangpur), begin by washing 1 cup of parboiled rice and soaking it for 20–30 minutes, then drain well. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds, and sauté until fragrant. Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook until light brown, then stir in 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, ½ teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste. Mix in the drained rice, coating each grain with the spice mixture, and add a splash of water to form a slightly thick bhuna masala. Cook on low heat, stirring occasionally, until the rice absorbs the flavors, becomes semi-dry, and slightly toasted. Garnish with freshly chopped coriander leaves and sliced green chilies before serving for the classic Rangpuri-style spicy and aromatic Chal Bhuna.

To prepare Sylheti-style Chal Bhuna, wash and soak 2 cups of atop or kalijira rice for 30 minutes, then drain well. Heat 4 tablespoons of ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 2 bay leaves, 3 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, and a small cinnamon stick, then fry 1 finely sliced onion until golden. Add the drained rice and stir-fry on medium heat for 6–7 minutes until the grains are lightly toasted and aromatic. Pour in 4 cups of hot water, add 1 teaspoon of salt and ½ teaspoon of turmeric, then cover and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes until the rice is fluffy and separate. Rest for 5 minutes, fluff gently with a fork, and serve hot with meat curry or dal.

To prepare Chal Bhuna (Tribal), begin by washing 1 cup of sticky or glutinous rice and soaking it for 30 minutes, then drain well. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil or sesame oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, and sauté until aromatic. Stir in ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of crushed red chili, ½ teaspoon of ground coriander, and salt to taste, mixing well with a splash of water to form a thick bhuna masala. Add the drained rice and toss gently to coat each grain with the spicy mixture. Cook on low heat, stirring occasionally, until the rice becomes tender and the masala clings to it, forming a semi-dry, richly flavored dish. Finish by garnishing with freshly chopped coriander and a few sliced green chilies for the traditional Tribal-style smoky and spicy flavor.

To prepare Chal Dry (Barisal), start by washing 1 cup of coarse local rice and soaking it for 20–30 minutes, then drain well. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds and 1 finely chopped onion, and sauté until the onion turns golden brown. Mix in 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the drained rice and stir gently to coat each grain with the spices. Cook on low heat, stirring occasionally, until the rice is fully cooked, dry, and fluffy. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and sliced green chilies for a light, aromatic Barisal-style dry rice dish.

To prepare Chal Dry (Dhaka), start by washing 1 cup of short-grain rice and soaking it for 15–20 minutes, then drain thoroughly. Heat 2 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil in a pan, add ½ teaspoon of cumin seeds and a pinch of ground cardamom, and sauté briefly. Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook until golden brown, then stir in 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the drained rice and mix gently so each grain is coated with the spices. Cook on low heat, stirring occasionally, until the rice is dry, fluffy, and fully cooked. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and a few sliced green chilies for the classic Dhaka-style aromatic dry rice.

To prepare Chal Dry (Hill Tracts), start by washing 1 cup of sticky or glutinous hill rice and soaking it for 30–40 minutes, then drain well. Heat 3 tablespoons of sesame oil or mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, and sauté until aromatic. Mix in ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of crushed red chili, ½ teaspoon of ground coriander, and salt to taste. Add the drained rice and toss gently to coat each grain with the spices. Cook on low heat, stirring occasionally, until the rice is fully cooked, dry, and slightly firm, retaining a nutty, smoky flavor. Finish by garnishing with freshly chopped coriander and sliced green chilies for the traditional Hill Tracts-style dry rice.

To prepare traditional Rangpur-style Chal Dry, start by washing 2 cups of atap or chinigura rice thoroughly and soaking it for 20 minutes, then drain well. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan and add 2 medium onions finely sliced, frying until golden brown; reserve half for garnish. To the remaining onions, add 2–3 green chilies, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, stirring briefly. Add the drained rice directly to the pan and dry-fry on medium heat for 6–8 minutes, stirring continuously so the grains get coated in the spiced oil but do not break. Cook until the rice develops a slightly crisp texture and a nutty aroma. Add the reserved fried onions on top, along with a drizzle of mustard oil, and serve warm.

To prepare Chal Fry (Chattogram), begin by washing 1 cup of aromatic long-grain rice and soaking it for 20 minutes, then drain well. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a deep pan, add ½ teaspoon of whole cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf, and sauté for a few seconds. Add 1 finely chopped onion and fry until golden brown, then mix in 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, ½ teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste. Stir in the drained rice, coating it evenly with the spices, and add 2 cups of water. Bring it to a boil, then reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer until the rice is fully cooked and fluffy. Garnish with sliced green chilies, fried onions, and fresh coriander leaves before serving hot.

To prepare Chal Fry (Dhaka), start by washing 1 cup of short-grain rice and soaking it for 15–20 minutes, then drain thoroughly. Heat 2 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds and a pinch of crushed cardamom, and sauté briefly. Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook until golden brown, then stir in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste. Mix in the drained rice so that each grain is coated with the spices, then pour 2 cups of water and bring to a boil. Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer until the rice is tender and fluffy. Finish by garnishing with fried onions, chopped coriander, and a few slit green chilies for the classic Dhaka-style flavor.

To prepare Hill Tracts–style Chal Fry, wash 2 cups of atop or desi rice thoroughly, then drain and spread for 10–15 minutes to remove excess water. Heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee in a heavy pan, add 2 sliced onions and fry until golden, then stir in 2 slit green chilies, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and salt to taste. Add the drained rice and fry on medium heat for 8–10 minutes, stirring gently until the grains are lightly toasted and aromatic. Pour in 4 cups of hot water, cover the pan tightly, and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes until the rice is fluffy and separate. Let it rest for 5 minutes before fluffing, then serve hot with tribal-style curries or vegetables.

To prepare Chal Fry (Sylhet), start by washing and soaking 1 cup of parboiled rice for 20–30 minutes, then drain it well. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds, and let them splutter. Add 1 finely chopped onion and sauté until golden brown, followed by 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, cooking until the raw aroma disappears. Mix in 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the drained rice, stirring well to coat each grain with the spice mixture, then pour 2 cups of water and bring it to a boil. Reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook until the rice is tender and the water is absorbed. Finish by fluffing the rice gently with a fork and garnishing with chopped fresh coriander and sliced green chilies for added flavor.

To prepare Chal Grilled (Barisal), begin by washing 1 cup of coarse local rice and soaking it for 30 minutes, then draining well. In a bowl, mix the rice with 2 tablespoons of mustard oil, 2 tablespoons of freshly grated coconut, 1 teaspoon of crushed green chili, 1 teaspoon of roasted coriander powder, ½ teaspoon of turmeric, and salt to taste. Add 2 tablespoons of onion paste and a squeeze of lemon juice to give it the distinctive Barisali tang. Stir well so the rice absorbs the flavors. Heat a flat tawa or skillet on medium heat, lightly grease it with a few drops of oil, and spread the rice mixture evenly in a thin layer. Grill gently until the bottom becomes crisp and lightly golden, then flip and cook the other side until aromatic and slightly smoky. The Barisal-style version is coastal in flavor—spicy, tangy, and coconut-rich—traditionally served with fried dry fish or green chili-onion relish.

To prepare Chal Grilled (Dhaka), first wash 1 cup of miniket or chinigura rice and soak it for 20 minutes, then drain well. In a bowl, combine the rice with 2 tablespoons of ghee, 1 tablespoon of yogurt, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of roasted cumin powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili flakes, a pinch of turmeric, and salt to taste. Mix thoroughly so that every grain is coated with the rich Dhaka-style marinade. Heat a non-stick pan or tawa on medium flame, lightly grease it with ghee, and spread the spiced rice mixture evenly into a thin, round layer. Press gently with a spatula and cook on low heat until the bottom turns crisp and golden brown. Flip carefully and grill the other side until aromatic and slightly charred at the edges. This Dhakai version has a buttery, mildly spicy flavor with a touch of tang from yogurt, usually served with mint chutney or fried eggplant slices.

To prepare Chal Grilled (Hill Tracts), start by washing 1 cup of sticky hill rice (jum rice or glutinous rice) and soaking it for 1 hour, then draining completely. In a bowl, mix the rice with 2 tablespoons of sesame oil, 1 teaspoon of crushed dry red chili, 1 teaspoon of roasted bamboo shoot paste (optional but traditional), 1 teaspoon of salt, and 2 tablespoons of freshly grated coconut. Wrap small portions of the seasoned rice mixture in banana leaves, folding them into flat rectangular parcels and securing the edges with toothpicks or threads. Place the parcels on a preheated grill or directly over low charcoal heat and cook for 8–10 minutes on each side, turning carefully until the banana leaves are slightly charred and the rice inside becomes firm and aromatic. Remove from the heat, unwrap, and serve hot—the rice will have a smoky, nutty flavor unique to the Hill Tracts region, often paired with chili-garlic chutney or smoked fish.

To prepare Chal Grilled (Mymensingh), begin by washing 1 cup of aromatic atop rice and soaking it for 20 minutes, then draining well. In a mixing bowl, combine the rice with 3 tablespoons of thick coconut milk, 1 tablespoon of mustard oil, 1 teaspoon of green chili paste, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, salt to taste, and a handful of finely chopped onions and coriander leaves. Mix everything thoroughly so that the rice absorbs the flavors. Heat a greased flat pan or tawa on medium heat, spread the marinated rice mixture evenly into a round layer about half an inch thick, and press lightly with a spatula. Grill on low flame until the bottom forms a crisp, golden crust, then flip gently and cook the other side until lightly browned and aromatic. This Mymensingh-style version has a soft, flavorful inside with a smoky outer crust, often enjoyed with spicy lentil chutney or mashed fried fish.

To prepare Chal Grilled (Rangpur), start by washing and soaking 1 cup of parboiled rice for 30 minutes, then drain it well. In a bowl, mix the rice with 2 tablespoons of mustard oil, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of roasted cumin powder, 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic, salt to taste, and a pinch of turmeric, ensuring the rice is evenly coated with the spices. Heat a flat iron griddle or non-stick pan, brush it with a little oil, and spread the marinated rice evenly in a thin layer. Press it gently with the back of a spatula and cook on low flame until the bottom turns crispy and golden brown. To prepare traditional Tribal-style Chal Grilled, start with 4–6 fresh eggs. Boil them for 8–10 minutes until hard-boiled, then peel and set aside.

In a small bowl, prepare a marinade with 1–2 tablespoons mustard oil, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, 1–2 finely chopped local green chilies, and a pinch of salt. Optionally, add a few chopped local herbs for authentic tribal flavor. Coat the boiled eggs evenly with the marinade.

Place the marinated eggs on a banana leaf or aluminum foil and grill over medium heat for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally, until lightly charred and aromatic.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Tribal-style Chal Grilled experience.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Chal Jhol, start with 1.5 cups of rice. Wash thoroughly and soak for 20 minutes, then drain.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until hot. Add 1 medium onion finely chopped and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add the drained rice and stir gently. Pour in 3 cups of hot water or light stock. Cover and cook over medium heat until the water is mostly absorbed. Reduce the heat to low, cover tightly, and simmer for another 10–15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and fluffy.

Optionally, garnish with chopped coriander leaves or a few fried onions before serving.

Serve hot for an authentic Barisal-style Chal Jhol experience.

To prepare Hill Tracts–style Chal Jhol, wash 2 cups of atop or kalijira rice thoroughly and set aside. Add the drained rice and stir-fry gently for 5–6 minutes until aromatic. Pour in 4 cups of hot water and salt to taste, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes until the rice is soft, separate, and slightly soupy. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and serve hot with meat or vegetable curries typical of Hill Tracts cuisine.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Chal Jhol, wash 2 cups of atop or kalijira rice thoroughly and set aside. Add the drained rice and stir-fry gently for 5–6 minutes until the grains are lightly toasted. Pour in 4 cups of hot water, season with salt, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes until the rice is soft, separate, and slightly soupy. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and serve hot with light curries or bhartas typical of Rajshahi cuisine.

To make traditional Sylheti Chal Jhol, begin by washing 1 cup of coarse rice (chal), preferably parboiled or local aromatic rice, and soak it for 10 minutes, then drain. In a medium pot, heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil until it reaches smoking point, then lower the heat. Add 1 small onion finely sliced and sauté lightly until translucent.

Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, and 1–2 slit green chilies, stirring gently for about a minute until aromatic. Add the soaked rice and stir for 1–2 minutes so the grains are lightly coated with oil and spices.

Pour in 3½ to 4 cups of hot water and add salt to taste (about ¾ teaspoon). Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat to low and let it simmer uncovered for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice grains are soft and the dish reaches a soupy, jhol-like consistency.

Once the rice is fully cooked and slightly broken (a hallmark of authentic Chal Jhol), drizzle 1 teaspoon of raw mustard oil on top and let it rest for 2 minutes before serving. The final texture should be light, comforting, and mildly spiced.

Serve hot as a standalone comfort dish or alongside fried fish, shutki, or green chili, as traditionally enjoyed in Sylheti households.

To make traditional Barisal-style Chal Khichuri, begin by washing 1 cup of coarse rice (chal), preferably parboiled or local Barisal rice, and soaking it for 10 minutes, then draining well. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil until it reaches smoking point, then lower the heat. Add 1 medium onion thinly sliced and fry until lightly golden.

Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, and 1½ teaspoons red chili powder, sautéing gently for 2–3 minutes until fragrant. Add ½ cup split moong dal (washed and drained) and stir for another 1–2 minutes so the dal is well coated with the spices.

Add the soaked rice and mix everything thoroughly. Pour in 4½ to 5 cups of hot water and add salt to taste (about 1½ teaspoons). Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low and cook uncovered for 15–18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice and dal are fully cooked and reach a soft, slightly mashed khichuri consistency.

Once done, add 2–3 slit green chilies and drizzle 1 teaspoon of raw mustard oil on top for aroma. Cover and let it rest for 5 minutes before serving.

Serve hot with fried hilsa (ilish bhaja), beguni, or mashed vegetables, as traditionally enjoyed in Barisal households.

To make traditional Chattogram-style Chal Khichuri, begin by washing 1 cup of coarse rice (chal) and ½ cup split moong dal separately, then soaking both together for 10 minutes and draining well. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil until it reaches smoking point, then lower the heat. Add 2 medium onions thinly sliced and fry until deep golden brown, as Chattogram khichuri is known for its richer flavor.

Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons red chili powder, and 1 teaspoon ground cumin-coriander mix. Sauté on low heat for 3–4 minutes until the oil separates and the masala becomes aromatic.

Add the soaked rice and dal, stirring well so they are evenly coated with the spice mixture. Pour in 5 to 5½ cups of hot water and add salt to taste (about 1½ teaspoons). Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low and cook uncovered for 18–20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice and dal are fully cooked and the khichuri becomes soft, slightly mushy, and rich.

Once cooked, add 3–4 slit green chilies and drizzle 1 teaspoon of raw mustard oil for a strong coastal aroma. Cover and let it rest for 5 minutes before serving.

Serve hot with beef curry, dried fish bhorta, or fried eggplant, as traditionally enjoyed in Chattogram households.

Serve hot with dried fish bhorta, fried shrimp, or simple vegetable curry, as traditionally enjoyed in Khulna households.

To make traditional Chattogram-style Chal Korma, begin by washing 1 cup of coarse rice (chal) and soaking it for 10–15 minutes, then draining. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil until it reaches smoking point, then lower the heat. Add 1 medium onion thinly sliced and sauté until golden brown.

Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and 1 teaspoon ground coriander. Sauté gently for 2–3 minutes until the spices release their aroma.

Pour in 3–3½ cups of hot water and add salt to taste (about 1 teaspoon). Cover and cook on low heat for 18–20 minutes until the rice is tender and the korma reaches a creamy, slightly thick consistency. Serve hot with fried fish, beef curry, or vegetable sides, as traditionally enjoyed in Chattogram households.

To make traditional Barisal-style Chal Paturi, begin by washing 1 cup of coarse rice (chal) and soaking it for 15 minutes, then draining well. Grind the soaked rice into a coarse paste using minimal water and keep aside.

Mix in ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and 1 tablespoon mustard oil.

In a bowl, combine the ground rice paste with the mustard mixture and add 2 tablespoons thick yogurt to give a soft, creamy texture. Adjust salt if needed.

Take banana leaves and lightly heat them over a flame to soften. Cut them into medium squares. Place a portion of the rice–mustard mixture in the center of each leaf, drizzle a few drops of mustard oil on top, and fold the leaf securely into a parcel, tying with thread if needed.

Steam the parcels in a steamer or covered pot for 25–30 minutes on medium heat until the rice is fully cooked and the aroma of mustard fills the dish. Once done, allow them to rest for a few minutes before opening.

To make traditional Rangpur-style Chal Polao, begin by washing 1 cup of aromatic rice (kalijira or basmati) and soaking it for 20 minutes, then draining well. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee until hot. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until lightly golden brown.

Add whole spices: 2 green cardamoms, 2 cloves, 1 small cinnamon stick, and 1 bay leaf. Sauté briefly until fragrant. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, ½ teaspoon garlic paste, and ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, stirring gently for a minute.

Add the soaked rice and sauté for 1–2 minutes so the grains are evenly coated with oil and spices. Pour in 2 cups of hot water (or light chicken stock) and add salt to taste (about ¾ teaspoon). Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat to low, cover tightly, and cook for 12–15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and fluffy.

Once done, drizzle 1 teaspoon of mustard oil or ghee on top and let it rest covered for 5 minutes. Fluff gently before serving.

Serve hot with fried fish, simple meat curry, or vegetable sides, as traditionally enjoyed in Rangpur households.

To make traditional Sylheti Chal Polao, begin by washing 1 cup of aromatic rice (kalijira or small-grain basmati) and soaking it for 20 minutes, then draining well. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee until hot. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until light golden brown.

Add whole spices: 2–3 green cardamoms, 2 cloves, 1 small cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf, and a pinch of nutmeg. Sauté briefly until fragrant. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, ½ teaspoon garlic paste, and ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, stirring gently for 1–2 minutes.

Add the soaked rice and sauté for 1–2 minutes so the grains are evenly coated with oil and spices. Pour in 2 cups of hot water (or light stock) and add salt to taste (about ¾ teaspoon). Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat to low, cover tightly, and cook for 12–15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and fluffy.

Once done, drizzle 1 teaspoon of mustard oil or ghee on top and let it rest covered for 5 minutes. Fluff gently before serving.

Serve hot with fish curry, chicken curry, or vegetable sides, as traditionally enjoyed in Sylhet households.

To make traditional Tribal-style Chal Polao, begin by washing 1 cup of coarse rice (chal) and soaking it for 15–20 minutes, then draining well. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 2–3 tablespoons of mustard oil until hot. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté lightly until golden brown.

Prepare a simple spice mix by adding ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and a pinch of salt. Unlike urban versions, Tribal-style polao emphasizes simplicity and natural flavors rather than complex spices. Sauté the spices with the onions for 1–2 minutes.

Add the soaked rice to the pot and stir gently to coat the grains with the spiced oil. Pour in 2 cups of hot water and cover the pot. Cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and fluffy.

Optionally, finish with a few drops of mustard oil or locally foraged herbs for added aroma.

Serve hot with forest vegetables, smoked fish, or simple lentil preparations, as traditionally enjoyed in tribal communities.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Chal Steamed (Chal Bhapa), take 2 cups of rice flour (preferably freshly ground parboiled rice flour), add ½ teaspoon salt, and gradually mix in 1 to 1¼ cups of lukewarm water while rubbing the flour between your fingers until it becomes moist and crumbly, resembling damp sand rather than a dough; lightly grease small steel bowls or molds with oil, loosely fill them with the rice mixture without pressing, and place them in a steamer over boiling water, then cover and steam on medium heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice cakes are firm, aromatic, and easily release from the sides, after which they should be rested briefly and served hot.

To prepare Dhaka-style Chal Steamed (Chal Bhapa), take 2 cups of fine rice flour, add ½ teaspoon salt and 1 teaspoon sugar, then gradually mix in 1 to 1¼ cups of lukewarm water while gently rubbing the flour with your fingers until it becomes soft, moist, and slightly lighter in texture than the Barisal version; lightly grease small bowls or molds, loosely fill them with the mixture, and for the Dhaka style add a thin layer of grated coconut or a few raisins on top before steaming, then place the molds in a steamer over boiling water, cover tightly, and steam on medium heat for 18–22 minutes until the chal steamed turns fluffy, mildly sweet, and fragrant, after which it is unmolded and served warm.

To prepare Hill Tracts–style Chal Steamed, take 2 cups of coarsely ground rice flour (traditionally hand-pounded rice), add ½ teaspoon salt, and gradually sprinkle in 1 to 1¼ cups of warm water while gently mixing with your fingers until the flour becomes lightly moist and airy, not compact; line small bamboo cups or metal molds with banana leaves for aroma, loosely fill them with the rice mixture, and place them in a steamer over vigorously boiling water, then cover tightly and steam on medium heat for 22–25 minutes until the rice becomes firm yet fluffy with a clean, natural rice aroma, after which it is unmolded and served hot, typically accompanied by boiled vegetables, bamboo shoot bhorta, or simple fermented fish preparations, reflecting the minimal-spice cooking traditions of the Hill Tracts.

To prepare Khulna-style Chal Steamed, wash 2 cups of atop or kalijira rice thoroughly and soak for 20–30 minutes, then drain. Mix the drained rice with 2 tablespoons mustard oil, ½ teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, 2 slit green chilies, and salt to taste. Wrap the seasoned rice in banana leaves or place in a greased steaming bowl, then steam over low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice is soft, fluffy, and aromatic. Let it rest for 5 minutes, fluff gently, and serve hot with curries, dal, or bhartas.

Place the seasoned rice in a greased steaming bowl or wrap in banana leaves, then steam over low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice is soft, fluffy, and aromatic. Let it rest for 5 minutes, fluff gently, and serve hot with curries, dal, or bhartas typical of Rajshahi cuisine.

To prepare Chattogram-style Chal Stuffed, wash 2 cups of atop or kalijira rice thoroughly and soak for 20–30 minutes, then drain. Prepare a stuffing by mixing 1 cup cooked spiced vegetables or minced meat with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, 2 slit green chilies, 2 tablespoons mustard oil, and salt to taste. Take small portions of the soaked rice, flatten slightly, and place the stuffing in the center, then shape and seal carefully. Wrap each stuffed rice portion in banana leaves or place in a greased steaming tray, then steam over low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice is tender, aromatic, and infused with the flavors of the stuffing. Serve hot with curries or dal.

To prepare a delicious Rangpur-style Khichuri Bhuna, which can be considered a "stuffed" rice dish due to its rich and flavorful contents, begin by washing 1 cup of fragrant rice and ½ cup of moong dal (yellow split lentils); drain well. In a large pot, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil and add a whole onion, finely chopped. Once the onion is golden, add 1 tablespoon of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of cumin powder, and a pinch of salt. Sauté the spices until fragrant. Now, add the washed rice and moong dal, and stir for 2-3 minutes to toast them lightly. Pour in 3 cups of hot water, add a few small chunks of potatoes and any optional vegetables like carrots or green beans, and stir everything together. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to a low simmer, cover the pot tightly, and let it cook for 20-25 minutes, or until all the water is absorbed and the rice and lentils are tender. The final dish will be a rich, thick, and spicy bhuna where the rice and vegetables are "stuffed" with flavor. Serve hot with pickle or achar.

To prepare a unique Sylhet-style rice dish that feels as though it is "stuffed" with savory flavors, you can create a delicious Akhni Pulao. Begin by washing 2 cups of fragrant rice, such as Chinigura or Basmati. In a large pot, heat 4 tablespoons of oil or ghee and add 2 large sliced onions, frying them until they turn golden. Now add 1 kg of beef or mutton cut into small pieces, and sauté with a paste of ginger, garlic, and a blend of spices including turmeric, cumin, coriander, and garam masala. Once the meat is half-cooked, add the washed rice, a few potato chunks, and stir everything together until the rice is lightly toasted. Pour in 4 cups of hot water, add salt to taste, and bring the mixture to a boil. Reduce the heat to a low simmer, cover the pot tightly, and let it cook for 20-25 minutes, or until all the water is absorbed and the rice is tender. The meat and spices are cooked with the rice, giving the dish a deeply flavorful, "stuffed" feel throughout. Garnish with fried onions before serving.

To prepare Barisal-style Chal Tok, wash 2 cups of atop or kalijira rice thoroughly and soak for 20–30 minutes, then drain. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, 2 slit green chilies, and ½ teaspoon turmeric, frying until aromatic. Add the drained rice and stir-fry gently for 5–6 minutes, then pour in 4 cups of hot water with a pinch of salt. Cover and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes until the rice is soft, tender, and slightly sticky with a lightly spiced flavor. Serve hot with fish, meat, or vegetable curries typical of Barisal cuisine.

To prepare Chattogram-style Chicken Bhuna, take 500 grams of chicken pieces, wash and pat them dry. Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 2 sliced onions, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, frying until golden brown and aromatic. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin-coriander powder, and salt to taste. Add the chicken and cook on medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 15–20 minutes until the chicken is browned and coated with the spices. Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer for another 10 minutes until the chicken is fully cooked and the bhuna develops a rich, thick, and aromatic texture. Serve hot with plain rice or paratha.
