To prepare traditional Barisal-style Chicken Dry, start with 700–800 grams of chicken cut into medium pieces. Wash and drain well.

In a bowl, marinate the chicken with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, and salt to taste. Let it rest for 20 minutes.

Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until hot. Add 2 medium onions thinly sliced and sauté until deep golden brown. Add the marinated chicken and cook on medium heat, stirring frequently, until the chicken releases moisture and the water dries up.

Lower the heat and continue cooking uncovered for 15–20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken becomes tender, well-coated with spices, and slightly crispy on the outside. Add 2–3 slit green chilies toward the end for aroma.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice or rice-based dishes for an authentic Barisal-style Chicken Dry experience.

To prepare traditional Chattogram-style Chicken Dry, start with 700–800 grams of chicken cut into medium pieces. Wash and drain well.

In a bowl, marinate the chicken with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons red chili powder (Chattogram style is spicier), 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, and salt to taste. Let it rest for 20 minutes.

Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until hot. Add 2 medium onions thinly sliced and sauté until deep golden brown. Add the marinated chicken and cook on medium heat, stirring frequently, until the chicken releases moisture and the water dries up.

Lower the heat and continue cooking uncovered for 20–25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is tender, well-coated with spices, and slightly crispy on the outside. Add 3–4 slit green chilies and a pinch of garam masala toward the end for strong aroma.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Chattogram-style Chicken Dry experience.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Chicken Fry, start with 700–800 grams of chicken cut into medium pieces. Wash and drain well.

In a bowl, marinate the chicken with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 tablespoon lemon juice (optional), and salt to taste. Let it rest for 30 minutes.

Heat enough mustard oil in a deep frying pan or kadai over medium heat. Once the oil is hot, carefully add the marinated chicken pieces and fry in batches. Fry until the chicken turns golden brown and crispy on the outside while remaining juicy inside.

Remove the fried chicken and drain on paper towels. Serve hot with plain rice, puffed rice (muri), or traditional Barisal-style sides.

To prepare traditional Dhaka-style Chicken Fry, start with 700–800 grams of chicken cut into medium pieces. Wash and drain well.

In a bowl, marinate the chicken with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 2 tablespoons plain yogurt, 1 tablespoon lemon juice, and salt to taste. Let it rest for 30–45 minutes.

Heat enough refined oil or mustard oil in a deep frying pan over medium heat. Carefully add the marinated chicken pieces and fry in batches, turning occasionally, until the chicken becomes golden brown and crispy on the outside while fully cooked inside.

Remove from oil and drain on paper towels. Serve hot with sliced onions, green chilies, and lemon wedges for an authentic Dhaka-style Chicken Fry experience.

Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan or kadai, then fry the chicken on medium heat, turning occasionally, for 12–15 minutes until the pieces are golden brown, crisp on the outside, and fully cooked inside. Garnish with sliced onions and green chilies, and serve hot with plain rice or paratha for a flavorful Hill Tracts-style meal.

To prepare Chattogram-style Chicken Grilled, take 500 grams of chicken pieces, wash and pat dry. Marinate them with 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, 1 teaspoon roasted cumin-coriander powder, 1 tablespoon yogurt, and salt to taste for at least 30 minutes. Preheat a grill or oven to medium-high heat, then place the chicken pieces on the grill and cook for 12–15 minutes per side, basting occasionally with the leftover marinade, until the chicken is fully cooked, slightly charred, and aromatic. Serve hot with plain rice, salad, or chutney as a flavorful Chattogram-style meal.

To prepare Barisal-style Chicken Jhol, take 500 grams of chicken pieces, wash and pat dry. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin-coriander powder, and salt to taste. Add the chicken and cook on medium heat for 10–12 minutes, then pour in 2–2.5 cups of water and simmer covered for 15–20 minutes until the chicken is tender and the curry has a thin, flavorful consistency. Garnish with fresh coriander leaves and serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Chicken Jhol, a light and aromatic Dhaka-style chicken curry, start with 500 grams of chicken (preferably on the bone for richer flavor), cleaned and cut into medium pieces. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3–4 tablespoons of mustard oil until lightly smoking, then add 2 medium onions finely sliced and fry until golden brown. Stir in 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 tablespoon garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons red chili powder, 2 teaspoons coriander powder, and salt to taste, frying the spices with a splash of water until oil separates. Add the chicken pieces, coat them well with the masala, and fry on medium-high heat for 8–10 minutes until slightly browned. Then pour in 2–3 cups of warm water, depending on desired thinness of the gravy, along with 2–3 slit green chilies. Cover and simmer on low heat until the chicken is tender and the jhol (broth) becomes light yet flavorful. Finish with a sprinkle of fresh coriander leaves and a drizzle of ghee if desired. Serve hot with plain bhaat for a classic homestyle meal.

To make traditional Hill Tracts-style Chicken Jhol, begin by washing and cutting 500 grams of chicken into medium pieces. In a large pot, heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil until it reaches smoking point, then reduce the heat. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until golden brown.

Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1½ teaspoons red chili powder, and 1 teaspoon ground coriander. Sauté for 2–3 minutes until aromatic.

Add the chicken pieces and stir well to coat with the spices. Cook for 8–10 minutes until the chicken changes color and releases some juices. Add 2–3 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon salt (adjust according to taste), and 2 cups of hot water. To make traditional Barisal-style Chingri Jhol, begin by cleaning and deveining 500 grams of medium-sized prawns (chingri). Lightly rinse and pat them dry. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil until it reaches smoking point, then reduce the heat. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until light golden brown.

Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and ½ teaspoon ground coriander. Sauté gently for 1–2 minutes until aromatic.

Add the prawns and stir gently to coat with the spices. Cook for 5–6 minutes until the prawns turn pink and slightly firm. Add 2–3 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon salt (adjust according to taste), and 1½ cups of hot water. Cover and simmer on low heat for 8–10 minutes until the prawns are cooked through and the broth is flavorful.

Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and a few fresh coriander leaves for aroma.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice, as traditionally enjoyed in Barisal households.

To make traditional Dhaka-style Chingri Jhol, begin by cleaning and deveining 500 grams of medium-sized prawns (chingri). Lightly rinse and pat them dry. Add the prawns and stir gently to coat with the spices. Cook for 5–6 minutes until the prawns turn pink and slightly firm. Add the prawns and sauté for 3–4 minutes until they turn pink, then pour in 2 cups of warm water and bring to a gentle boil. Add 2–3 more slit green chilies for heat, cover, and simmer on low until the prawns are tender and the jhol develops a light, aromatic broth. Garnish with fresh coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed plain bhaat.

To prepare Dhaka-style Chingri Khichuri, wash 1 cup of rice and ½ cup of moong dal (yellow lentils) thoroughly and soak for 20–30 minutes. Drain the soaked rice and lentils, add them to the pot along with 4 cups of hot water, cover, and cook on low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice and lentils are soft and infused with the prawn flavors. Serve hot with a drizzle of ghee for a traditional Dhaka-style meal.

To make traditional Mymensingh-style Chingri Khichuri, begin by washing 1 cup of coarse rice (chal) and ½ cup split moong dal separately, then soak both together for 10 minutes and drain well. Clean and devein 300–400 grams of medium prawns (chingri) and pat dry.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil until it reaches smoking point, then reduce the heat. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and ½ teaspoon ground cumin, sautéing gently for 2–3 minutes until aromatic.

Add the prawns and stir lightly, cooking for 4–5 minutes until they turn pink. Remove prawns temporarily and set aside. Add the soaked rice and dal to the pot, stir to coat with the spices, and pour in 4 cups of hot water. Add salt to taste (about 1–1½ teaspoons) and bring to a gentle boil.

Cover and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes until the rice and dal are soft. Return the cooked prawns to the pot and mix gently, letting them warm through for 3–4 minutes. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and a few slit green chilies for flavor.

Serve hot as a complete meal, as traditionally enjoyed in Mymensingh households.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Chingri Polao, start by washing and soaking 2 cups of basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and set aside.

To prepare Chingri Stuffed (Dhaka style), begin by taking 300–400 grams of medium-sized prawns (chingri), clean them thoroughly, and remove the veins while keeping the shells intact. Gently slit each prawn along the back without cutting through completely and stuff the spice mixture evenly inside. Heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, lightly fry the stuffed prawns on medium heat until they turn golden and the spices are aromatic, then cover and cook for 5–7 minutes until fully cooked. To prepare Dal Bhuna (Chattogram style), begin by washing ½ cup moong dal or red lentils and draining them well. Boil the lentils in 2–3 cups of water with a pinch of turmeric and salt until soft. In a separate pan, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil, add 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves, and sauté until golden and aromatic. Add the cooked dal and stir-fry on medium heat for 5–7 minutes, reducing the moisture to create a thick, slightly dry, and richly spiced consistency characteristic of Chattogram cuisine. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil or ghee for flavor and serve hot with plain rice or polao.

To prepare Dal Grilled (Hill Tracts style), begin by cooking ½ cup moong dal or red lentils in 2–3 cups of water with a pinch of turmeric and salt until soft but still holding their shape. Shape the mixture into small patties or logs, lightly brush with oil, and grill on a preheated grill or non-stick pan over medium heat for 3–5 minutes on each side until golden and slightly crisp. Serve hot as a side with plain rice or as a light snack.

Shape the mixture into small patties or logs, then lightly brush with mustard oil. Preheat a grill or non-stick pan and cook the dal patties on medium heat for 3–5 minutes on each side until golden and slightly crisp on the outside. Serve hot as a side with plain rice or as a snack.

To prepare Dal Jhol in Chattogram style, wash 1 cup of red lentils (masoor dal) and boil with 4 cups of water, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and salt until the dal softens but remains light and soupy. In a separate pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil, add 1 dried red chili, ½ teaspoon of mustard seeds, ½ teaspoon of nigella seeds, and a sprig of curry leaves, then let them splutter before adding 1 finely chopped onion, 2–3 green chilies, and 1 chopped tomato, frying until soft and aromatic. Mix this tempering into the boiled dal, add a little more hot water if needed for a thin consistency, and simmer for 5–7 minutes to bring out the flavors. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and fresh coriander leaves, then serve hot with plain rice and fried fish or vegetables.

To prepare Dal Jhol (Rajshahi style), begin by washing ½ cup red lentils (masoor dal) or yellow moong dal and draining them well. In a medium pot, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil, add a pinch of turmeric, 1–2 sliced green chilies, and salt to taste, sautéing briefly to release the aroma. Pour in 3 cups of water and bring to a gentle boil, then add the lentils. Simmer on low heat, skimming foam occasionally, until the lentils are fully cooked and soft but still slightly soupy, keeping the consistency light and rustic as preferred in Rajshahi cuisine. Finish with a small drizzle of mustard oil for flavor and serve hot with plain rice or seasonal bhorta.

To prepare Dal Jhol (Sylhet style), begin by washing ½ cup red lentils (masoor dal) or yellow moong dal and draining them well. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil or ghee for aroma and serve hot with plain rice or steamed vegetables.

To prepare Dal Khichuri (Barisal style), begin by washing 1 cup rice and ½ cup lentils (often moong dal) and draining them well. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a deep pot, add sliced onions and sauté until lightly golden, then add garlic paste, green chilies, turmeric, and a small pinch of cumin, keeping the seasoning simple and slightly robust as preferred in Barisal. Stir in the rice and lentils, mix thoroughly, then pour in about 4½ cups of water and add salt to taste. Bring to a gentle boil, reduce the heat, and cook covered until the rice and dal soften into a creamy, comforting khichuri. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil, allow it to rest briefly, and serve hot with fried hilsa, shutki, or seasonal bhorta.

To prepare Dal Khichuri (Chattogram style), begin by washing 1 cup rice and ½ cup lentils (preferably moong dal) and draining them well. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pot, add sliced onions and sauté until lightly golden, then stir in ginger-garlic paste, green chilies, turmeric, coriander, and a small pinch of cumin, keeping the spices balanced and aromatic rather than heavy. Add the rice and lentils, mix well to coat them in the spices, then pour in about 4½ cups of hot water and season with salt. Bring to a gentle boil, reduce the heat, and cook covered until the rice and dal break down into a soft, slightly loose khichuri typical of Chattogram cuisine. Finish with a drizzle of ghee or mustard oil, rest briefly, and serve hot with bhorta or fried vegetables.

To prepare Dal Khichuri (Dhaka style), begin by washing 1 cup rice and ½ cup moong dal, then soak them separately for 15–20 minutes. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil and sauté 1 sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. Add the soaked dal and rice, 2½–3 cups water, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and salt to taste. Cover and cook on low heat until the rice and dal are soft and fluffy. For a more flavorful Dhaka-style khichuri, lightly fry 300 g cleaned prawns or small fish and add them on top during the final steaming. Serve hot with fried or sautéed vegetables or mustard oil drizzled over the top.

To prepare Dal Khichuri (Hill Tracts style), begin by washing 1 cup rice and ½ cup moong dal, then soak them separately for 15–20 minutes. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or local vegetable oil, and sauté 1 sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. Add the soaked rice and dal, 2½–3 cups water, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and salt to taste. Cover and cook on low heat until the rice and dal are soft and fluffy. Optionally, lightly fry 300 g local freshwater fish or small prawns and place them on top during the final steaming to infuse flavor. Serve hot with a drizzle of mustard oil.

To prepare Dal Khichuri (Mymensingh style), begin by washing 1 cup rice and ½ cup moong dal separately and soaking them for 15–20 minutes. Add the soaked rice and dal, 2½–3 cups water, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and salt to taste. Cover and cook on low heat until the rice and dal are soft and fluffy. For added flavor, lightly fry 300 g cleaned fish or prawns and layer them on top of the khichuri during the final steaming. Serve hot with a drizzle of mustard oil.

Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Dal Korma in Sylheti style, wash 2 cups of moong dal thoroughly and dry roast it in a pan until fragrant and golden, then boil with 5 cups of water and a little salt until soft but not mushy. In another pan, heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee, fry 2 finely sliced onions until golden, then add 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric, 2 teaspoons of roasted cumin powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and stir until the spices release oil. Add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook to a thick masala, then mix in the boiled dal and simmer on low heat for 10–12 minutes, adjusting consistency with water if needed. To enrich the korma, add ½ cup of beaten yogurt or coconut milk along with 1 teaspoon of garam masala and a handful of fried onions, stirring gently so the dal remains creamy. Garnish with fresh coriander leaves and green chilies, then serve hot with plain rice, polao, or paratha.

To prepare Tribal-style Dal Korma, take 1 cup of moong dal (yellow lentils), wash thoroughly, and soak for 20–30 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon mild red chili powder, ½ teaspoon cumin-coriander powder, and salt to taste. Add the soaked dal along with 3 cups of water, cover, and simmer on low heat for 20–25 minutes until the dal is soft. Reduce heat, add ½ cup coconut milk or cream (optional) to enrich the korma, and cook for another 5–7 minutes until the gravy becomes thick, creamy, and aromatic. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Tribal-style meal.

To prepare Barisal-style Dal Paturi, wash 1 cup of soaked moong dal (yellow lentils) and 1 cup of rice thoroughly and soak for 20–30 minutes. Grind 2 tablespoons mustard seeds with 1–2 green chilies into a smooth paste and mix with 2 tablespoons mustard oil, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and salt to taste. Spread the mustard-spiced dal evenly on cleaned banana leaves, roll or fold securely, and steam or grill over low heat for 20–25 minutes until the dal is fully cooked, tender, and infused with the aromatic mustard flavor. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Barisal-style meal.

Grind 2 tablespoons mustard seeds with 1–2 green chilies into a smooth paste and mix with 2 tablespoons mustard oil, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and salt to taste. Spread the mustard-spiced dal evenly on cleaned banana leaves, roll or fold securely, and steam or grill over low heat for 20–25 minutes until the dal is fully cooked, tender, and infused with the aromatic mustard flavor. To prepare Hill Tracts–style Dal Paturi, wash 1 cup of soaked moong dal (yellow lentils) and 1 cup of rice thoroughly and soak for 20–30 minutes. To prepare Chattogram-style Dal Polao, wash 2 cups of basmati or atop rice thoroughly and soak for 20–30 minutes, then drain. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil or ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add 1 cup cooked moong dal (yellow lentils) and mix gently with the spices. Add the soaked rice and 4 cups of hot water, cover, and cook on low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice is tender and infused with the mildly spiced dal. Serve hot garnished with fried onions for a traditional Chattogram-style Dal Polao.

To prepare Dal Polao (Dhaka style), begin by washing 1 cup Basmati or fragrant rice and soaking it for 15–20 minutes. Separately, boil ½ cup moong dal or red lentils in 2 cups water with a pinch of turmeric and salt until tender. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. Add the soaked rice and cooked dal to the pot, along with 2½–3 cups water and salt to taste. Cover and cook on low heat until the rice is fluffy and fully cooked. Optionally, garnish with fried onions or a drizzle of mustard oil. Serve hot as a wholesome main dish.

To prepare Dal Polao (Mymensingh style), begin by washing 1 cup Basmati or fragrant rice and soaking it for 15–20 minutes. Separately, boil ½ cup moong dal or red lentils in 2 cups water with a pinch of turmeric and salt until tender. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. Add the soaked rice and cooked dal to the pot, along with 2½–3 cups water and salt to taste. Cover and cook on low heat until the rice is fluffy and fully cooked. Optionally, garnish with fried onions or a drizzle of mustard oil for added flavor. Serve hot as a wholesome main dish.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. To prepare Dal Polao (Sylhet style), begin by washing 1 cup fragrant rice and soaking it for 15–20 minutes. Separately, boil ½ cup moong dal until soft with a pinch of turmeric and salt. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. Add the soaked rice and cooked dal, pour in 2½–3 cups water, season with salt, cover, and cook on low heat until the rice is fluffy and fully cooked, allowing the subtle Sylheti aroma to develop. Serve hot as a comforting main dish with light curries or vegetables.

To prepare Dal Steamed (Khulna style), begin by washing ½ cup moong dal or red lentils and soaking them for 15–20 minutes. Drain and place the dal in a heatproof bowl, then season with a pinch of salt, ½ teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon mustard paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 chopped green chilies. Drizzle 1 teaspoon mustard oil over the mixture and mix gently. Place the bowl in a steamer or over a pot of boiling water, cover, and steam on medium heat for 20–25 minutes until the dal is soft, set, and lightly aromatic. Serve hot as a simple, protein-rich side dish with plain rice.

To prepare Dal Steamed (Sylhet style), begin by washing ½ cup moong dal or red lentils and soaking them for 15–20 minutes. Drain and place the dal in a heatproof bowl, then season with a pinch of salt, ½ teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon mustard paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 chopped green chilies. Add 1–2 tablespoons yogurt or a little coconut milk for a soft, Sylheti richness, and drizzle 1 teaspoon mustard oil over the mixture. Mix gently, then steam the bowl over boiling water for 20–25 minutes until the dal is soft, set, and lightly aromatic. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Dal Stuffed (Chattogram style), begin by cooking ½ cup moong dal or red lentils with a pinch of turmeric and salt until soft but not mushy, then mash lightly. In a bowl, mix the cooked dal with 1 small finely chopped onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon mustard paste, and salt to taste. Take vegetables commonly used for stuffing (such as lau or pointed gourd), slit them lengthwise, and fill generously with the dal mixture. Heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil in a pan, place the stuffed vegetables gently, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes, turning occasionally, until the vegetables are tender and the stuffing is well infused with the mild coastal flavors typical of Chattogram cuisine. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Dal Stuffed (Rajshahi style), begin by cooking ½ cup moong dal or red lentils with a pinch of turmeric and salt until soft, then mash lightly. In a bowl, mix the cooked dal with 1 small finely chopped onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and salt to taste, keeping the flavors simple as preferred in Rajshahi cuisine. Take vegetables suitable for stuffing (such as lau or pointed gourd), slit them lengthwise, and fill generously with the dal mixture. Heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil in a pan, arrange the stuffed vegetables, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes, turning occasionally, until the vegetables are tender and the stuffing is fully cooked. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Dal Stuffed (Rangpur style), soak and boil 1 cup chana dal until soft but intact, then mash lightly. Mix the dal with finely chopped onion, green chili, garlic paste, cumin powder, coriander powder, turmeric, salt, and a little mustard oil. Traditionally in Rangpur, the stuffing is shaped into small patties or used to stuff vegetables (like potol or lau), then lightly shallow-fried. After frying, the stuffed pieces are simmered briefly in a thin gravy made with onion, ginger, garlic, turmeric, and a touch of red chili, keeping the spices mild and earthy, characteristic of northern Bengal cuisine. Serve with steamed rice.

To prepare Dal Stuffed in the Tribal style, soak 1 cup of red lentils (masoor) or chickpeas for 20–25 minutes. Cook the lentils until soft and blend into a smooth paste. In a bowl, mix the lentil paste with 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste to form a thick stuffing. Cut small slits in boiled or lightly steamed potatoes and fill them with this lentil mixture. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil in a pan and lightly fry the stuffed potatoes until golden. Garnish with chopped fresh coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Dal Tok in the Barisal style, soak 1 cup of red lentils (masoor) or chickpeas for 20–25 minutes. Cook the lentils until soft and leave slightly chunky or mash into a paste. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1/2 teaspoon mustard seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds, and let them splutter. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until translucent. Stir in 1/2 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Pour in 1/2 cup tamarind pulp and 1/2 cup water, and simmer gently until the curry develops a lightly tangy-spicy flavor. Add the cooked lentils and simmer for 5–6 minutes so the flavors blend well. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dal Tok in the Dhaka style, soak 1 cup of red lentils (masoor) or chickpeas for 20–25 minutes. Cook the lentils until soft, leaving them slightly chunky or mash into a paste. Stir in 1/2 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. To prepare Khulna-style Dal Tok, wash 1 cup of red lentils (masoor dal) and boil with 4 cups of water, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and salt until soft and light. In a small pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil, add ½ teaspoon mustard seeds, ½ teaspoon nigella seeds, 2 dried red chilies, and a few curry leaves, letting them splutter, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook until soft and tangy. Pour this tempering into the boiled dal, mix well, and simmer for 5–6 minutes to combine the sourness with the lentils. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dal Tok (Rajshahi style), begin by washing ½ cup moong dal or red lentils and draining them well. Boil the dal in 2–3 cups of water with a pinch of turmeric and salt until soft. In a separate pan, heat 2 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil, add 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves, sautéing until aromatic. Pour the cooked dal into the pan, stir well, and cook on medium heat until slightly thickened, then simmer uncovered for a few minutes so the dal acquires a thin, tangy, and lightly spiced consistency typical of Rajshahi’s “tok” style. Serve hot with plain rice.

Cook uncovered for a few minutes to thicken slightly, giving the dish a light, tangy, and spiced consistency typical of Tribal-style dal tok. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Barisal-style Dim Bhuna, boil 4 eggs, peel them, and rub lightly with a pinch of salt and turmeric. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, fry the eggs until golden, then remove and set aside. In the same oil, fry 2 sliced onions until brown, add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 2 teaspoons chili powder, 1 teaspoon roasted cumin-coriander powder, and salt to taste, stirring until the spices release oil. Add 2 chopped tomatoes and 2–3 slit green chilies, cooking until soft and thick, then return the fried eggs, coat them well with the masala, and cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes until the gravy clings to the eggs. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and serve hot with plain rice or parathas.

To prepare Chattogram-style Dim Bhuna, take 4–5 medium-sized eggs, boil them until hard, peel, and set aside. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon cumin–coriander powder, and salt to taste. Slice the boiled eggs in halves or quarters and gently add them to the pan, frying on medium heat until the eggs are lightly golden and fully coated with the spices in a thick, bhuna-style layer. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Chattogram-style meal.

To prepare Dim Bhuna in the Rangpur style, boil 3 eggs, peel them, and cut them in halves. Heat 2 tablespoons oil in a pan and lightly fry the eggs until slightly golden, then set aside. In the same pan, add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until light brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Add a splash of water to form a smooth masala. Return the fried eggs to the pan and gently cook for 3–4 minutes on low heat so the eggs absorb all the flavors. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dim Dry in the Barisal style, boil 3 eggs, peel them, and cut them in halves. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan and lightly fry the eggs until slightly golden, then set aside. Once the gravy has completely dried, garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dim Fry in the Hill Tracts style, boil 3 eggs and peel them. Heat 3 tablespoons oil in a pan. Add the eggs, whole or halved, and fry on medium heat for 5–6 minutes until lightly golden on the outside. Then add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds to splutter. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until lightly brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, and sauté for 2–3 minutes. Mix the spices well with the eggs. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dim Grilled (Barisal style), begin by boiling 4–6 eggs until hard-boiled, then peel and set them aside. Make a marinade by mixing 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon mustard oil, a pinch of salt, and ½ teaspoon ginger-garlic paste. Coat the boiled eggs evenly with the marinade. Preheat a grill or heavy pan, lightly grease with mustard oil, and grill the eggs on medium heat, turning occasionally, until they develop a golden, slightly charred exterior. Serve hot as a snack or side dish with plain rice or bread.

To prepare Dim Grilled in the Chattogram style, boil 3 eggs and peel them. Heat 2 tablespoons oil in a pan. Add the eggs, whole or halved, and grill on medium heat for 5–6 minutes until the outside is lightly golden and slightly crispy. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds to splutter. Stir in 1 teaspoon garlic paste and 1 teaspoon ginger paste lightly. Sprinkle a little salt, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and chopped coriander leaves on top of the eggs and grill for 2–3 minutes. Serve hot with steamed rice or bread.

To prepare Dim Grilled in the Dhaka style, boil 3 eggs and peel them. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil (or any neutral cooking oil) in a pan. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds to splutter. Stir in 1 teaspoon garlic paste and 1 teaspoon ginger paste lightly. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds to splutter. Stir in 1 teaspoon garlic paste and 1 teaspoon ginger paste lightly. Sprinkle a little salt, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and chopped coriander leaves on top of the eggs and grill for 2–3 minutes. Serve hot with steamed rice or bread.

To prepare Dim Grilled in the Tribal style, boil 3 eggs and peel them. Heat 2 tablespoons local oil or mustard oil in a pan. Add the eggs, whole or halved, and grill on medium heat for 5–6 minutes until lightly golden and slightly crispy on the outside. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds to splutter. Stir in 1 teaspoon garlic paste and 1 teaspoon ginger paste lightly. Sprinkle a little salt, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and chopped coriander leaves on top of the eggs and grill for 2–3 minutes. Serve hot with steamed rice or bread.

To prepare Dim Jhol in the Hill Tracts style, boil 3 eggs and peel them. Heat 2 tablespoons local oil or mustard oil in a pan. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds to splutter. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until translucent. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Add 1/2 cup water and 1/2 cup coconut milk, and simmer gently for 3–4 minutes. Add the boiled eggs and cook for another 5 minutes to let the eggs absorb the flavors. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dim Jhol in the Khulna style, boil 3 eggs and peel them. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds to splutter. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until translucent. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Add 1/2 cup water and 1/2 cup coconut milk, and simmer gently for 3–4 minutes. Add the boiled eggs and cook for another 5 minutes to let the eggs absorb the flavors. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dim Jhol in the Mymensingh style, boil 3 eggs and peel them. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds to splutter. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until translucent. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Add 1/2 cup water and 1/2 cup coconut milk, and simmer gently for 3–4 minutes. Add the boiled eggs and cook for another 5 minutes to let the eggs absorb the flavors. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dim Jhol in the Rajshahi style, boil 3 eggs and peel them. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds to splutter. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until translucent. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Add 1/2 cup water and 1/2 cup coconut milk, and simmer gently for 3–4 minutes. Add the boiled eggs and cook for another 5 minutes to let the eggs absorb the flavors. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare a traditional Rangpur-style Dim Jhol, a light and simple egg curry, start by boiling 4-5 eggs until they are hard-boiled. Peel the eggs and make small slits on the surface. In a pan, heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil and add the eggs, frying them gently until they are a light golden color; set them aside. In the same pan, add a little more oil if needed and temper with a few whole green chilies and ½ teaspoon of panch foron (Bengali five-spice mix). As the spices splutter, add 1 finely chopped medium onion and sauté until soft. Now, add 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste, stirring well. Add 1.5 cups of water and bring the gravy to a boil. Gently place the fried eggs back into the jhol, cover the pan, and let it simmer for 5-7 minutes, allowing the flavors to meld. The final dish will have a thin, light gravy that is perfect for a weeknight meal and is a great accompaniment to rice.

To prepare traditional Sylhet-style Dim Jhol, start with 4–6 eggs. Boil them for 8–10 minutes until hard-boiled, then peel and set aside.

Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan. Add 1 medium onion finely chopped and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add 2 medium tomatoes chopped and cook until soft. Pour in 1.5–2 cups of water and bring to a gentle simmer. Add the boiled eggs and let them cook in the gravy for 5–7 minutes to absorb the flavors. Optionally, add 1–2 slit green chilies for extra aroma.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Sylhet-style Dim Jhol experience.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Dim Khichuri, start by washing 1.5 cups of rice and 0.5 cup of moong dal (yellow lentils) thoroughly and soak for 20 minutes, then drain.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until hot. Add 1 medium onion finely chopped and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add 4–5 boiled and peeled eggs, cut into halves or quarters. Stir gently to coat the eggs with the spices. Add the drained rice and dal mixture, and pour in 3 cups of hot water. Cover and cook over medium heat until the water is mostly absorbed. Reduce the heat to low, cover tightly, and simmer for another 10–15 minutes until the rice and dal are fully cooked and fluffy.

Optionally, garnish with fried onions or chopped coriander leaves before serving.

Serve hot for an authentic Barisal-style Dim Khichuri experience.

To prepare traditional Dhaka-style Dim Khichuri, start by washing 1.5 cups of rice and 0.5 cup of moong dal (yellow lentils) thoroughly and soak for 20 minutes, then drain.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until hot. Add 1 medium onion finely chopped and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add 4–5 boiled and peeled eggs, cut into halves or quarters. Stir gently to coat the eggs with the spices. Add the drained rice and dal mixture, and pour in 3 cups of hot water. Cover and cook over medium heat until the water is mostly absorbed. Reduce the heat to low, cover tightly, and simmer for another 10–15 minutes until the rice and dal are fully cooked and fluffy.

Optionally, garnish with fried onions or chopped coriander leaves before serving.

Serve hot for an authentic Dhaka-style Dim Khichuri experience.

To prepare Dim Khichuri (Mymensingh), also known as Egg Khichuri, begin by washing and soaking 2 cups of rice (e.g., Basmati or regular white rice) and 1 cup of Masoor Dal (red lentils) together for about 15−20 minutes, then drain; separately, hard-boil 4-5 eggs and peel them, or fry the eggs lightly after coating them with a little salt and turmeric; in a large pot or pressure cooker, heat 1/3 cup of oil or a mix of oil and ghee, temper with 2 bay leaves, cinnamon sticks, cardamom, and cloves, then add 1 cup of sliced onion and sauté until light brown; stir in 2 teaspoons each of ginger and garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon each of red chili powder and cumin powder, and salt to taste, cooking the spices until the raw smell is gone; add the drained rice and dal mixture and fry gently for 3−4 minutes until aromatic; pour in about 6 cups of hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low heat until the rice and dal are tender (about 15−20 minutes, or for 2-3 whistles in a pressure cooker); once cooked, mix in the boiled or fried eggs and 5-6 whole green chilies, cover again, and let it rest on very low heat or simply off the heat for 5−10 minutes to let the flavors settle, then garnish with fresh coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Dim Khichuri, wash and soak 1½ cups of small-grain rice (such as miniket) and ½ cup moong dal separately for about 20 minutes, then drain. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pot, add 1 bay leaf, 2 dried red chilies, and a pinch of cumin seeds, then sauté 1 medium sliced onion until lightly golden. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, ½ teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, salt to taste, and a pinch of red chili powder, cooking briefly until fragrant. Add the soaked rice and dal, stir well, then pour in about 5 cups hot water. Let it simmer on medium heat until the grains soften and thicken into a creamy consistency. Meanwhile, boil 4 eggs, peel them, lightly fry in a little oil with a pinch of turmeric and salt, then add them to the khichuri. Finish with 1 tablespoon ghee and a sprinkle of fried onions, cover, and cook on low heat for 5 more minutes. Serve hot with green chili and lemon for a comforting Rajshahi-style Dim Khichuri.

To prepare Sylhet-style Dim Khichuri, begin by washing and soaking ½ cup aromatic rice and ¼ cup moong dal together for about 15 minutes, then drain well. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pot and add 1 small sliced onion, sautéing until lightly golden, followed by 1 teaspoon ginger paste, a pinch of garlic paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and green chilies to taste. Add the soaked rice and dal, stirring gently to coat them with the spices, then pour in about 2½ cups hot water and salt as needed. Bring to a gentle boil, reduce the heat, cover, and let it simmer until the rice and dal soften into a thick, comforting consistency. Meanwhile, lightly fry or boil 2 eggs; crack them gently into the khichuri during the final few minutes so they absorb the broth without breaking apart. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil for Sylheti aroma, rest for a few minutes, and serve hot with lemon wedges or simple bhorta.

To prepare Tribal-style Dim Khichuri, begin by washing ½ cup local rice and ¼ cup lentils (often mixed or forest-grown varieties) and draining them well. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil or local vegetable oil in a deep pot, add crushed garlic, sliced onions, and fresh green chilies, and sauté lightly until aromatic without heavy browning. Stir in a pinch of turmeric and salt, then add the rice and lentils, mixing gently before pouring in about 2½ cups of water. Let it come to a soft boil, then simmer covered on low heat until the grains and lentils break down into a rustic, slightly coarse khichuri. Add 2 lightly boiled eggs, gently cracked so they absorb the broth, and cook for a few more minutes. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil or a touch of forest herbs if available, rest briefly, and serve hot as a simple, nourishing meal.

To prepare Dim Korma (Chattogram style), begin by boiling 4 eggs until just set, then peel and lightly score them so they absorb flavor. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil or refined oil in a pan, add sliced onions and sauté until golden, followed by ginger-garlic paste, green chilies, and a light blend of spices such as turmeric, coriander, and a small pinch of garam masala, keeping the heat gentle to avoid over-roasting. Stir in beaten yogurt or coconut milk gradually to form a smooth, mildly creamy gravy typical of Chattogram cuisine, then add salt to taste. Gently place the eggs into the sauce, cover, and simmer on low heat for 8–10 minutes so the eggs soak up the rich, aromatic korma flavors. Finish with a drizzle of ghee or oil and rest briefly before serving hot with plain bhaat or polao.

To prepare Dim Korma (Khulna style), begin by boiling 4 eggs until firm, peeling them, and lightly frying them in mustard oil until the surfaces turn lightly golden. In the same pan, add more mustard oil if needed, then sauté finely sliced onions until deep golden, followed by ginger-garlic paste, green chilies, turmeric, coriander, and a small pinch of cumin powder, creating a fragrant spice base typical of Khulna cooking. Stir in beaten yogurt mixed with a little water to form a smooth, mildly tangy gravy, then add salt to taste and simmer gently until the oil begins to separate. Add the fried eggs, cover, and cook on low heat for 8–10 minutes so the eggs absorb the rich korma flavors. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and let it rest briefly before serving hot with plain bhaat.

To prepare Dim Korma (Mymensingh style), begin by boiling 4 eggs until firm, peeling them, and lightly scoring the surface. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil or ghee in a pan, add thinly sliced onions and sauté until soft and lightly golden, then stir in ginger paste, a small amount of garlic, green chilies, turmeric, coriander, and a touch of cumin, keeping the spice level mild in keeping with Mymensingh tradition. Add beaten yogurt or lightly diluted milk gradually to form a smooth, gently creamy gravy, season with salt, and simmer on low heat until aromatic and slightly thickened. Gently add the eggs, cover, and cook for about 8–10 minutes so they absorb the subtle korma flavors, then finish with a drizzle of ghee and allow it to rest briefly before serving hot with plain bhaat or soft polao.

To prepare Dim Korma (Rangpur style), begin by hard-boiling 4 eggs, peeling them, and lightly scoring the sides. Heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil in a pan, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. Add 2–3 tablespoons yogurt or onion paste, followed by ½ teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, stirring to form a smooth, mildly spiced gravy. Gently add the boiled eggs, cover, and simmer on low heat for 8–10 minutes until the eggs absorb the flavors and the korma thickens. Serve hot with plain rice or paratha.

To prepare Dim Korma (Sylhet style), begin by hard-boiling 4 eggs, peeling them, and lightly scoring the sides. Heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. Add 2–3 tablespoons yogurt or a little coconut milk, along with ½ teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, stirring to form a smooth, mildly rich gravy typical of Sylheti cooking. Gently add the boiled eggs, cover, and simmer on low heat for 8–10 minutes until the eggs absorb the flavors and the korma thickens. Serve hot with plain rice or paratha.

To prepare Dim Korma (Tribal style), begin by hard-boiling 4 eggs, peeling them, and lightly scoring the sides. Heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil in a pan, sauté 1 small chopped onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until fragrant. Add 2–3 tablespoons onion paste or lightly beaten yogurt, then season with ½ teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, stirring gently to create a simple, rustic gravy. Add the boiled eggs, cover, and simmer on low heat for 8–10 minutes until the eggs absorb the flavors and the korma thickens slightly, reflecting the earthy simplicity of Tribal-style cooking. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Dim Paturi (Dhaka style), begin by hard-boiling 4 eggs, peeling them, and lightly slicing each egg lengthwise. In a bowl, mix 2 tablespoons mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1–2 crushed garlic cloves, salt to taste, and 1 teaspoon mustard oil to form a thick marinade. Coat the eggs gently with this mixture. Place the marinated eggs on lightly greased banana leaves, wrap them securely, and tie if needed. Cook the parcels on a pan or grill over low to medium heat for 10–12 minutes, turning carefully, until the eggs absorb the mustardy flavor and release a light aroma. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Dim Paturi (Khulna), a Bengali egg delicacy where eggs are steamed in banana leaves, begin by preparing the spice paste: soak and then blend 1.5 tablespoons of mixed yellow and black mustard seeds, 1/2 cup of shredded coconut, 4−6 green chillies, a pinch of salt, and 1/4 teaspoon of turmeric powder with a splash of water and a few drops of mustard oil until smooth. Take 4−6 boiled eggs, gently score them, and coat them thoroughly with the mustard-coconut paste and 2−3 tablespoons of mustard oil, allowing them to marinate for at least 30 minutes. Lightly heat large squares of banana leaves to make them pliable, place one marinated egg with a spoonful of extra paste and an optional whole chilli onto a leaf, fold it into a tight parcel, and secure it with a string. Place the secured parcels in a steamer or a covered pan over low heat with a tablespoon of hot oil; steam for 15−20 minutes or pan-fry for 7−10 minutes on each side until the leaves are charred and the paste is cooked. Once done, remove from heat, let it rest for 5 minutes, then unwrap and serve hot, often as an accompaniment to rice.

To prepare traditional Mymensingh-style Dim Paturi, start with 4–6 fresh eggs. Boil them for 8–10 minutes until hard-boiled, then peel and set aside.

In a small bowl, prepare a paste with 1 teaspoon mustard oil, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, 1–2 finely chopped green chilies, and a pinch of salt. Optionally, add a little grated coconut or chopped coriander leaves for extra flavor.

Spread the paste evenly on a banana leaf (or foil if unavailable). Place the boiled eggs on the leaf and wrap securely to seal the flavors. Steam or grill over medium heat for 10–12 minutes until the flavors are absorbed.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Mymensingh-style Dim Paturi experience.

To prepare traditional Rangpur-style Dim Paturi, start with 4–6 boiled eggs. Boil them for 8–10 minutes until hard-boiled, then peel and set aside.

In a small bowl, prepare a paste with 1–2 tablespoons mustard oil, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder (slightly spicier for Rangpur style), 1–2 finely chopped green chilies, and a pinch of salt. Optionally, add a few chopped coriander leaves or grated coconut for extra flavor. Coat the boiled eggs evenly with this paste.

Place the marinated eggs on banana leaves or aluminum foil, fold securely, and steam or grill over medium heat for 10–12 minutes until the eggs absorb the flavors and develop a slight aroma from the leaf.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Rangpur-style Dim Paturi experience.

To prepare Barisal-style Dim Polao, rinse 2 cups of basmati or long-grain rice and soak for 20 minutes. Boil 3 eggs, peel, and set aside. In a large pan, heat 3 tablespoons of oil, add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds to temper. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until light brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger-garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the soaked rice and 3 cups of water, cover, and cook on medium heat for 10–12 minutes. Finally, add the boiled eggs to the polao, cover, and cook another 5 minutes to allow the flavors to blend. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Dim Polao in the Rangpur style, boil 3 eggs and peel them. Wash 1 cup Basmati rice and soak it in water for 30 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons oil in a pan. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds, 1/2 teaspoon cinnamon, 2–3 cloves, and 1 bay leaf and let them splutter. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until lightly brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste and sauté for 1–2 minutes. Add 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon garam masala, then add 1 cup water. When water starts boiling, add the soaked rice, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes until the rice is tender. Place the boiled eggs on top and cover for another 2–3 minutes to allow the flavors to infuse.

To prepare Barisal-style Dim Steamed, beat 4 eggs in a bowl with ½ teaspoon salt, ½ teaspoon turmeric, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and 2 finely chopped green chilies, then mix in ½ cup of chopped onions and a handful of coriander leaves. Add ½ cup of water or milk to make the mixture light, pour it into a greased steel bowl, and drizzle 1 tablespoon of mustard oil on top for aroma. Place the bowl in a steamer or over boiling water in a covered pot, letting it steam gently on low heat for 20–25 minutes until the eggs set into a soft, fluffy pudding-like texture. Once cooked, cut into slices and serve hot with plain rice and dal.

To prepare Chattogram-style Dim Steamed, boil 3 eggs and peel them. In a bowl, mix 1/2 cup milk, 1/2 teaspoon salt, a pinch of black pepper, and 1/2 teaspoon sugar to form a smooth mixture. Pour this mixture into a steaming dish and place the boiled eggs on top. Cover and steam over boiling water for 12–15 minutes until the surrounding milk sets into a soft custard-like texture. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice or flatbread.

To prepare Hill Tracts-style Dim Steamed, boil 3 eggs and peel them. In a bowl, mix 1/2 cup milk, 1/2 teaspoon jaggery, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and a pinch of black pepper to form a smooth mixture. Pour this mixture into a steaming dish and place the boiled eggs on top. Cover and steam over boiling water for 12–15 minutes on low heat until the milk mixture gently sets into a soft custard-like texture. Garnish with finely chopped local herbs or coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice or flatbread.

To prepare traditional Khulna-style Dim Steamed, start with 4–6 fresh eggs. Wash them thoroughly and set aside.

In a bowl, whisk the eggs lightly with 1 teaspoon salt, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder (optional), and 1–2 finely chopped green chilies for mild heat. You may also add a tablespoon of finely chopped onion or coriander leaves for extra flavor.

Grease a heatproof bowl or small containers with 1 teaspoon mustard oil and pour the egg mixture in. Place the bowl in a steamer or a large covered pot with 1–2 cups of water at the bottom. Steam on medium heat for 12–15 minutes or until the eggs are fully set and cooked through.

Remove from the steamer, let cool slightly, and serve hot with plain rice or roti for an authentic Khulna-style Dim Steamed experience.

To prepare traditional Mymensingh-style Dim Steamed, start with 4–6 fresh eggs. Wash them thoroughly and set aside.

In a bowl, whisk the eggs lightly with 1 teaspoon salt, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder (optional), and 1–2 finely chopped green chilies for mild heat. You may also add a tablespoon of finely chopped onion or coriander leaves for extra flavor.

Grease a heatproof bowl or small containers with 1 teaspoon mustard oil and pour the egg mixture in. Place the bowl in a steamer or a large covered pot with 1–2 cups of water at the bottom. Steam on medium heat for 12–15 minutes or until the eggs are fully set and cooked through.

Remove from the steamer, let cool slightly, and serve hot with plain rice or roti for an authentic Mymensingh-style Dim Steamed experience.

To prepare Tribal-style Dim Steamed, boil 3 eggs and peel them. In a bowl, mix 1/2 cup thick milk, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and a small amount of jaggery to form a smooth mixture. Pour this mixture into a steaming dish and place the boiled eggs on top. Cover and steam over boiling water for 12–15 minutes until the milk mixture sets gently into a soft custard-like texture. Garnish with finely chopped local herbs or coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice or flatbread.

To prepare Chattogram-style Dim Stuffed, make lengthwise slits in 6 medium green chilies or small eggplants and hollow out the centers slightly. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup chhena (fresh cottage cheese), 1 tablespoon roasted gram flour, 1/2 teaspoon ginger paste, a pinch of salt, and 1/2 teaspoon sugar to make a soft, smooth stuffing. Fill the vegetables with this milk-based mixture. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and 1 dried red chili for tempering, then arrange the stuffed vegetables in the pan. Cover and cook on low heat for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally until the filling sets properly. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Hill Tracts-style Dim Stuffed, make lengthwise slits in 6 medium green chilies or local hill gourds and gently hollow the centers. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup grated coconut, 1 tablespoon roasted rice flour, 1/2 teaspoon ginger paste, a pinch of salt, and 1/2 teaspoon jaggery to form a soft, smooth, lightly sweet stuffing. Fill the vegetables with this mixture. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 dried red chili and a pinch of wild cumin for tempering. Arrange the stuffed vegetables, cover, and cook on low heat for 12–15 minutes, turning occasionally until the filling sets and a subtle smoky aroma develops. Garnish with local herbs or chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Khulna-style Dim Stuffed, make lengthwise slits in 6 medium green chilies or small eggplants and hollow out the centers slightly. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup chhena (fresh cottage cheese), 1 tablespoon roasted gram flour, 1/2 teaspoon ginger paste, a pinch of salt, and 1/2 teaspoon sugar to make a soft, smooth stuffing. Fill the vegetables with this mixture. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and 1 dried red chili for tempering, then arrange the stuffed vegetables. Cover and cook on low heat for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally until the filling sets properly. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Dim Stuffed, make lengthwise slits in 6 medium green chilies or small eggplants and slightly hollow out the centers. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup chhena (fresh cottage cheese), 1 tablespoon roasted gram flour, 1/2 teaspoon ginger paste, a pinch of salt, and 1/2 teaspoon sugar to make a soft, smooth stuffing. Fill the vegetables with this mixture. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and 1 dried red chili for tempering, then arrange the stuffed vegetables. Cover and cook on low heat for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally until the filling sets properly. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dim Stuffed in the Tribal style, boil 3 eggs, peel them, and cut them in halves. Remove the yolks and place them in a bowl. Mix the yolks with 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste to form a thick stuffing. Fill the egg whites with this spiced yolk mixture. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan and lightly fry the stuffed eggs until golden. Garnish with chopped fresh coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice or flatbread.

To prepare Dim Tok in the Chattogram style, begin by boiling 3 eggs, peeling them, and cutting them in halves. Heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan and lightly fry the eggs until slightly golden, then set aside. In the same oil, add 1/2 teaspoon mustard seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until translucent. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, adding a splash of water to form a smooth masala. Pour in 1/2 cup tamarind pulp and 1/2 cup water and simmer gently until the curry develops a balanced sour-spicy flavor. Add the fried eggs and cook for 3–4 minutes so they absorb the tangy gravy. Garnish with chopped fresh coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dim Tok in the Dhaka style, begin by boiling 3 eggs, peeling them, and keeping them whole or cutting them in halves as preferred. Heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan and lightly fry the eggs until the outer surface turns slightly golden, then set aside. In the same oil, add 1/2 teaspoon of mustard seeds and 1/2 teaspoon of nigella seeds and let them splutter, followed by 1 medium finely chopped onion sautéed until translucent. Add 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste, mixing with a splash of water to form a smooth masala. Pour in 1/2 cup of tamarind pulp and 1/2 cup of water, allowing the curry to simmer gently until it develops a balanced sour-spicy flavor. Add the fried eggs and cook for another 3–4 minutes so they absorb the tangy gravy. Finish with chopped fresh coriander leaves and serve hot with plain steamed rice.

To prepare Dim Tok in the Rajshahi style, begin by boiling 3 eggs, peeling them, and cutting them in half. Heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan and lightly fry the eggs until the surfaces turn slightly golden, then set them aside. In the same oil, add 1/2 teaspoon of nigella seeds and 2 dried red chilies, allowing them to crackle, then add 1 medium-sized chopped onion and sauté until soft. Stir in 1/2 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste, adding a little water to prevent burning and cook until the spices are well blended. Add 1/2 cup of tamarind pulp (or raw mango sour juice) and bring to a gentle boil. Once the gravy becomes lightly sour and thin, add the fried eggs and simmer for 3–4 minutes so the eggs absorb the tangy flavors. Finish by garnishing with fresh coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

Dim Tok (Sylhet style) is a light, tangy egg curry known for its sharp sourness rather than heavy spices. Boiled eggs are lightly fried and then simmered in a thin gravy made with onion, green chili, turmeric, and minimal red chili. The sour taste traditionally comes from tenga ingredients such as lime juice, tok doi (sour yogurt), or sometimes tamarind, with Sylhet cuisine favoring a clean, citrusy finish. Mustard oil is often used for aroma, and the curry is kept watery, making it ideal with plain rice.

To prepare Duck Bhuna (Dhaka style), begin by cleaning and cutting 1 kg duck into medium pieces. Marinate the duck with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1½ teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and salt to taste for 20 minutes. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil, sauté 1 large sliced onion until deep golden, then add the marinated duck and cook on medium heat, stirring frequently, until the meat releases its juices. Continue cooking uncovered on low heat for 35–40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the duck becomes tender and the gravy thickens into a rich, dark bhuna coating typical of Dhaka-style cooking. Serve hot with plain rice or khichuri.

To prepare Duck Bhuna (Hill Tracts style), begin by cleaning and cutting 1 kg duck into medium pieces. Marinate the duck with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1½ teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and salt to taste for 20 minutes. Heat 3–4 tablespoons vegetable or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, sauté 1 large sliced onion until lightly browned, then add the marinated duck. Cook on medium heat, stirring frequently, until the duck releases its juices. Continue cooking uncovered on low heat for 35–40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the duck becomes tender and the gravy reduces to a thick, dark, bhuna-style coating with a slightly smoky, earthy flavor characteristic of Hill Tracts cooking. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Duck Bhuna (Mymensingh style), begin by cleaning and cutting 1 kg duck into medium pieces. Marinate the duck with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1½ teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and salt to taste for 20 minutes. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil, sauté 1 large sliced onion until golden, then add the marinated duck and cook on medium heat, stirring frequently, until the duck releases its own fat and moisture. Continue cooking uncovered on low heat for 35–40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the meat becomes tender and the gravy thickens and coats the duck pieces in a rich, dark bhuna-style finish. Serve hot with plain rice or khichuri.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Duck Bhuna, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a pan and sauté 1 large chopped onion until light brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. Mix in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck pieces and cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes. Add 1/2 cup chopped tomatoes and 3 slit green chilies, stirring occasionally until the oil separates and the meat is cooked through. Finish with 1/2 teaspoon garam masala and garnish with chopped coriander leaves before serving hot.

To prepare Rangpur-style Duck Bhuna, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a pan and sauté 1 large chopped onion until light brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. Mix in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck pieces and cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes. Add 1/2 cup chopped tomatoes and 3 slit green chilies, stirring occasionally until the oil separates and the meat is cooked through. Finish with 1/2 teaspoon garam masala and garnish with chopped coriander leaves before serving hot.

To prepare Tribal-style Duck Bhuna, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan and sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. Mix in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck pieces and cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes. Add 1/2 cup chopped tomatoes and 3 slit green chilies, stirring occasionally until the oil separates and the meat is cooked through. Finish with 1/2 teaspoon garam masala and garnish with local coriander leaves before serving hot.

To prepare Hill Tracts-style Duck Dry, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. Mix in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck pieces and cook on low heat for 8–10 minutes until the meat is fully cooked and the spices are well absorbed. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Duck Dry, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. Add the duck pieces and fry on medium heat for 8–10 minutes until the meat is fully cooked and lightly golden. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

Add the duck pieces and fry on medium heat for 8–10 minutes until the meat is fully cooked and slightly golden. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Khulna-style Duck Fry, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. Mix in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. To prepare Mymensingh-style Duck Fry, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. To prepare Sylhet-style Duck Fry, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown.
