To prepare Barisal-style Duck Grilled, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Marinate the meat with 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste for 30 minutes. Heat a little oil in a grill pan or skillet, and grill the marinated duck pieces for 8–10 minutes, turning on both sides until lightly golden and aromatic. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Dhaka-style Duck Grilled, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Marinate the meat with 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste for 30 minutes. Heat a little oil in a grill pan or skillet, and grill the marinated duck pieces for 8–10 minutes, turning on both sides until lightly golden and aromatic. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Hill Tracts-style Duck Grilled, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Marinate the meat with 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste for 30 minutes. Heat a little oil in a grill pan or skillet, and grill the marinated duck pieces for 8–10 minutes, turning on both sides until lightly golden and aromatic. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Duck Grilled, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Marinate the meat with 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste for 30 minutes. Heat a little oil in a grill pan or skillet, and grill the marinated duck pieces for 8–10 minutes, turning on both sides until lightly golden and aromatic. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare a delicious Rangpur-style duck dish that is slow-cooked to a dark, caramelized finish, resembling a "grilled" texture, start with a whole duck (about 1.5 kg), cleaned and cut into pieces. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil until it smokes, then add 2 large sliced onions and sauté until golden. Add 1 tablespoon of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of cumin powder, and a few whole garam masala spices like cinnamon sticks, cardamom, and cloves. Cook the spices until fragrant, adding a splash of water to prevent burning. Now, add the duck pieces and cook on high heat, stirring continuously until the meat is well-seared on all sides. Pour in 1 cup of warm water, reduce the heat to low, and cover the pot to let the duck simmer for 1 to 1.5 hours, or until it becomes very tender and the gravy thickens to a rich, dark brown color. The long cooking process gives it a deep, almost roasted flavor that is characteristic of this region's cuisine. Serve hot with rice or paratha.

To prepare Duck Jhol (Chattogram style), begin by cleaning and cutting 1 kg duck into medium pieces. In a large pot, heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil, sauté 1 large sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until golden and aromatic. Add the duck pieces, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, and cook on medium heat for 5–7 minutes. Pour in 2–3 cups water, cover, and simmer on low heat for 35–40 minutes until the duck is tender and the gravy is flavorful but slightly thin, characteristic of Chattogram-style “jhol.” Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Hill Tracts-style Duck Jhol, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a pan. Sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1 teaspoon turmeric powder. Stir in 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck pieces and cook for 10–12 minutes. Then add 2 cups of water and 1/2 cup chopped tomatoes, cover, and simmer for 20 minutes. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Duck Jhol, cut 500 g duck meat into medium-sized pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan and sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown, then add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste and cook well. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck meat and bhuna on medium heat for 10–12 minutes. Pour in 2–2½ cups of hot water, cover, and simmer gently for about 25 minutes until the meat is tender and the gravy turns aromatic. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Duck Jhol, cut 500 g duck meat into medium pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a pan and sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown, then add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste and cook well. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck meat and bhuna on medium heat for 10–12 minutes. Add 2 cups of hot water, cover, and simmer for 20–25 minutes until the meat becomes tender and the gravy reaches a medium consistency. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Rangpur-style Duck Jhol, cut 500 g duck meat into medium-sized pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan and sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste and cook well. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck meat and bhuna on medium heat for 10–12 minutes. Pour in 2–2½ cups of hot water, cover, and simmer for about 25 minutes until the meat becomes tender and the gravy turns thick and aromatic. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Sylhet-style Duck Jhol, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a pan. Sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1 teaspoon turmeric powder. Stir in 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck pieces and cook for 10–12 minutes. Then add 2 cups of water and 1/2 cup chopped tomatoes, cover, and simmer for 20 minutes. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Barisal-style Duck Khichuri, wash and soak 200 g rice and 50 g lentils for 20 minutes. Cut 250 g duck meat into medium pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pot and sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder. Add the duck meat, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste, and cook for 8–10 minutes. Mix in the soaked rice and lentils, add 2½ cups of hot water, cover, and cook on medium heat for 18–20 minutes until the khichuri becomes soft and thick. Finish with a little ghee and chopped coriander leaves, and serve hot.

To prepare Chattogram-style Duck Khichuri, soak 200 g uncooked rice and 50 g lentils for 20 minutes. Cut 250 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a pan, sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder. Add the duck meat, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste, and cook for 8–10 minutes. Mix in the soaked rice and lentils, add 2 cups of water, cover, and cook for 15–20 minutes until soft. Before serving, drizzle a little ghee and garnish with chopped coriander leaves.

To prepare Dhaka-style Duck Khichuri, wash and soak 200 g rice and 50 g lentils for 20 minutes. Cut 250 g duck meat into medium-sized pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of oil or ghee in a heavy pot and sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder. Add the duck meat, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, and cook for 8–10 minutes. Add the soaked rice and lentils along with 2½ cups of hot water, cover, and cook on medium heat for 18–20 minutes until the khichuri is soft, fluffy, and aromatic. Finish with a drizzle of ghee and chopped coriander leaves, and serve hot.

To prepare traditional Mymensingh-style Duck Khichuri, start by cutting about 600 g of deshi duck meat into medium pieces, cleaning thoroughly, and patting dry. Wash 1.5 cups of kalijira or atap rice and ½ cup of moong dal (lentils), then soak them together for 20 minutes; drain and set aside. In a heavy-bottomed pan, dry roast the dal for 2–3 minutes until aromatic, then set aside. Heat 5 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee in the same pan and fry 2 medium onions finely sliced until golden brown; remove one-third for garnish. To the remaining onions, add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 2–3 green chilies, 2 bay leaves, 3–4 cardamoms, 2 cinnamon sticks, and 3–4 cloves, sautéing until fragrant. Mix in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste, cooking with a splash of water until the oil separates. Add the duck pieces and fry for 8–10 minutes, stirring until the meat is well coated with spices. Next, add the roasted dal and soaked rice, stir gently for 2–3 minutes, and then pour in 5 cups of hot water. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low, cover with a tight-fitting lid, and let it cook for 25–30 minutes until the rice, dal, and duck are tender and the khichuri has a rich, thick texture. After turning off the heat, let it rest for 5 minutes, then fluff gently and garnish with the reserved fried onions before serving hot.

To prepare Rangpur-style Duck Khichuri, wash and soak 200 g atap rice and 50 g lentils for 20 minutes. Cut 250 g duck meat into medium pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pot and sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder. Add the duck meat, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, and bhuna for about 10 minutes. Mix in the soaked rice and lentils, add 2½ cups of hot water, cover, and cook on medium heat for 20–22 minutes until the khichuri is soft, slightly fluffy, and aromatic. Finish with a drizzle of ghee and serve hot.

To prepare Sylhet-style Duck Khichuri, wash and soak 200 g atap rice and 50 g lentils for 20 minutes. Cut 250 g duck meat into medium-sized pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pot and sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder. Add the duck meat, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, and bhuna for 10–12 minutes. Add the soaked rice and lentils with 3 cups of hot water, cover, and cook on medium heat for 22–25 minutes until the khichuri becomes soft, fluffy, and aromatic. Finish with a drizzle of ghee and chopped coriander leaves, and serve hot.

To prepare Tribal-style Duck Khichuri, wash and soak 200 g coarse atap rice and 50 g local lentils for 20 minutes. Cut 250 g duck meat into medium pieces. Heat 2 tablespoons of oil or wild sesame oil in a pot and lightly sauté crushed garlic and chopped onion. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck meat and bhuna on medium heat for about 10 minutes. Mix in the soaked rice and lentils, add 3 cups of hot water, cover, and cook slowly for 25–30 minutes until the khichuri becomes soft, thick, and naturally aromatic. Serve hot without heavy spices.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Duck Korma, clean and cut 500 g duck meat into medium pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pot, add 2 bay leaves, 4 green cardamoms, and 4–5 sliced onions, and fry until lightly golden. Add 2 tablespoons onion paste, 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and salt; bhuna well. Add the duck meat and cook covered on medium heat for 20–25 minutes until oil separates. Then add 1 cup thick coconut milk and 1/2 cup yogurt, stir gently, cover, and cook slowly for another 15 minutes until the meat is tender and the gravy becomes rich and creamy. Serve hot with plain rice or polao.

To prepare a traditional Chattogram-style Duck Korma, a rich and creamy curry, start with 1 kg of duck, cleaned and cut into pieces. In a large pot, heat 4 tablespoons of ghee or oil and add whole spices like 2-3 green cardamom pods, 2 cinnamon sticks, and 4-5 cloves. Once they release their aroma, add 2 large sliced onions and fry until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon of ginger-garlic paste and cook until the raw smell disappears. Now, add the duck pieces and brown them on all sides. In a bowl, mix 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of cumin powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste with a little water to form a paste, then add it to the pot and sauté well. To create the korma's signature rich gravy, pour in 1 cup of coconut milk and 1 cup of fresh milk, stirring to combine. Cover the pot and let it simmer on low heat for 1 to 1.5 hours, or until the duck is very tender and the gravy has thickened to a rich consistency. Finish by garnishing with a pinch of garam masala before serving hot with pulao, paratha, or rice.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Duck Korma, clean and cut 500 g duck meat into medium pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pot, add 2 bay leaves, 3 green cardamoms, and 1 cinnamon stick, then add 2 medium onion pastes and sauté until lightly golden. Stir in 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1/2 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt, cooking until aromatic. Add the duck meat, cover, and cook on medium heat for 25–30 minutes until oil releases. Then add 1/2 cup yogurt and 1 cup thin coconut milk, mix gently, cover, and simmer for another 15 minutes until the meat becomes tender and the gravy thickens. Serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Duck Korma, clean and cut 500 g duck meat into medium pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 3 cardamoms, and 1-inch cinnamon stick to release fragrance. Then add 2 tablespoons onion paste and sauté until lightly golden. Stir in 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt, cooking well. Add the duck meat, cover, and cook on medium heat for 25–30 minutes until oil separates. Then mix in 1/2 cup yogurt and 1 cup thick coconut milk, cover, and simmer for another 15 minutes until the meat is tender and the gravy thickens. Serve hot with steamed rice or polao.

To prepare Rangpur-style Duck Korma, clean and cut 500 g duck meat into medium pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 3 green cardamoms, and 1-inch cinnamon stick to release aroma. Then add 2 tablespoons onion paste and sauté until lightly golden. Stir in 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt, and bhuna well. Add the duck meat, cover, and cook on medium heat for 25–30 minutes until oil separates. Then mix in 1/2 cup yogurt and 1 cup coconut milk, cover, and simmer for another 15 minutes until the meat is tender and the gravy thickens. Serve hot with steamed rice or polao.

To prepare Sylhet-style Duck Korma, clean and cut 500 g duck meat into medium pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 3 green cardamoms, and 1-inch cinnamon stick to release fragrance. Then add 2 tablespoons onion paste and sauté until lightly golden. Stir in 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt, and cook well. Add the duck meat, cover, and cook on medium heat for 25–30 minutes until oil separates. Then add 1 cup thick coconut milk and 1/2 cup yogurt, stir gently, cover, and simmer for another 15 minutes until the meat is tender and the gravy thickens. Serve hot with steamed rice or polao.

To prepare Barisal-style Duck Paturi, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Marinate the meat with 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon mustard oil, and let it sit for 20 minutes. Heat leaves in a bowl or use banana leaves. Place the marinated meat on the leaves, wrap tightly, and secure. Steam in a preheated steamer for 25–30 minutes. Once cooked, unwrap the leaves and serve hot with rice or polao.

To prepare Dhaka-style Duck Paturi, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Marinate the meat with 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon mustard oil, and let it sit for 20–30 minutes. Lightly warm the leaves (banana or other suitable leaves). Place the marinated meat on the leaves and wrap tightly. Steam in a preheated steamer for 25–30 minutes. Once cooked, unwrap and serve hot with rice or polao.

To prepare Hill Tracts-style Duck Paturi, cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Marinate the meat with 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon wild or mustard oil, and let it sit for 20 minutes. Lightly warm banana leaves or other suitable leaves. Place the marinated meat on the leaves and wrap tightly. Steam in a preheated steamer for 25–30 minutes. Once cooked, unwrap and serve hot with rice or polao.

To prepare Khulna-style Duck Paturi, take a small whole duck (about 1–1.2 kg), clean it thoroughly, and pat dry. Prepare a stuffing by mixing ½ cup finely chopped onions, 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon freshly ground mustard paste, 2–3 crushed garlic cloves, 1-inch ginger paste, and salt to taste. Loosen the skin of the duck slightly and stuff the mixture into the cavity evenly. Wrap the stuffed duck in banana leaves (or foil if unavailable) and secure with kitchen string. Steam or cook the wrapped duck over low heat for 50–60 minutes until tender and fully infused with the mustard and spice flavors. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Khulna-style meal.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Duck Paturi, take a small whole duck (about 1–1.2 kg), clean it thoroughly, and pat dry. Prepare a stuffing by mixing ½ cup finely chopped onions, 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon freshly ground mustard paste, 2–3 crushed garlic cloves, 1-inch ginger paste, and salt to taste, keeping the seasoning balanced and mildly aromatic as preferred in Rajshahi cuisine. Loosen the skin of the duck slightly and stuff the mixture into the cavity evenly. Wrap the stuffed duck in banana leaves (or foil if unavailable) and secure with kitchen string. Steam or cook the wrapped duck over low heat for 50–60 minutes until tender and fully infused with the spices. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Rajshahi-style meal.

To prepare Rangpur-style Duck Paturi, cut 1 kilogram of duck meat into medium pieces and wash thoroughly, then marinate with 3 tablespoons of mustard paste, 2 tablespoons of yogurt, 1 tablespoon of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 2 teaspoons chili powder, 1 teaspoon roasted cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, salt to taste, 3–4 slit green chilies, and 3 tablespoons of mustard oil, leaving it for at least 1 hour. Wrap the marinated duck pieces in banana leaves, securing each parcel with thread or toothpicks, then place them on a hot tawa, pan, or griddle, cooking on very low heat for 40–50 minutes, turning occasionally until the duck is tender, smoky, and infused with mustard flavor. Serve hot with plain rice for a rustic, traditional taste.

To prepare Sylheti-style Duck Paturi, take a small whole duck (about 1–1.2 kg), clean it thoroughly, and pat dry. Prepare a stuffing by mixing ½ cup finely chopped onions, 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon freshly ground mustard paste, 2–3 crushed garlic cloves, 1-inch ginger paste, and salt to taste, keeping the flavors aromatic and slightly bold as is typical in Sylheti cuisine. Loosen the skin of the duck slightly and stuff the mixture evenly into the cavity. Wrap the stuffed duck in banana leaves (or foil if unavailable) and secure with kitchen string. Steam or cook the wrapped duck over low heat for 50–60 minutes until tender and fully infused with the mustard and spice flavors. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Sylheti-style meal.

To prepare Dhaka-style Duck Polao, begin by cleaning a small whole duck (about 1–1.2 kg) and cutting it into pieces. Marinate the duck pieces with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1-inch ginger paste, 2–3 crushed garlic cloves, and salt to taste for 15–20 minutes. Heat 4 tablespoons ghee or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, sauté 1 sliced onion until golden, then add the marinated duck and fry until lightly browned. Wash and soak 2 cups of aromatic rice such as basmati or kalijira for 20–30 minutes, drain, and add it to the pan along with 4 cups of hot water. Cover and simmer on low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice is tender and infused with the duck’s flavors. Garnish with fried onions or boiled eggs if desired, and serve hot.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Duck Polao, begin by cleaning a small whole duck (about 1–1.2 kg) and cutting it into pieces. Marinate the duck with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1-inch ginger paste, 2–3 crushed garlic cloves, and salt to taste, letting it rest for 15–20 minutes. Heat 4 tablespoons ghee or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, sauté 1 sliced onion until golden, then add the marinated duck and fry until lightly browned. Wash and soak 2 cups of aromatic rice such as basmati or kalijira for 20–30 minutes, drain, and add it to the pan with 4 cups of hot water. Cover and simmer on low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice is tender and infused with the duck’s flavors. Garnish with fried onions or boiled eggs if desired, and serve hot.

To prepare Tribal-style Duck Polao, begin by cleaning a small whole duck (about 1–1.2 kg) and cutting it into pieces. Marinate the duck with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1-inch ginger paste, 2–3 crushed garlic cloves, and salt to taste, keeping the seasoning simple and earthy, and let it rest for 15–20 minutes. Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, sauté 1 sliced onion until golden, then add the marinated duck and lightly fry until browned. Wash and soak 2 cups of aromatic rice such as kalijira for 20–30 minutes, drain, and add it to the pan along with 4 cups of hot water. Cover and simmer on low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice is tender and infused with the duck’s flavors. Serve hot with plain rice or a light vegetable side for a traditional Tribal-style meal.

To prepare Dhaka-style Duck Steamed, take a small whole duck (about 1–1.2 kg), clean it thoroughly, and pat dry. Prepare a light, aromatic marinade by mixing 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1-inch ginger paste, 2–3 crushed garlic cloves, and salt to taste, keeping the flavors mildly pungent as preferred in Dhaka cuisine. Rub the marinade evenly over the duck, including inside the cavity, and let it rest for 20–30 minutes. Place the duck in a heatproof dish, set it inside a steamer or a covered pan with a little water at the bottom, and steam on medium heat for 50–60 minutes until tender, fully cooked, and aromatic. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Dhaka-style meal.

To prepare Hill Tracts–style Duck Steamed, take a small whole duck (about 1–1.2 kg), clean it thoroughly, and pat dry. Prepare a simple, earthy marinade by mixing 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1-inch ginger paste, 2–3 crushed garlic cloves, and salt to taste, keeping the flavors rustic as preferred in Hill Tracts cooking. Rub the marinade evenly over the duck, including inside the cavity, and let it rest for 20–30 minutes. Place the duck in a heatproof dish, set it inside a steamer or a covered pan with a little water at the bottom, and steam on medium heat for 50–60 minutes until tender, fully cooked, and aromatic. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Hill Tracts-style meal.

Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Tribal-style meal.

To prepare Chattogram-style Duck Stuffed, begin by taking a whole small duck (about 1–1.2 kg), clean it thoroughly, and pat dry. Prepare a stuffing by mixing ½ cup finely chopped onions, 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon ground cumin, 1 teaspoon garam masala, 2–3 crushed garlic cloves, 1-inch ginger paste, and salt to taste. Loosen the skin of the duck slightly and carefully stuff this mixture into the cavity, ensuring it is evenly distributed. Tie the legs with kitchen string to secure the stuffing. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan or Dutch oven, sear the duck on all sides until golden brown, then cover and cook on low heat for 45–50 minutes, occasionally basting with its own juices, until the duck is tender and the stuffing fully cooked. Serve hot with plain rice or traditional polao for a rich Chattogram-style meal.

To prepare Duck Stuffed (Dhaka style), begin by cleaning and gutting a medium-sized duck (about 1–1.2 kg). Prepare a stuffing with 1 small chopped onion, 2–3 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger-garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 2 tablespoons mustard paste, and salt to taste. Stuff the mixture into the duck cavity and secure with kitchen twine. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, sear the duck on all sides, then cover and cook on low heat for 45–50 minutes, turning occasionally until the duck is tender and fully cooked, and the stuffing is infused throughout. Serve hot with plain rice or paratha.

An authentic Hilly duck curry, inspired by the cuisine of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, uses indigenous ingredients and cooking methods to create a uniquely flavorful dish. To prepare it, take a cleaned and cut duck, and marinate it with a paste of ginger, garlic, turmeric powder, and a generous amount of dani morich (bird's eye chilies) from the hills. For the stuffing or filling, a blend of bamboo shoots, finely chopped onion, and nappi or sidol (fermented fish paste) is often used, which you would stuff into the duck pieces before cooking. In a pot, heat mustard oil and fry sliced onions until they soften, then add the marinated duck pieces and any remaining stuffing mixture. Sauté the duck well, adding a little water if needed to prevent the spices from burning. Once the duck is cooked and tender, a taaba style of preparation might involve adding a simple, watery broth to finish. Alternatively, for a richer bhuna style, continue to cook until the gravy thickens and the oil separates, a technique common in Bengali cooking. Finally, for an authentic touch, wrap the cooked duck pieces in banana leaves (hebaang) and briefly place them over hot coals to infuse a smoky aroma. This dish is usually served with plain rice.

To prepare Khulna-style Duck Stuffed, clean and cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and lightly sauté. Add 1/2 cup chopped vegetables (carrot, eggplant, beans) and cook for 5 minutes while stirring. Stuff this mixture into the duck meat and place in a large pot or steamer, cover, and cook on medium heat for 25–30 minutes until the meat is tender. Serve hot with rice or bread.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Duck Stuffed, clean and cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and lightly sauté. Add 1/2 cup chopped vegetables (carrot, eggplant, beans) and cook for 5 minutes while stirring. Stuff this mixture into the duck meat and place in a large pot or steamer, cover, and cook on medium heat for 25–30 minutes until the meat is tender. Serve hot with rice or bread.

To prepare Sylhet-style Duck Stuffed, clean and cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. To prepare Tribal-style Duck Stuffed, clean and cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 1 tablespoon wild or mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and lightly sauté. Add 1/2 cup chopped local vegetables (carrot, eggplant, beans, or chili) and cook for 5–7 minutes while stirring. Stuff this mixture into the duck meat, cover in a large pot or wrap in leaves, and steam on medium heat for 25–30 minutes until the meat is tender. Serve hot with rice or polao.

To prepare Chattogram-style Duck Tok, clean and cut 500 g duck meat into small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and sauté lightly. Add 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the duck meat and cook on medium heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring occasionally. Then add 2 tablespoons yogurt, cover, and cook for another 5–7 minutes. Serve hot with lightly thickened gravy and tender meat alongside steamed rice or polao.

To prepare Duck Tok (Hill Tracts), begin by cleaning and cutting 500 grams of duck meat into medium pieces and boiling it with salt and enough water until the meat is tender, then drain and set aside. Heat 3 tablespoons of sesame oil or mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, and sauté until fragrant. Add 2–3 chopped green chilies, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of crushed dry red chili, and salt to taste, stirring well on low heat. Add the boiled duck pieces and bhuna them gently until the spices coat the meat and the oil slightly separates. Pour in 1–1½ tablespoons of lemon juice or fermented bamboo shoot water (traditional in Hill Tracts) to create the signature sour flavor, and simmer for a few minutes until the dish becomes semi-dry and aromatic. Finish with a handful of chopped coriander or local herbs and serve hot as a bold, tangy Hill Tracts delicacy.

To prepare Duck Tok (Mymensingh), begin by cleaning and cutting 500 grams of duck meat into medium pieces and boiling it with salt and enough water until the meat is tender, then drain and keep aside. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, and sauté until aromatic. Add 2–3 slit green chilies, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste, stirring well on low heat. Add the boiled duck pieces and bhuna them gently so the spices coat the meat evenly. Pour in 1–2 tablespoons of lemon juice or tamarind water to create the characteristic Mymensingh-style sourness, and simmer for a few minutes until the dish becomes semi-dry and flavorful. Finish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot as a traditional tangy duck dish.

To prepare Duck Tok (Rajshahi), start by cleaning and cutting 500 grams of duck meat into medium pieces and boiling it with salt and enough water until tender, then drain and set aside. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, and sauté until fragrant. Add 2–3 chopped green chilies, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, ½ teaspoon of roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste, mixing well on low heat. Add the boiled duck pieces and bhuna them gently until the spices coat the meat and oil begins to separate. Pour in 1–2 tablespoons of tamarind water or sour plum (tok boroi) extract, a signature Rajshahi touch, and simmer briefly until the dish becomes semi-dry and tangy. Finish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot as a bold, spicy, and sour Rajshahi-style delicacy.

To prepare Duck Tok (Sylhet), begin by cleaning and cutting 500 grams of duck meat into medium pieces and boiling it with salt and enough water until the meat is tender, then drain and set aside. Pour in 1–2 tablespoons of lemon juice or shatkora juice (a signature Sylheti citrus), and simmer for a few minutes until the dish becomes semi-dry, tangy, and fragrant. Finish with chopped fresh coriander leaves and serve hot as a classic Sylheti sour duck delicacy.

To prepare Dudh Bhuna (Dhaka), begin by heating 2 liters of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan and bringing it to a gentle boil, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. Lower the heat and continue simmering, stirring frequently, until the milk reduces to about one-third of its original volume and becomes thick and creamy. Add ¾ cup of sugar (adjust to taste), 2–3 crushed green cardamom pods, and a small pinch of salt, stirring continuously so the milk does not burn. Cook on low heat until the mixture turns light golden and takes on a rich, bhuna-style texture with a slightly caramelized flavor. Finish by stirring in 1 tablespoon of ghee for aroma, then remove from heat and allow it to cool slightly before serving. This Dhaka-style Dudh Bhuna is rich, mildly sweet, and deeply aromatic, often enjoyed warm or chilled as a traditional dessert.

To prepare Dudh Bhuna (Hill Tracts), begin by heating 2 liters of fresh full-cream milk in a heavy pan and bringing it to a slow boil, stirring regularly to prevent sticking. Reduce the heat and simmer gently until the milk reduces to about one-third and thickens noticeably. Add ½ cup of sugar (adjust to taste), a pinch of salt, and 1–2 crushed cardamom pods, stirring continuously. Continue cooking on low heat until the milk takes on a slightly grainy texture and a light caramelized color, reflecting the traditional hill-style bhuna cooking. Finish by stirring in 1 tablespoon of sesame oil or ghee for a subtle nutty aroma, then remove from heat and allow it to cool slightly before serving. This Hill Tracts version is less sweet, richly concentrated, and deeply aromatic.

To prepare Dudh Bhuna (Mymensingh), begin by heating 2 liters of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan and bringing it to a gentle boil, stirring often so it does not stick. Add ¾ cup of sugar (adjust to taste), a small pinch of salt, and 2–3 crushed green cardamom pods, mixing well. This Mymensingh-style Dudh Bhuna is rich, mildly sweet, and traditionally enjoyed warm as a comforting dessert.

Lower the heat and simmer slowly, stirring continuously, until the milk reduces to about one-third of its original volume and becomes thick and creamy. Add ½ cup of sugar (Rangpur style is slightly less sweet), a small pinch of salt, and 2 crushed green cardamom pods, mixing well. Continue cooking on low heat until the milk develops a lightly caramelized color and a rich bhuna texture with a deep aroma. Finish by stirring in 1 tablespoon of ghee for added richness, then remove from heat and allow it to cool slightly before serving. This Rangpur-style Dudh Bhuna is mildly sweet, dense, and traditionally enjoyed warm.

To prepare Dudh Dry (Barisal), start by heating 2 liters of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat, stirring frequently to prevent sticking. Reduce the heat and simmer gently until the milk thickens and reduces to about one-third of its original volume. Add ½ cup of sugar (adjust to taste) and a pinch of salt, stirring continuously. Continue cooking on low heat until the milk becomes thick, slightly grainy, and completely dry, taking on a light golden color with a concentrated, caramelized flavor. Finish by stirring in 1 tablespoon of ghee for aroma, then remove from heat and allow it to cool slightly before serving. This Barisal-style Dudh Dry is dense, rich, and mildly sweet, perfect as a traditional dessert.

To prepare Dudh Dry (Rangpur), start by heating 2 liters of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan, stirring frequently to prevent sticking. Reduce the heat and simmer gently until the milk thickens and reduces to about one-third of its original volume. Add ½ cup of sugar (slightly less for Rangpur style) and a pinch of salt, stirring continuously. Continue cooking on low heat until the milk becomes thick, slightly grainy, and almost dry, with a light golden color and concentrated flavor. Finish by stirring in 1 tablespoon of ghee for aroma, then remove from heat and let it cool slightly before serving. This Rangpur-style Dudh Dry is rich, dense, and mildly sweet, with a deeply caramelized taste.

To prepare Dudh Dry (Sylhet), begin by heating 2 liters of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan, stirring frequently to prevent sticking. Reduce the heat and simmer slowly, stirring continuously, until the milk thickens and reduces to about one-third of its original volume. Add ½–¾ cup of sugar (adjust to taste) and a pinch of salt, mixing well. Continue cooking on low heat until the milk becomes thick, slightly grainy, and dry, taking on a light golden color and rich aroma. Finish by stirring in 1 tablespoon of ghee for extra flavor, then remove from heat and let it cool slightly before serving. This Sylheti-style Dudh Dry is dense, mildly sweet, and deeply flavorful, perfect as a traditional dessert.

To prepare Dudh Fry (Barisal), start by heating 2 liters of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat, stirring frequently to prevent sticking or burning. Reduce the heat and simmer gently until the milk thickens slightly but still retains a pourable consistency. Add ½ cup of sugar (adjust to taste), a pinch of salt, and 2–3 crushed green cardamom pods, stirring well. Continue cooking on low heat until the milk achieves a creamy, lightly thickened texture with a mild caramelized aroma. Finish by stirring in 1 tablespoon of ghee for richness and flavor, then remove from heat. Serve warm as a traditional Barisal-style mildly sweet, creamy milk dessert.

To prepare Dudh Fry (Chattogram), begin by heating 2 liters of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat, stirring frequently to prevent sticking. Finish by stirring in 1 tablespoon of ghee for richness and flavor, then remove from heat. Serve warm as a traditional Chattogram-style mildly sweet, creamy milk dessert.

Reduce the heat and simmer gently until the milk thickens slightly but remains pourable. Add ½ cup of sugar (adjust to taste), a pinch of salt, and 2–3 crushed green cardamom pods, stirring well. Continue cooking on low heat until the milk develops a creamy, lightly thickened texture with a subtle caramelized aroma, characteristic of Rajshahi-style milk desserts. Finish by stirring in 1 tablespoon of ghee for extra richness, then remove from heat. Serve warm as a mildly sweet, aromatic, and comforting Rajshahi-style milk dessert.

To prepare traditional Rangpur-style Dudh Fry, start with 500 ml of fresh full-fat milk. Pour the milk into a heavy-bottomed pan and bring it to a boil over medium heat, stirring occasionally to prevent burning.

Once the milk starts boiling, reduce the heat to low and simmer until it thickens slightly. Add 2 tablespoons ghee or clarified butter, 4 tablespoons sugar (adjust to taste), ½ teaspoon cardamom powder, and a pinch of saffron strands (optional) for aroma and flavor. Continue stirring gently to avoid sticking.

For Rangpur-style richness, some cooks add a small handful of crushed nuts like almonds or cashews during the final 5 minutes of cooking. Simmer until the milk thickens to a creamy consistency suitable for serving as a dessert.

Serve warm or chilled in small bowls for an authentic Rangpur-style Dudh Fry experience.

To prepare Dudh Grilled (Barisal), start by boiling 2 liters of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan, stirring frequently to prevent sticking. Reduce the heat and simmer until the milk thickens and reduces to about half its original volume. Add ½ cup of sugar (adjust to taste), a pinch of salt, and 2–3 crushed green cardamom pods, stirring well. Continue cooking on low heat until the mixture becomes dense, creamy, and slightly caramelized. Pour the thickened milk into a greased flat tray and spread it evenly, then allow it to cool and set slightly. Cut into square or rectangular pieces, lightly brush with ghee, and grill on a hot flat pan or grill until both sides develop a light golden crust. Serve warm or at room temperature as a rich, aromatic Barisal-style milk dessert.

Reduce the heat and simmer until the milk thickens and reduces to about half its original volume. Add ½ cup of sugar (adjust to taste), a pinch of salt, and 2–3 crushed green cardamom pods, stirring well. Continue cooking on low heat until the milk becomes dense, creamy, and slightly caramelized. Cut into square or rectangular pieces, lightly brush with ghee, and grill on a hot flat pan or grill until both sides develop a light golden crust. Reduce the heat and simmer until the milk thickens and reduces to about half its original volume. Add ½–¾ cup of sugar (to taste), 2–3 crushed green cardamom pods, and a small pinch of salt, and continue cooking on low heat until the mixture becomes dense, smooth, and slightly glossy. Pour the thickened milk into a greased flat tray, spread it evenly, and allow it to cool and set completely. Cut into square or rectangular pieces, lightly brush with ghee, and grill on a hot flat pan or grill until both sides develop a light golden crust. Serve warm or at room temperature as a rich, mildly sweet Dhaka-style milk dessert with a caramelized exterior and soft interior.

Reduce the heat and simmer until the milk thickens and reduces to about half its volume. Pour the thickened milk into a greased flat tray and spread it evenly, then allow it to cool and set slightly. Cut into square or rectangular portions, brush lightly with ghee, and grill on a hot flat pan or grill until both sides develop a light golden crust. Serve warm or at room temperature as a rustic Rangpur-style milk delicacy with a caramelized exterior and soft interior.

To prepare Barisal-style Dudh Jhol, heat 500 ml milk thoroughly. In a pan, heat 1 tablespoon oil or ghee, add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and lightly sauté. Add 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Gradually pour the hot milk into the pan while stirring to prevent it from burning. Cook on medium heat for 5–7 minutes. Finish with a drizzle of ghee and chopped coriander leaves, and serve hot with rice or bread.

To prepare Chattogram-style Dudh Jhol, heat 500 ml milk thoroughly on the stove. In a pan, heat 1 tablespoon oil, add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and lightly sauté. Add 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Gradually pour the hot milk into the pan, stirring continuously to prevent burning. Cook on medium heat for 5–7 minutes. Optionally, drizzle a little ghee and garnish with chopped coriander leaves, and serve hot.

To prepare Khulna-style Dudh Jhol, take 500 ml milk, 1 tablespoon yogurt, and 1 teaspoon turmeric powder in a pan and heat on medium flame. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste and mix well. Stir in 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Cook gently for 5–7 minutes while stirring continuously until the milk thickens and the spices are well incorporated. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Dudh Khichuri (Mymensingh), start by washing 1 cup of rice and ½ cup of moong dal (split yellow lentils) thoroughly and soaking them for 15–20 minutes. Drain well. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil and add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, and 2–3 slit green chilies, sautéing until aromatic. Add 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, and a pinch of salt. Stir in the drained rice and lentils, coating them evenly with the spices. Pour in 3 cups of milk and 1 cup of water, bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat and simmer, covered, until the rice and dal are fully cooked and the mixture becomes creamy. Finish by adding 1 tablespoon of ghee and garnish with chopped coriander leaves. Serve hot as a comforting, mildly sweet, and aromatic Mymensingh-style milk khichuri.

To prepare a traditional Sylhet-style Dudh Khichuri, start by thoroughly washing 1 cup of Basmati or local fragrant rice and ½ cup of moong dal. In a large pot, heat 2 tablespoons of ghee. Add 2 bay leaves, 2 cardamom pods, and a small cinnamon stick, and fry until fragrant. Add the washed rice and moong dal, and toast them on medium heat for 3-4 minutes until the moong dal turns a light golden color and a nutty aroma fills the air. Pour in 3 cups of water and 2 cups of milk. Add a pinch of salt and a little sugar to balance the flavors. Stir well and bring to a boil. Reduce the heat to a low simmer, cover the pot, and cook for about 20-25 minutes, or until the rice and dal are soft and the mixture has thickened to a creamy consistency. Be sure to stir occasionally to prevent sticking. For a final touch, heat a small amount of ghee in a separate pan, add a few fried cashews and raisins, and pour this over the khichuri. You can also garnish with more ghee and a sprinkle of garam masala before serving. Serve hot.

To prepare Dudh Khichuri (Tribal), start by washing 1 cup of sticky or glutinous rice and ½ cup of split yellow lentils (moong dal), then soak them for 20–30 minutes and drain well. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2–3 tablespoons of sesame oil or mustard oil and add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 2–3 chopped green chilies, and a pinch of salt, sautéing until aromatic. Add the drained rice and lentils, stirring gently to coat with the spices. Pour in 3 cups of fresh full-cream milk and 1 cup of water, bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat and simmer, covered, until the rice and lentils are fully cooked and the mixture turns creamy and slightly thick. Finish by adding 1 tablespoon of ghee or sesame oil and garnish with freshly chopped coriander or local herbs. Serve hot as a rich, comforting, and mildly spiced Tribal-style milk khichuri.

To prepare Barisal-style Dudh Korma, take 500 ml milk, 1 tablespoon yogurt, and 1 teaspoon turmeric powder in a pan and heat on medium flame. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste and mix well. Stir in 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Cook gently for 5–7 minutes while stirring continuously until the milk thickens and the spices are well incorporated. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare a traditional Chattogram-style Dudh Korma, start with 500g of chicken or mutton, cut into medium-sized pieces. In a large pot or pan, heat 3 tablespoons of ghee or oil. Add 2-3 whole cardamom pods, 2 cinnamon sticks, and 4-5 cloves, frying briefly until fragrant. Add 2 finely sliced medium onions and fry until translucent. Add 1 tablespoon of ginger-garlic paste and cook until the raw smell disappears. Mix in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste, stirring well. Add the meat pieces and brown them on all sides. Pour in 1 cup of coconut milk and 1 cup of fresh milk, stirring to combine. Cover the pot and let it simmer on low heat for 30-40 minutes (for chicken) or 1-1.5 hours (for mutton) until the meat is tender and the gravy has thickened. Garnish with a pinch of garam masala and fresh coriander leaves before serving. Serve hot with pulao, paratha, or rice.

To prepare Dhaka-style Dudh Korma, take 500 ml milk, 1 tablespoon yogurt, and 1 teaspoon turmeric powder in a pan and heat on medium flame. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste and mix well. Stir in 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Cook gently for 5–7 minutes while stirring continuously until the milk thickens and the spices are well incorporated. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Dudh Korma, heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a pan. Sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. Mix in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add 1 cup thick milk and 1/2 cup coconut milk, and simmer gently for 5 minutes until the korma thickens and becomes smooth. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Sylhet-style Dudh Korma, heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a pan. Sauté 1 large chopped onion until lightly brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking until the raw smell disappears. Mix in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add 1 cup thick milk and 1/2 cup coconut milk, stirring gently and simmer on low heat for 5 minutes until the korma thickens smoothly. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Dudh Korma, a traditional tribal dish known for its rich, creamy texture and subtle sweetness, begin by heating 2 tablespoons of ghee or clarified butter in a medium-sized pot over low heat. Add 1 small cinnamon stick, 2–3 green cardamom pods, and 2 cloves, sautéing for about a minute until fragrant. Then add 1 small finely chopped onion and cook until translucent. Stir in 250 grams of bone-in chicken pieces (or goat meat, depending on regional preference), and cook until lightly browned on all sides. Next, add 1 teaspoon each of ginger and garlic paste, and sauté for another 2–3 minutes. Pour in 1 cup of full-fat milk and ½ cup of water, season with salt to taste, and bring the mixture to a gentle boil. Reduce the heat to low, cover, and let it simmer for 25–30 minutes or until the meat is tender and the milk has thickened slightly into a light gravy. Stir occasionally to prevent the milk from scorching. Once cooked, garnish with a sprinkle of freshly ground nutmeg or black pepper (optional) and serve hot with plain bhaat or flatbread.

To prepare Barisal-style Dudh Paturi, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup coconut milk, 1 teaspoon jaggery, and a pinch of salt in a bowl to form a smooth mixture. Divide this mixture among 4 medium-sized banana leaves. Optionally, sprinkle some chopped nuts or roasted sesame seeds on top. Wrap each banana leaf and steam for 10–12 minutes or cook on low heat in a pan until the milk mixture sets into a soft custard-like texture. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves or fresh coconut and serve hot.

To prepare Dudh Paturi (Chattogram), start by heating 1 liter of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan and bringing it to a gentle boil. Reduce the heat and simmer until it thickens slightly. Add ½ cup of sugar, 2–3 crushed green cardamom pods, and a small pinch of salt, stirring well. Pour a portion of the thickened milk onto a greased banana leaf, fold it carefully into a parcel, and steam the parcel over medium heat for 15–20 minutes until the milk sets into a soft, creamy pudding. Repeat with the remaining milk mixture. Serve the parcels warm, enjoying the subtle aroma of banana leaves combined with the sweet, creamy Dudh Paturi, a signature Chattogram-style dessert.

To prepare Dudh Paturi (Hill Tracts), start by heating 1 liter of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan, stirring frequently, and bringing it to a gentle boil. Reduce the heat and simmer until the milk thickens slightly. Add ½ cup of sugar, a pinch of salt, and 2 crushed cardamom pods, mixing well. Pour portions of the thickened milk onto greased banana leaves, fold them carefully into parcels, and steam over medium heat for 15–20 minutes until the milk sets into a soft, creamy pudding. Optionally, sprinkle a few crushed roasted sesame seeds or local nuts inside the parcels for added flavor. Serve warm, enjoying the rich, slightly nutty, and aromatic Hill Tracts-style Dudh Paturi.

To prepare Khulna-style Dudh Paturi, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup coconut milk, 1 teaspoon jaggery, and a pinch of salt in a bowl to form a smooth mixture. Divide this mixture among 4 medium-sized banana leaves. Optionally, sprinkle some chopped nuts or sesame seeds on top. Wrap each banana leaf and steam for 10–12 minutes or cook covered in a pan on low heat until the milk mixture sets into a soft custard-like texture. Before serving, garnish with a little fresh coconut or chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

Garnish with chopped coriander leaves or fresh coconut and serve hot.

To prepare Tribal-style Dudh Paturi, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup coconut milk, 1/2 teaspoon jaggery, and a pinch of salt to form a smooth mixture. Wrap each banana leaf, cover, and steam on low heat for 10–12 minutes or cook in a pan until the milk mixture sets into a soft custard-like texture. Garnish with local herbs or chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Barisal-style Dudh Polao, rinse 2 cups of basmati or long-grain rice and soak for 20 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons of ghee or oil in a pan, add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon ground cardamom for tempering. Sauté 1 medium chopped onion until light brown. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup coconut milk, 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and a little sugar to create a milk-based mixture. Combine this mixture with the soaked rice, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes until the rice is soft and aromatic. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves or nuts and serve hot.

To prepare Chattogram-style Dudh Polao, rinse 2 cups of basmati or long-grain rice and soak for 20 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons of oil or ghee in a pan, add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon ground cardamom for tempering. Sauté 1 medium chopped onion until light brown. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup coconut milk, 1/2 teaspoon salt, 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, and a little sugar to make a milk-based mixture. Combine this mixture with the soaked rice, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes until the rice is soft and aromatic. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves or roasted nuts and serve hot.

To prepare Tribal-style Dudh Polao, rinse 2 cups of basmati or long-grain rice and soak for 20 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil in a pan, add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon ground cardamom for tempering. Sauté 1 medium chopped onion until light brown. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup coconut milk, 1/2 teaspoon salt, 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, and a little jaggery to make a milk-based mixture. Garnish with finely chopped local herbs or coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Dudh Steamed, a simple and beloved Barisal-style milk pudding, begin by boiling 1 liter of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat, stirring continuously until it reduces slightly and thickens for a creamier texture. Once thickened, let it cool to a lukewarm state. In a separate bowl, whisk 3 large eggs with ½ cup of sugar until smooth and frothy, then slowly add the cooled milk while stirring to form a uniform custard mixture. Add ½ teaspoon of cardamom powder and, if desired, a few drops of rose water for aroma. Pour the mixture into a greased steel bowl or heatproof dish, cover it tightly with foil or a lid, and place it in a steamer. Steam gently for 25–30 minutes, or until the custard is set and a toothpick inserted comes out clean. Let it cool slightly before unmolding, and garnish with chopped nuts or raisins if preferred. This soft and delicate dessert is best served chilled after a meal.

To prepare traditional Dhaka-style Dudh Steamed, start with 500 ml of fresh full-fat milk. Pour the milk into a heavy-bottomed pan and bring it to a boil over medium heat, stirring occasionally to prevent burning.

Once the milk starts boiling, reduce the heat to low. Add 2 tablespoons sugar (adjust to taste) and ½ teaspoon cardamom powder. Stir gently and continue simmering until the milk thickens slightly. For Dhaka-style richness, you can also whisk in 1–2 tablespoons of cream or khoya (optional).

Pour the thickened milk mixture into a heatproof bowl or small containers. Cover and steam over medium heat for 10–12 minutes until the milk sets into a soft, custard-like consistency.

Serve warm or chilled for an authentic Dhaka-style Dudh Steamed experience.

To prepare a unique Hill Tracts-style dish that is steamed with milk, you can make a flavorful fish or chicken steamed in coconut milk, which is a more authentic interpretation. Start by marinating small pieces of fish or chicken with a paste made from dani morich (bird's eye chilies), ginger, garlic, and salt. For the "milk," prepare a rich coconut milk by blending fresh coconut with a little water and straining it. In a steamer, or in a pot using the traditional hebaang method of wrapping in a banana leaf, layer the marinated fish or chicken pieces with slices of onion and some freshly cut bamboo shoots. Pour the thick coconut milk over the mixture. Cover the steamer and cook for 20-25 minutes until the fish or chicken is tender and has absorbed the flavors of the coconut milk and spices. This dish is rich, slightly spicy, and creamy, and is a perfect accompaniment to steamed rice.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Dudh Steamed, boil 3 eggs and peel them. In a bowl, mix 1/2 cup thick milk, 1/2 teaspoon salt, 1/2 teaspoon jaggery, and a pinch of black pepper to form a smooth mixture. Pour this mixture into a steaming dish and place the boiled eggs on top. Cover and steam over boiling water for 12–15 minutes until the milk mixture sets into a soft custard-like texture. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice or flatbread.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Dudh Steamed, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup coconut milk, a pinch of salt, and 1/2 teaspoon jaggery in a bowl. Pour the mixture into a banana leaf wrap or a heatproof steaming dish, cover, and steam over boiling water for 15–20 minutes on low heat until the milk gently sets into a soft, pudding- or custard-like consistency. Optionally, sprinkle a little roasted sesame seeds or lightly toasted nuts on top before serving. This simple, naturally flavored dish can be enjoyed either with plain steamed rice or as a light standalone dessert.

To prepare Tribal-style Dudh Steamed, mix 1 cup thick milk with 1/2 cup fresh coconut milk, a pinch of salt, and 1/2 teaspoon jaggery in a bowl. Pour the mixture into a banana leaf wrap or a heatproof steaming dish, cover, and steam over boiling water for 15–18 minutes until the milk gently sets into a soft, pudding-like texture. For added flavor, lightly sprinkle roasted sesame seeds or rice flour on top before serving. This simple, naturally flavored dish is enjoyed either as a light standalone item or alongside plain steamed rice.

To prepare Hill Tracts–style Dudh Stuffed, begin by making lengthwise slits in 6 medium green chilies or local hill gourds and gently hollowing the centers. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup coconut milk, 1 tablespoon roasted rice flour, 1/2 teaspoon ginger paste, a pinch of salt, and 1/2 teaspoon jaggery to form a mildly sweet, thick stuffing. Fill the vegetables with this milk-based mixture. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan or stone pot, add 1 dried red chili and a pinch of wild cumin, then arrange the stuffed vegetables, cover, and cook on low heat for 12–15 minutes, turning occasionally until the filling sets and develops a subtle smoky aroma. Finish with a sprinkle of local herbs or coriander leaves and serve hot with plain steamed rice.

To prepare Khulna-style Dudh Stuffed, begin by making lengthwise slits in 6 medium green chilies or pointed gourds and gently hollowing the centers. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 2 tablespoons thick coconut milk, 1 tablespoon roasted gram flour, 1/2 teaspoon ginger paste, a pinch of salt, and 1/2 teaspoon sugar to form a smooth, mildly sweet stuffing. Fill the vegetables with this milk-based mixture. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and 1 dried red chili, then arrange the stuffed vegetables in the pan. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally until the coconut–milk filling sets and the vegetables are tender. Finish with a light sprinkle of garam masala and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Dudh Stuffed, begin by making lengthwise slits in 6 medium green chilies or pointed gourds and gently hollowing the center. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 1/2 cup fresh chhena, 1 tablespoon roasted gram flour, 1/2 teaspoon ginger paste, a pinch of salt, and 1/2 teaspoon sugar to form a soft, smooth stuffing. Fill the vegetables with this milk-based mixture. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and 1 dried red chili, then arrange the stuffed vegetables in the pan. Cover and cook on medium-low heat for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally until the filling sets and the vegetables are cooked through. Finish with a light sprinkle of garam masala and chopped green chilies, and serve hot with plain steamed rice.

To prepare Sylheti-style Dudh Stuffed, begin by making lengthwise slits in 6 medium green chilies or small eggplants, gently hollowing the center. In a bowl, mix 1 cup thick milk, 2 tablespoons khoya, 1 tablespoon roasted gram flour, 1/2 teaspoon ginger paste, a pinch of salt, and 1/2 teaspoon sugar to form a smooth stuffing. Fill the vegetables with this milk-based mixture. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and 1 dried red chili, then arrange the stuffed vegetables in the pan. Cover and cook on low heat for 8–10 minutes, turning occasionally, until the filling sets and the outer surface turns lightly golden. Finish with a sprinkle of 1/2 teaspoon garam masala and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Dudh Tok in the Rangpur style, begin by whisking 1 cup of slightly sour milk or yogurt until smooth. Heat 1 tablespoon mustard oil in a pan and add 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and 2 dried red chilies for tempering. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until softened. Lower the heat and mix in 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder and salt to taste with a little water to prevent burning. Slowly add the whisked milk, stirring continuously to avoid curdling. Pour in 1/2 cup water along with 1 tablespoon tamarind water or a few raw mango pieces, then simmer gently for 5–7 minutes until the curry becomes mildly sour and smooth. Remove from heat and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Gur Bhuna in the Barisal style, break 1 cup of date palm jaggery into small pieces. Heat 1 tablespoon mustard oil in a pan and add 1/2 cup grated coconut along with 1 tablespoon sesame seeds, roasting gently on low heat until aromatic. Add the jaggery and stir continuously so it melts and combines evenly with the coconut and sesame. For balanced flavor, add a pinch of salt and 1/4 teaspoon cardamom powder, continuing to cook until the mixture becomes thick and semi-dry. Remove from heat, allow to cool slightly, and serve.

To prepare Gur Bhuna in the Hill Tracts style, break 1 cup date palm or cane jaggery into small pieces. Heat 1 tablespoon local oil or ghee in a pan. Add 1/2 cup grated coconut and roast slowly on low heat until the coconut becomes lightly dry and aromatic. Add the jaggery and stir continuously so it melts and blends evenly with the coconut. For added aroma, mix in 1/4 teaspoon cardamom powder and a little finely chopped ginger. Cook until the mixture becomes thick and dry. Remove from heat and serve once slightly cooled.

To prepare Gur Bhuna in the Mymensingh style, break 1 cup date palm jaggery into small pieces. Heat 1 tablespoon ghee in a pan. Add 1/2 cup grated coconut and sauté on low heat until lightly golden and aromatic. Add the jaggery and stir continuously so it melts and blends well with the coconut. For extra flavor, add 1/2 teaspoon finely chopped ginger and 1/4 teaspoon cardamom powder. Cook until the mixture thickens and starts to release a little ghee. Turn off the heat and serve warm or at room temperature.

To prepare Gur Dry in the Barisal style, break 1 cup date palm jaggery or cane jaggery into small pieces. Heat 1 tablespoon ghee or coconut oil lightly in a pan. Add 1/2 cup grated coconut and sauté on low heat until the coconut becomes lightly dry and aromatic. Add the jaggery and stir continuously so it melts and coats the coconut evenly. For flavor, add 1/4 teaspoon cardamom powder. Cook until the mixture becomes thick and dry. Turn off the heat and allow it to cool slightly before serving.

To prepare Gur Dry (Mymensingh), start by heating 500 grams of jaggery (gur) with ½ cup of water in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat until it melts completely. Strain the liquid to remove impurities. Continue cooking the jaggery syrup on low heat, stirring frequently, until it thickens and reaches a semi-dry consistency with a slightly sticky texture. Optionally, add ½ teaspoon of cardamom powder for aroma. Once thickened, pour the mixture onto a greased tray or plate and allow it to cool slightly. Serve as a rich, aromatic, and mildly sweet Mymensingh-style Gur Dry dessert.

To prepare Gur Dry (Rajshahi), start by heating 500 grams of jaggery (gur) with ½ cup of water in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat until it melts completely. Strain the syrup to remove impurities, then continue cooking on low heat, stirring frequently, until it thickens and reaches a semi-dry, slightly sticky consistency. Add ½ teaspoon of cardamom powder or a small pinch of nutmeg for a subtle aromatic flavor, characteristic of Rajshahi-style desserts. Pour the thickened jaggery mixture onto a greased tray or plate and allow it to cool slightly before serving. Enjoy as a rich, sweet, and fragrant traditional Gur Dry treat.

To prepare Gur Dry (Rangpur), start by heating 500 grams of jaggery (gur) with ½ cup of water in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat until it melts completely. Strain the syrup to remove any impurities, then continue cooking on low heat, stirring frequently, until it thickens to a semi-dry, slightly sticky consistency. Add ½ teaspoon of crushed green cardamom or a pinch of roasted cumin powder for the signature Rangpuri aroma. Pour the thickened jaggery mixture onto a greased tray or plate and allow it to cool slightly. Serve as a rich, aromatic, and traditional Rangpur-style Gur Dry dessert.

To prepare Gur Dry (Tribal), start by heating 500 grams of jaggery (gur) with ½ cup of water in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat until it melts completely. Strain the syrup to remove any impurities, then continue cooking on low heat, stirring frequently, until it thickens to a semi-dry, slightly sticky consistency. For a traditional Tribal touch, add ½ teaspoon of crushed roasted sesame seeds or a small pinch of local spices for aroma. Pour the thickened jaggery mixture onto a greased tray or plate and allow it to cool slightly. Serve as a rich, aromatic, and mildly sweet Tribal-style Gur Dry dessert.

To prepare Gur Fry (Barisal), begin by breaking 400–500 grams of soft jaggery (gur) into small pieces. Heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan over low heat, then add the jaggery and let it melt slowly, stirring continuously. Add 2–3 tablespoons of water to help dissolve the gur evenly, and continue cooking on low heat until it thickens slightly and turns glossy. Stir in a pinch of salt and ½ teaspoon of crushed cardamom for aroma, allowing the mixture to gently fry until it reaches a smooth, sticky, semi-liquid consistency without becoming dry. Remove from heat and let it cool slightly before serving. This Barisal-style Gur Fry is rich, aromatic, and deeply caramelized, traditionally enjoyed as a rustic sweet treat.

To prepare Gur Fry (Khulna), start by breaking 400–500 grams of soft jaggery (gur) into small pieces. Heat 2 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan over low heat, then add the jaggery and let it melt slowly while stirring continuously. Add 2–3 tablespoons of water to help dissolve the gur evenly, and continue cooking on low heat until it thickens slightly and develops a glossy texture. Stir in a pinch of salt and ½ teaspoon of crushed cardamom or a pinch of roasted sesame seeds for the signature Khulna aroma. Allow the mixture to gently fry until it reaches a smooth, sticky, semi-liquid consistency. Remove from heat, let it cool slightly, and serve warm as a rich, caramelized Khulna-style sweet delicacy.

To prepare a traditional Rajshahi-style Gur Pitha, a sweet treat that involves frying and a jaggery glaze, start by making the dough by mixing 1 cup of rice flour with a pinch of salt and enough warm water to form a soft, pliable dough; rest it for 15 minutes. For the sweet filling, cook 1 cup of grated coconut with ½ cup of crushed jaggery until the mixture thickens and becomes sticky. Now, take small balls of the rice flour dough, flatten each into a small disc, place a spoonful of the coconut-jaggery filling in the center, and fold the edges to form a half-moon shape, sealing them well. Alternatively, you can use a different shape like a Gokul Pitha, which is typically round. Heat a pan with enough oil to deep fry. Fry the prepared pithas on medium heat until they are golden brown on both sides. In a separate pot, melt about 1 cup of jaggery with ½ cup of water to create a thin syrup. Once the pithas are fried, immediately dip them into the warm jaggery syrup, ensuring they are well-coated. Remove them and let them cool slightly before serving.

To prepare Gur Grilled (Chattogram), start by breaking 400–500 grams of soft jaggery (gur) into small pieces and dissolving it in ½ cup of water over low heat in a heavy-bottomed pan, stirring until fully melted and smooth. Strain the syrup to remove impurities. Pour the jaggery mixture onto a greased flat tray or banana leaf and allow it to cool slightly until it thickens but is still pliable. Cut into square or rectangular portions, lightly brush with ghee, and grill on a hot tawa or grill pan until both sides develop a light caramelized crust. Serve warm as a rich, aromatic, and slightly smoky Chattogram-style Gur Grilled dessert.

To prepare Gur Jhol (Barisal), start by breaking 400–500 grams of soft jaggery (gur) into small pieces and dissolving it in 2 cups of water over low heat in a heavy-bottomed pan, stirring until fully melted and smooth. Strain the syrup to remove any impurities. Add ½ teaspoon of crushed cardamom or a small pinch of ground cinnamon for aroma. Simmer gently on low heat for 5–7 minutes until the mixture thickens slightly but remains pourable, forming a sweet, syrupy consistency. Serve warm or at room temperature as a traditional Barisal-style lightly sweetened and aromatic jaggery syrup, perfect as a dessert or to drizzle over other treats.

Simmer gently on low heat for 5–7 minutes until the mixture thickens slightly but remains pourable, forming a sweet, syrupy consistency. To prepare Gur Khichuri (Chattogram), start by washing 1 cup of rice and ½ cup of moong dal (split yellow lentils) thoroughly and soaking them for 15–20 minutes. Drain well. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds, 2–3 green chilies, and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, sautéing until aromatic. Add the drained rice and dal, stirring gently to coat with the spices. Dissolve 100 grams of jaggery (gur) in ½ cup of water and pour the syrup over the rice and dal mixture. Add 2½ cups of water and a pinch of salt, bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat, cover, and simmer until the rice and dal are cooked and the mixture is creamy and slightly sweet. Finish with a drizzle of ghee before serving hot as a traditional Chattogram-style Gur Khichuri.

To prepare Dhaka-style Gur Khichuri, wash 1 cup of moong dal and dry roast it until golden and fragrant, then wash 1 cup of atop rice or kalijira rice and keep aside. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons of ghee, add 2 bay leaves, 2 cardamom pods, 2 cloves, and a small cinnamon stick, then stir in the roasted dal and rice, frying gently for 3–4 minutes. Pour in 4 cups of hot water, add ½ teaspoon turmeric and a pinch of salt, and cook covered on low heat until the rice and dal are soft and fluffy. Finally, stir in ½ cup of liquid date palm jaggery (gur) or grated solid jaggery, letting it melt and blend into the khichuri to give a sweet, rich flavor. Serve warm as a winter comfort dish, often paired with fried eggplant or pickles.

To prepare Gur Khichuri (Mymensingh), start by washing 1 cup of rice and ½ cup of moong dal (split yellow lentils) thoroughly and soaking them for 15–20 minutes. Drain well. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds, 2–3 green chilies, and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, sautéing until aromatic. Add the drained rice and dal, stirring gently to coat with the spices. Dissolve 100 grams of jaggery (gur) in ½ cup of water and pour the syrup over the rice and dal mixture. Add 2½ cups of water and a pinch of salt, bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat, cover, and simmer until the rice and dal are cooked and the mixture is creamy and slightly sweet. Finish with a drizzle of ghee before serving hot as a traditional Mymensingh-style Gur Khichuri.

To prepare Gur Korma (Khulna), start by cleaning and cutting 500 grams of mutton or beef into medium-sized pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 1 finely sliced onion, and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, cooking until aromatic. Reduce the heat and stir in ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the meat and bhuna thoroughly until the spices coat it evenly and the oil begins to separate. Dissolve 2–3 tablespoons of jaggery (gur) in ½ cup of warm water and pour over the meat, then add 1–1½ cups of milk and simmer on low heat until the meat is tender and the gravy turns rich, mildly sweet, and glossy. Finish with ½ teaspoon of garam masala and a drizzle of ghee before serving hot as a fragrant Khulna-style Gur Korma.

To prepare Gur Paturi (Barisal), start by heating 1 liter of full-cream milk in a heavy-bottomed pan until it comes to a gentle boil. Reduce the heat and simmer until the milk thickens slightly. Add 100–150 grams of jaggery (gur), stirring constantly until fully dissolved, along with 2–3 crushed green cardamom pods for aroma. Grease banana leaves or a heatproof tray lightly with ghee, pour portions of the milk-jaggery mixture onto them, and fold into parcels if using leaves. Steam the parcels over medium heat for 15–20 minutes until the mixture sets into a soft, creamy pudding. Serve warm as a rich, aromatic Barisal-style Gur Paturi dessert.

To prepare Gur Polao (Hill Tracts), start by washing 2 cups of fragrant rice (such as basmati) and soaking it for 20–30 minutes. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons of sesame oil or mustard oil, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds, 2–3 whole green cardamoms, 2–3 cloves, and a small cinnamon stick, sautéing until aromatic. Drain the rice and add it to the pan, stirring gently to coat with the oil and spices. Dissolve 150 grams of jaggery (gur) in ½ cup of water over low heat and pour this syrup over the rice. Add 2½ cups of water and a pinch of salt, bring to a boil, then reduce the heat, cover, and simmer until the rice is cooked and has absorbed the jaggery flavor, forming a slightly sweet, fragrant Hill Tracts-style Gur Polao. To prepare Gur Steamed (Chattogram), start by breaking 400–500 grams of soft jaggery (gur) into small pieces and dissolving it in ½ cup of water over low heat in a heavy-bottomed pan, stirring until fully melted and smooth. Strain the syrup to remove any impurities. Grease a heatproof tray or small bowls lightly with ghee, pour in the jaggery syrup, and place them in a steamer. Steam over medium heat for 15–20 minutes until the mixture sets into a firm yet slightly sticky texture. Optionally, sprinkle a few crushed roasted sesame seeds or a pinch of cardamom powder for added aroma before steaming. Serve warm or at room temperature as a traditional Chattogram-style steamed jaggery dessert.

To prepare Gur Stuffed (Barisal), begin by dissolving 150 grams of grated jaggery (gur) in 2–3 tablespoons of water over low heat until it melts into a thick filling, then set aside to cool. In a bowl, mix 2 cups of rice flour with a pinch of salt and gradually add warm water to form a soft, pliable dough. Divide the dough into small balls, flatten each one, place a spoonful of the jaggery filling in the center, and carefully seal and shape into round or oval dumplings. Steam the stuffed dumplings for 12–15 minutes until cooked through, then lightly brush with ghee and shallow-fry on a pan until the outside turns lightly golden and aromatic. Serve warm as a sweet, comforting Barisal-style Gur Stuffed delicacy.

To prepare Gur Tok (Chattogram), start by slicing 2–3 medium-sized eggplants (begun) into thin rounds or small pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste, sautéing briefly to release the aroma. Add the eggplant slices and cook on medium heat until they become soft and slightly browned. Dissolve 2–3 tablespoons of jaggery (gur) in a small splash of water and pour over the cooked eggplants, stirring gently to coat evenly. Simmer for 5–7 minutes until the mixture thickens and the gur melds with the spices, forming a sweet and tangy semi-dry dish. Garnish with fresh coriander leaves and serve hot as a traditional Chattogram-style Gur Tok.
