Marinate the fish with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, a pinch of salt, and 1 teaspoon sesame oil for 15–20 minutes. Preheat a grill pan or oven to medium-high heat. Lightly brush the fish pieces with sesame oil and place them on the grill. Cook for 5–7 minutes on each side, or until the fish is cooked through, slightly charred, and aromatic. Optionally, sprinkle a few crushed roasted local spices for extra flavor. Serve hot as a traditional Hill Tracts-style Ilish Grilled dish.

To prepare Ilish Grilled (Khulna), start by cleaning 500 grams of hilsa fish (ilish) and cutting it into medium-sized pieces. Marinate the fish with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, a pinch of salt, and 1 teaspoon mustard oil for 15–20 minutes. Preheat a grill pan or oven to medium-high heat. Lightly brush the fish pieces with mustard oil and place them on the grill. Cook for 5–7 minutes on each side, or until the fish is cooked through, slightly charred, and aromatic. Optionally, sprinkle a few crushed roasted spices like cumin or black pepper for extra flavor. Serve hot as a traditional Khulna-style Ilish Grilled dish.

To prepare Ilish Grilled (Sylhet), start by cleaning 500 grams of hilsa fish (ilish) and cutting it into medium-sized pieces. Marinate the fish with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, a pinch of salt, and 1 teaspoon mustard oil for 15–20 minutes. Preheat a grill pan or oven to medium-high heat. Lightly brush the fish pieces with mustard oil or ghee and place them on the grill. Cook for 5–7 minutes on each side, or until the fish is cooked through, slightly charred, and aromatic. Optionally, sprinkle a few crushed roasted spices like cumin or black pepper for extra flavor. Serve hot as a traditional Sylhet-style Ilish Grilled dish.

To prepare Ilish Grilled (Tribal), start by cleaning 500 grams of hilsa fish (ilish) and cutting it into medium-sized pieces. Marinate the fish with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, a pinch of salt, and 1 teaspoon sesame oil for 15–20 minutes, reflecting the Tribal preference for light, earthy flavors. Preheat a grill pan or open charcoal grill to medium-high heat. Lightly brush the grill and the fish pieces with sesame oil, then grill for 5–7 minutes on each side until the fish is cooked through, lightly charred, and aromatic. Avoid heavy spices to keep the natural flavor of hilsa prominent. Serve hot as a traditional Tribal-style Ilish Grilled dish.

To prepare Ilish Jhol (Barisal), start by cleaning 500 grams of hilsa fish (ilish) and cutting it into medium-sized pieces. Lightly marinate the fish with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and a pinch of salt for 10 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until it reaches a smoky point, then carefully add the fish pieces and lightly fry for 1–2 minutes on each side; remove and set aside. In the same oil, add 1 finely sliced onion and sauté until soft, followed by 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1–2 slit green chilies. Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, stirring briefly. Pour in 2–2½ cups of water and bring to a gentle boil. Add the lightly fried hilsa pieces back into the pan and simmer on low heat for 6–8 minutes until the gravy is light, fragrant, and infused with mustard oil aroma. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and serve hot as an authentic Barisal-style Ilish Jhol.

To prepare Ilish Jhol (Hill Tracts style), clean 500 grams of hilsa (ilish) fish and cut into medium pieces. Lightly marinate the fish with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and a pinch of salt for about 10 minutes.

Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a deep pan until it reaches smoking point, then reduce the heat. Gently fry the fish pieces until lightly golden on both sides and remove them from the pan.

In the same oil, add 2 crushed green chilies and, if available, a small amount of hill herbs or wild coriander (optional but traditional). Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and stir briefly. Pour in 2–2½ cups of water and bring to a gentle boil. Season with salt to taste.

Carefully add the fried fish back into the gravy and simmer for 6–8 minutes on low heat until the broth becomes light, aromatic, and slightly mustardy. Finish with ½ teaspoon mustard oil drizzled on top.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Hill Tracts–style Ilish Jhol experience.

To make traditional Khulna-style Ilish Jhol, begin by cleaning and washing 6–8 pieces of fresh hilsa (ilish) fish thoroughly, then lightly rub them with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and ½ teaspoon salt and keep aside for 5 minutes. Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a deep pan until it reaches smoking point to remove its sharp raw flavor, then reduce the heat to medium. Carefully add the hilsa pieces and lightly fry them for about 1–2 minutes per side—just enough to seal the fish without overcooking. Remove the fish and keep aside.

In the same oil, add 1 teaspoon mustard seeds and 2–3 dried green chilies, letting them splutter to release their aroma. Add 1 medium onion (thinly sliced, optional but common in Khulna style) and sauté until lightly translucent. Then add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon salt (adjust to taste), and 1 tablespoon mustard paste (made from soaked mustard seeds and green chilies). Sauté the spices gently for 1–2 minutes, being careful not to burn the mustard.

Pour in 2 cups of hot water and bring the gravy to a gentle boil. Once the broth starts simmering, carefully slide the fried hilsa pieces back into the pan. Cover and cook on low heat for 8–10 minutes, allowing the fish to absorb the mustardy, pungent flavors typical of Khulna-style jhol. Avoid stirring too much to prevent breaking the delicate fish. Finish with 2–3 slit green chilies for aroma, then turn off the heat.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for the most authentic experience.

To make traditional Rajshahi-style Ilish Jhol, start by cleaning and washing 6–8 pieces of fresh hilsa (ilish) fish, then lightly marinate them with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and ½ teaspoon salt for about 5 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a deep pan until lightly smoking, then reduce the heat and gently fry the fish pieces for 1 minute per side—just enough to firm them. Remove and keep aside.

In the same oil, add ½ teaspoon nigella seeds (kalojira) and 2 dried red chilies, allowing them to crackle and release their aroma. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and ½ teaspoon salt, stirring briefly on low heat. Now add 1 medium potato, cut into medium wedges (a signature element of Rajshahi-style jhol) and sauté for 2–3 minutes so the potatoes absorb the spices.

Pour in 2 to 2.5 cups of hot water, cover, and cook until the potatoes are nearly tender. Once the potatoes are soft, gently place the fried hilsa pieces into the gravy. Cover again and let everything simmer on low heat for 8–10 minutes, allowing the fish and potatoes to blend with the light, comforting broth. Add 2–3 slit green chilies toward the end for fragrance. Avoid stirring vigorously to keep the fish intact.

Turn off the heat once the gravy remains thin and clear, which is characteristic of Rajshahi-style ilish jhol. Serve hot with plain steamed rice.

To prepare Ilish Jhol (Sylhet), start by cleaning 500 grams of hilsa fish (ilish) and cutting it into medium pieces. Lightly marinate the fish with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and a pinch of salt for about 10 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee in a pan until hot. Add 1 finely sliced onion and sauté until soft and lightly golden, then add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1–2 slit green chilies, stirring until aromatic. Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Pour in 2–2½ cups of water and bring to a gentle boil. Carefully add the hilsa pieces and simmer on low heat for 6–8 minutes until the fish is cooked and the jhol remains light and slightly spicy, characteristic of Sylhet cuisine. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil or ghee and serve hot with steamed rice as a traditional Sylhet-style Ilish Jhol.

To make traditional Barisal-style Ilish Khichuri, begin by washing 1 cup of coarse rice (chal) and ½ cup split moong dal separately, then soaking them together for 10 minutes and draining well. Cut 4–5 pieces of hilsa fish (ilish) and lightly rub them with salt and ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, then shallow-fry them in 2 tablespoons of mustard oil until lightly golden. Set aside.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat the remaining mustard oil (add 1 more tablespoon if needed) until it reaches smoking point, then reduce the heat. Add 1 medium onion thinly sliced and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1–1½ teaspoons red chili powder, and ½ teaspoon ground cumin. Sauté gently for 2–3 minutes until aromatic.

Add the soaked rice and dal, stirring well so they are evenly coated with the spices. Pour in 4½–5 cups of hot water and add salt to taste (about 1½ teaspoons). Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat to low and cook uncovered for 15–18 minutes until the rice and dal are soft and slightly mushy.

Gently place the fried hilsa pieces on top of the khichuri, add 2–3 slit green chilies, cover, and cook on very low heat for another 5–7 minutes so the hilsa flavor infuses the khichuri. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil for the signature Barisal aroma.

Serve hot with lemon wedges, green chili, or simple vegetable bharta, as traditionally enjoyed in Barisal households.

To prepare traditional Dhaka-style Ilish Khichuri, start by washing and soaking 1½ cups of aromatic rice (kalijira or chinigura) and ½ cup of moong dal together for about 15–20 minutes, then drain and keep aside. Clean and cut 500 grams of fresh hilsa (ilish) fish into medium pieces, rub lightly with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and a pinch of salt, and shallow-fry the pieces in 3 tablespoons of mustard oil until just lightly golden; remove and keep aside.

In the same heavy-bottomed pot, add 2 tablespoons more mustard oil if needed and heat gently. Add 2 dried red chilies, 2 bay leaves, 4 green cardamoms, 1 cinnamon stick, and 4 cloves, allowing them to release their aroma. Add 1 large finely sliced onion and sauté until soft and lightly golden. Stir in 1 tablespoon ginger paste, then add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1½ teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and about 1½ teaspoons salt, cooking the spices for 2–3 minutes until fragrant.

Add the soaked rice and dal mixture to the pot and stir gently for 3–4 minutes so the grains are well coated with the spices. Pour in about 5 cups of hot water, mix carefully, and let it cook uncovered over medium heat. When the rice and dal are about 70% cooked and the mixture has a thick, porridge-like consistency, gently place the fried ilish pieces on top. Drizzle 1 teaspoon ghee over the khichuri, cover the pot, and cook on low heat for another 10–12 minutes, allowing the hilsa flavor to infuse into the khichuri.

Once done, turn off the heat and let it rest covered for 5 minutes. Gently mix before serving, being careful not to break the fish pieces. Serve hot with fried eggplant, beguni, green chili, and a squeeze of lemon for an authentic Dhaka experience.

To prepare Hill Tracts-style Ilish Khichuri, clean and wash 4–5 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Rinse and soak 1 cup atap rice and 1/2 cup red lentils together. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pot, add 2 dried chilies, 2 bay leaves, and 1 teaspoon crushed cumin seeds. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until lightly golden. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and salt to taste. Add the washed rice and lentils, sauté for 2–3 minutes, then add 3 cups hot water and cook covered on medium heat. When the khichuri is half cooked, place the hilsa pieces on top, cover, and simmer for another 10–12 minutes until the rice and lentils are soft and the fish flavor infuses the dish. Serve hot.

To prepare Khulna-style Ilish Khichuri, clean and wash 4–5 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Rinse and soak 1 cup atap rice and 1/2 cup red lentils together. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pot, add 2 dried chilies, 2 bay leaves, and 1 teaspoon crushed cumin seeds. Add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until lightly golden. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and salt to taste. Add the washed rice and lentils, sauté for 2–3 minutes, then add 3 cups hot water and cook covered on medium heat. When the khichuri is half cooked, add the hilsa pieces, 2–3 slit green chilies, and a little mustard paste, cover, and simmer for another 10–12 minutes until soft and aromatic. Serve hot.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Ilish Khichuri, clean and wash 4–5 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Rinse and soak 1 cup atap rice and 1/2 cup red lentils together. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pot, add 2 bay leaves, 2 dried chilies, and 1 teaspoon crushed cumin seeds. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until lightly golden. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and salt to taste. Add the washed rice and lentils, sauté well for 2–3 minutes, then add 3 cups hot water and cook covered on medium heat. When the khichuri is half cooked, place the hilsa pieces on top, cover, and simmer for another 10–12 minutes until the rice and lentils are soft and aromatic. Serve hot.

To prepare Chattogram-style Ilish Korma, clean and wash 5–6 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 3 green cardamoms, and a 1-inch cinnamon stick to release aroma. Add 2 tablespoons onion paste and sauté until lightly golden. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Once the spices are well cooked, gently mix in 1/2 cup yogurt. Carefully place the hilsa pieces into the gravy, cover, and cook on very low heat for 8–10 minutes. When the gravy thickens and oil rises, remove from heat and serve hot with steamed rice or polao.

To prepare Dhaka-style Ilish Korma, clean and wash 5–6 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Heat a mixture of 3 tablespoons ghee and mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 4 green cardamoms, and a 1-inch cinnamon stick to release aroma. Add 2 tablespoons onion paste and slowly sauté until golden. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Once the spices are well cooked, gradually mix in 1/2 cup yogurt. Gently place the hilsa pieces into the gravy, cover, and cook on very low heat for 8–10 minutes. When the gravy thickens and ghee aroma rises, remove from heat and serve hot with steamed rice or basmati polao.

To prepare Khulna-style Ilish Korma, clean and wash 5–6 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 3 green cardamoms, and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for tempering. Add 2 tablespoons onion paste and sauté slowly until lightly golden. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. When the spices are well cooked, gradually mix in 1/2 cup yogurt. Gently place the hilsa pieces into the gravy, cover, and cook on very low heat for 8–10 minutes. Once the gravy thickens and mustard oil aroma rises, remove from heat and serve hot with steamed rice or polao.

To prepare a traditional Mymensingh-style Ilish Korma, a rich and creamy Hilsa fish curry, start with 500g of fresh Ilish fish, cut into medium-sized steaks. In a large pan, heat 3 tablespoons of ghee or oil. Add 2 bay leaves, 2 cardamom pods, and a small cinnamon stick, frying briefly until fragrant. Now, add 1 large sliced onion and fry until it turns golden. Add 1 tablespoon of ginger-garlic paste and cook until the raw smell disappears. Add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste, stirring well. Now, add the fish pieces and gently cook them on both sides for a minute. In a separate bowl, whisk together ½ cup of thick yogurt and ½ cup of milk, and then pour this mixture into the pan. Bring the curry to a gentle simmer, cover the pan, and let it cook on low heat for 10-12 minutes, or until the fish is tender and the gravy has thickened to a rich, creamy consistency. Finish by garnishing with a few green chilies before serving hot with pulao or rice.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Ilish Korma, clean and wash 5–6 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 2 green cardamoms, and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for tempering. Add 2 tablespoons onion paste and sauté slowly until lightly brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. When the spices are well cooked, gradually mix in 1/2 cup yogurt. Gently place the hilsa pieces into the gravy, cover, and cook on very low heat for 8–10 minutes. Once the gravy thickens and releases a soft aroma, remove from heat and serve hot with steamed rice or polao.

To prepare Rangpur-style Ilish Korma, clean and wash 5–6 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 3 green cardamoms, and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for tempering. Add 2 tablespoons onion paste and sauté lightly until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Once the spices are well cooked, gradually mix in 1/2 cup yogurt. Gently place the hilsa pieces into the gravy, cover, and cook on low heat for 8–10 minutes. When the gravy thickens and the fish becomes tender, remove from heat and serve hot with steamed rice or polao.

To prepare Sylhet-style Ilish Korma, clean and wash 5–6 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 3 cardamoms, and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for tempering. Add 2 tablespoons onion paste and sauté lightly until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Once the spices are well cooked, gradually mix in 1/2 cup yogurt. Gently place the hilsa pieces into the gravy, cover, and cook on low heat for 8–10 minutes. When the gravy thickens and the fish becomes tender, remove from heat and serve hot with steamed rice or polao.

To prepare Barisal-style Ilish Paturi, clean and wash 4–5 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Lightly season the fish with salt. For the stuffing, mix 2 tablespoons mustard paste, 1 teaspoon chopped green chilies, and 1 teaspoon fresh yogurt into a smooth paste. Spread this mixture gently over the fish. Wrap the fish pieces in banana leaves or pati leaves and steam on low heat for 8–10 minutes until the fish is tender and the spices are infused. Serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare traditional Dhaka-style Ilish Paturi, start by cleaning 4 medium pieces (about 400 g) of fresh hilsa fish and patting them dry. Prepare a spice paste by grinding 3 tablespoons of mustard seeds (or using ready mustard paste) with 1 tablespoon of poppy seeds, 3–4 green chilies, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon salt, and 4 tablespoons of mustard oil into a smooth mixture; add a splash of water if necessary to make a thick paste. Coat the fish pieces thoroughly with this paste and let them marinate for 15–20 minutes. Meanwhile, prepare 4 large banana leaves by lightly heating them over an open flame or hot pan to make them pliable. Place each marinated fish piece with some spice paste onto a banana leaf, add a slit green chili on top, and fold the leaf into a tight parcel; secure with kitchen thread or toothpicks. In a heavy-bottomed pan, arrange the parcels, drizzle with 1–2 teaspoons of mustard oil, and cook on very low heat, covered, for 15–20 minutes, flipping once halfway through, until the fish is tender and infused with mustard aroma. Alternatively, the parcels can be steamed in a steamer for 20 minutes. Once cooked, carefully unwrap the banana leaves and serve the ilish hot with steamed rice.

Begin with 500 grams of fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium-sized steaks. Wash and pat dry. Prepare a spice paste by grinding together 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 2 tablespoons grated coconut, 2 green chilies, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, and a pinch of salt until smooth.

Spread large, cleaned banana leaves over a flat surface and lightly heat them to make them pliable. Place each hilsa piece on a banana leaf and coat generously with the mustard-coconut spice paste. Fold the leaf to fully enclose the fish and secure it with kitchen twine or toothpicks.

In a wide, heavy-bottomed pan, add a few tablespoons of water and place a steamer rack or small bowl to keep the wrapped fish above water. Arrange the banana leaf parcels on the rack, cover the pan tightly, and steam over medium-low heat for 15–20 minutes, until the fish is fully cooked and infused with the aromatic paste.

Serve hot, directly in the banana leaves for a rustic presentation, optionally garnished with a few mustard seeds fried in mustard oil for added aroma. Traditionally, this is enjoyed with plain rice.

Start with 500 grams of fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks. Wash and pat dry carefully. In a small bowl, prepare a paste with 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 2 tablespoons grated coconut, 1–2 green chilies (adjust to taste), 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, 1 teaspoon sugar, and ½ teaspoon salt. For Khulna style, adding a touch of raw mango paste (1 teaspoon) enhances the tangy coastal flavor. Grind or pound into a smooth mixture.

Take large banana leaves and warm them gently over fire or hot water to make them pliable. Spread the spice paste evenly over each fish piece and wrap securely in the banana leaf, folding the edges tightly.

Place the wrapped fish in a steamer or on a shallow layer of water in a heavy-bottomed pan, ensuring the parcels do not touch the water. Cover tightly and cook on medium-low heat for 12–15 minutes, until the fish is fully cooked and aromatic.

Serve hot, directly in the banana leaves for an authentic experience. Garnish with a few fried mustard seeds or sliced green chilies for extra fragrance. Traditionally paired with plain steamed rice.

Take 500 grams of fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks. Wash thoroughly and pat dry. Prepare a spice paste by grinding 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 1–2 green chilies (adjust to taste), 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, 1 tablespoon yogurt, ½ teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon poppy seeds (optional, a Rangpur specialty). Mix into a smooth paste.

Warm large banana leaves gently to make them pliable. Spread the spice paste evenly on each fish piece and wrap securely in the banana leaf, folding edges tightly. Rangpur style often uses a slight touch of mustard oil on the leaf for extra aroma.

Place the parcels on a steaming rack or shallow water layer in a heavy-bottomed pan, ensuring they don’t touch the water. Cover tightly and steam on medium-low heat for 12–15 minutes until the fish is fully cooked and infused with the paste’s flavor.

Serve hot, directly in the banana leaf. Garnish with a few fried poppy seeds or sliced green chilies for an authentic Rangpur aroma. Traditionally served with plain rice.

Begin with 500 grams of fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks. Wash and pat dry gently. Prepare a spice paste by grinding 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 1–2 green chilies (adjust to taste), 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, 1 tablespoon tamarind pulp, and ½ teaspoon salt. Sylhet style often incorporates a slight tanginess with tamarind or a few drops of lemon juice.

Warm large banana leaves gently to make them pliable. Spread the paste evenly over each fish piece and wrap securely, folding the edges tightly. Optional: smear a little mustard oil over the leaf for added aroma.

Place the parcels on a steaming rack or shallow water layer in a heavy-bottomed pan, ensuring they don’t touch the water. Cover tightly and steam on medium-low heat for 12–15 minutes, until the fish is fully cooked and fragrant.

Serve hot, directly in the banana leaf. Garnish with a few fried mustard seeds or finely sliced green chilies for aroma. Traditionally paired with plain steamed rice.

Begin by washing and soaking 2 cups of basmati or kalijira rice for 20 minutes, then drain and set aside. Take 500 grams of fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks, wash, and pat dry. Marinate the fish with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon salt, and a few drops of mustard oil for 10 minutes.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil until slightly smoky. Fry 2 thinly sliced medium onions until golden brown. Add 2 tablespoons ginger-garlic paste and gently sauté. Add the marinated hilsa fish carefully and fry for 3–5 minutes on medium heat until lightly browned. Remove the fish and set aside.

In the same oil, add 2–3 whole spices (4–5 cloves, 2–3 green cardamoms, 1-inch cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf) and sauté for a few seconds. Add the soaked rice and lightly toast for 1–2 minutes. Pour in 3 cups of hot water, 1 teaspoon salt, and ½ teaspoon sugar. Place the fried hilsa gently on top of the rice, cover, and cook over low heat for 15–20 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and aromatic.

Once done, fluff the rice gently with a fork. Garnish with fried onions, a few green chilies, and a drizzle of mustard oil for authentic Barisal aroma. Serve hot.

Start by washing and soaking 2 cups of basmati or kalijira rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside. Take 500 grams of fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks, wash, and pat dry. Marinate with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon mustard oil for 10–15 minutes.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil until slightly smoky. Fry 2 medium thinly sliced onions until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 tablespoon garlic paste, sautéing lightly. Add the marinated hilsa fish gently and fry for 3–5 minutes until lightly browned. Remove the fish and set aside.

Add whole spices—3 cloves, 2 green cardamoms, 1-inch cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf, and 1 small star anise—to the oil and sauté briefly. Add the soaked rice and lightly toast for 1–2 minutes. Pour in 3 cups of hot water, 1 teaspoon salt, and ½ teaspoon sugar. Place the fried hilsa gently on top of the rice, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and infused with aroma.

Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and garnish with fried onions, a few green chilies, and fresh coriander for a coastal Chattogram touch. Serve hot.

Begin by washing and soaking 2 cups of basmati or kalijira rice for 20 minutes, then drain and set aside. Take 500 grams of fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks, wash, and pat dry. Marinate with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon salt, and ½ teaspoon mustard oil for 10 minutes.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil until slightly smoky. Fry 2 medium thinly sliced onions until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 tablespoon garlic paste, sautéing lightly. Add the marinated hilsa fish and fry gently for 3–4 minutes until lightly browned. Remove the fish and set aside.

Add whole spices—4 cloves, 2 green cardamoms, 1–inch cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf, and 1 black cardamom—to the oil and sauté briefly. Add the soaked rice and lightly toast for 1–2 minutes. Pour in 3 cups of hot water, 1 teaspoon salt, and ½ teaspoon sugar. Place the fried hilsa gently on top of the rice, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and aromatic.

Once done, fluff the rice gently and garnish with fried onions, a few green chilies, and a drizzle of mustard oil for authentic Dhaka aroma. Serve hot.

Start by washing and soaking 2 cups of basmati or kalijira rice for 20 minutes, then drain. Take 500 grams of fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks, wash, and pat dry. Marinate with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon mustard oil for 10–15 minutes.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil until slightly smoky. Fry 2 thinly sliced medium onions until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 tablespoon garlic paste, sauté briefly.

Add the marinated hilsa and fry gently for 3–5 minutes until lightly browned. Remove the fish and set aside. Add whole spices—3–4 cloves, 2 green cardamoms, 1-inch cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf—to the pan and sauté briefly.

Add the soaked rice and lightly toast for 1–2 minutes. Pour in 3 cups hot water, 1 teaspoon salt, and ½ teaspoon sugar. Place the fried hilsa gently on top of the rice, cover, and cook over low heat for 15–20 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and aromatic.

Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and garnish with fried onions and sliced green chilies. Serve hot.

Wash and soak 2 cups of kalijira or basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well. Take 500 grams fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks, wash gently, and pat dry. Marinate the fish with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon salt, and ½ teaspoon mustard oil for about 10 minutes.

Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot until just lightly smoky. Add 2 medium onions, thinly sliced, and fry until light golden (not dark, as Rajshahi cooking prefers mild color). Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, sauté briefly until fragrant.

Add the marinated hilsa and fry gently for 3–4 minutes until just sealed. Remove the fish carefully and keep aside. In the same oil, add whole spices—3 cloves, 2 green cardamoms, 1 small cinnamon stick, and 1 bay leaf—and sauté for a few seconds.

Add the soaked rice and stir gently for 1–2 minutes. Pour in 3 cups hot water, 1 teaspoon salt, and ¾ teaspoon sugar (a hallmark of Rajshahi style). Place the fried hilsa pieces gently on top of the rice. Cover tightly and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes until the rice is fluffy and aromatic.

Once done, rest the polao for a few minutes, then fluff gently. Garnish with fried onions and whole green chilies. Serve hot with plain salad or light bhorta.

Take 500 grams fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks. Wash gently and pat dry. In a bowl, prepare a smooth paste using 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 2–3 green chilies (Dhaka style is moderately hot), 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, and ½ teaspoon salt. Some Dhaka kitchens add 1 teaspoon poppy seeds for softness, but this is optional.

Coat the hilsa pieces evenly with the mustard paste. Take large banana leaves and warm them slightly over flame to make them flexible. Place the fish pieces on the leaves, drizzle a little extra mustard oil on top, and fold tightly to seal.

Arrange the wrapped fish in a steamer or on a rack placed inside a heavy pot with a small amount of water (ensuring the parcels do not touch the water). Cover tightly and steam on medium heat for 15–18 minutes until the fish is fully cooked and aromatic.

Serve hot directly in the banana leaves. Traditionally enjoyed with plain steamed rice, green chili, and a simple dal or bhorta.

Take 500 grams fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks. Wash gently and pat dry. Prepare a coarse paste using 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 3–4 green chilies (Hill Tracts style is slightly sharper), 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, ½ teaspoon salt, and optionally 1 teaspoon crushed wild herbs or local leaves traditionally used by hill communities.

Rub the paste evenly over the hilsa pieces. Instead of heavy banana-leaf wrapping, Hill Tracts cooking often uses thin banana leaves or turmeric leaves, lightly warmed for flexibility. Place the fish inside, drizzle a little mustard oil, and fold tightly.

Arrange the parcels in a bamboo steamer or on a raised rack inside a covered pot with minimal water. Steam on medium heat for 12–15 minutes until the fish is just cooked, tender, and aromatic.

Serve hot in the leaf wrapping, traditionally paired with plain rice or sticky rice, green chili, and a light fermented side if available.

Take 500 grams fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks. Wash gently and pat dry. Prepare a paste using 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 2–3 green chilies, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, ½ teaspoon salt, and 1–2 tablespoons sour yogurt (tok doi)—a hallmark of Mymensingh cooking that adds gentle tang without heaviness.

Coat the hilsa pieces evenly with the mustard–yogurt paste. Lightly warm banana leaves to make them flexible. Place the fish on the leaves, drizzle a little extra mustard oil on top, and fold tightly to seal.

Arrange the parcels in a steamer or on a rack inside a covered pot with minimal water, ensuring the parcels do not touch the water. Steam over medium heat for 15–18 minutes until the fish is tender and aromatic.

Serve hot in the banana leaves. Traditionally enjoyed with plain steamed rice, green chili, and simple dal or mashed vegetables.

Take 500 grams fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks. Wash gently and pat dry. Prepare a slightly coarse paste using 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 1–2 green chilies (Rangpur style is milder in heat), 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, ½ teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon poppy seeds (posto)—a common northern addition that softens the mustard sharpness.

Coat the hilsa pieces evenly with the mustard–poppy seed paste. Warm banana leaves lightly over flame to make them pliable. Place the fish pieces on the leaves, drizzle a few drops of mustard oil, and fold tightly.

Arrange the parcels on a rack inside a covered pot or steamer with a small amount of water, ensuring the fish does not touch the water. Steam over medium heat for 15–18 minutes until the fish is tender and aromatic.

Serve hot in the leaf wrapping. Traditionally paired with plain rice, green chili, and simple lentil dal or mashed potato bhorta.

Take 500 grams fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks. Wash gently and pat dry. Prepare a coarse paste using 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 3 green chilies (tribal style is sharper but clean), ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, and ½ teaspoon salt. In some tribal kitchens, a pinch of crushed wild leaves or fermented herbs is added for an earthy note.

Rub the paste evenly over the hilsa pieces. Instead of thick banana leaves, use thin banana leaves, turmeric leaves, or forest leaves, lightly warmed to make them flexible. Place the fish inside, drizzle a few drops of mustard oil, and fold securely.

Arrange the parcels in a bamboo steamer or on a raised rack inside a covered pot with minimal water. Steam over medium heat for 12–15 minutes until the fish is tender, moist, and fragrant.

Serve hot in the leaf wrapping. Traditionally eaten with plain rice or sticky rice, green chilies, and very simple sides, letting the fish remain the focus.

To prepare an authentic Barisal-style Ilish, which is often cooked with a rich mustard paste that can be considered a flavorful "stuffing," begin with a fresh, whole Ilish fish (about 1 kg). Cut it into large steaks or use it whole, cleaning it well. For the paste, soak 3 tablespoons of yellow mustard seeds, 1 tablespoon of black mustard seeds, 4-5 green chilies, and a pinch of salt in warm water for 15 minutes. Drain the water and grind the mixture into a smooth paste. In a large pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil and carefully arrange the fish steaks. Spread the prepared mustard paste evenly over the fish, ensuring it coats all sides. Add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Pour about 1 cup of water into the pan, or just enough to create a thick gravy. Cover the pan and cook on medium-low heat for 10-15 minutes, gently flipping the fish once to cook both sides. The key is to avoid overcooking the delicate fish. The final dish should have a rich, pungent gravy that clings to the fish.

Take 500 grams of fresh hilsa fish, preferably medium-sized steaks. Wash and pat dry. Make small slits in each piece to allow the stuffing to penetrate.

For the stuffing: Grind together 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 1 tablespoon grated coconut, 1–2 green chilies (adjust to taste), 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, 1 teaspoon poppy seeds (optional), ½ teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon sugar into a smooth paste. Some Dhaka versions also add ½ teaspoon chopped fresh coriander for aroma.

Stuff each hilsa steak carefully with the prepared paste. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until slightly smoky. Gently place the stuffed hilsa pieces in the pan. Cook on medium-low heat for 8–10 minutes on each side until the fish is fully cooked and the stuffing is aromatic. Avoid excessive stirring to prevent the fish from breaking.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice, garnished with a drizzle of mustard oil and a few fried mustard seeds for extra flavor.

Take 500 grams of fresh hilsa fish, cut into medium steaks. Wash and pat dry carefully. Make small slits on each fish piece for stuffing.

For the stuffing: Pound or grind together 2 tablespoons mustard seeds, 1 tablespoon grated coconut, 2–3 green chilies (adjust to taste), 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 tablespoon mustard oil, ½ teaspoon salt, and a pinch of dried red chili flakes. Hill Tracts style may also include a small handful of crushed wild herbs or leaves for a subtle earthy aroma.

Stuff each hilsa steak generously with the prepared paste. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until slightly smoky. Carefully place the stuffed hilsa in the pan and cook on low to medium heat for 8–12 minutes on each side until the fish is fully cooked and the stuffing is aromatic. Avoid excessive stirring to keep the fish intact.

Serve hot, preferably with plain rice or steamed sticky rice. Garnish with a drizzle of mustard oil and a few fried mustard seeds for authentic Hill Tracts aroma.

To prepare Tribal-style Ilish Stuffed, clean and wash 4–5 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Make a deep slit in the middle of each fish for stuffing. For the stuffing, mix 2 tablespoons chopped onion, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste into a smooth paste. Fill this mixture into the slits of the fish. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan and cook the stuffed hilsa pieces on low heat for 8–10 minutes, covered, until the fish is cooked through and the spices are infused. Serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Barisal-style Ilish Tok, clean and wash 5–6 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 2 dried chilies and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds for tempering. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and salt to taste. Gently place the hilsa pieces into the pan and cook on low heat for 4–5 minutes. Then gradually mix in 1/2 cup sour yogurt or raw mango juice, cover, and simmer for another 5–7 minutes until the gravy turns lightly tangy and the fish becomes tender. Serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Khulna-style Ilish Tok, clean and wash 5–6 medium pieces of hilsa fish. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 2 dried chilies and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds for tempering. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, and salt to taste. Gently place the hilsa pieces into the pan and cook on low heat for 4–5 minutes. Then gradually mix in 1/2 cup sour yogurt or raw mango juice, cover, and simmer for another 5–7 minutes until the gravy turns lightly tangy and the fish becomes tender. Serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Kacchi Biryani, begin by marinating 1 kilogram of mutton pieces with 1 cup of yogurt, 3 tablespoons of ginger paste, 2 tablespoons of garlic paste, green chilies, 2 teaspoons of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon each of turmeric, coriander, and roasted cumin powder, 1 tablespoon of garam masala, ½ cup of fried onions, 4 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee, black pepper, and salt, then cover and refrigerate for 6 hours or overnight; meanwhile, wash and soak 1 kilogram of fragrant basmati or kalijira rice for 30 minutes and drain. In a heavy-bottomed pot greased with ghee, spread the raw marinated meat at the bottom, layer the soaked rice on top, sprinkle ½ cup of saffron or kewra-infused milk, add fried onions and drizzle more ghee, then seal the pot tightly with a lid and cook first on medium heat for 20 minutes before lowering to very gentle heat for 1.5 to 2 hours until the meat is tender and the rice fully cooked; let it rest for 10 minutes, then gently fluff before serving hot with salad or raita.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut them into medium chunks. Soak briefly in water with a little turmeric to prevent discoloration, then rinse and drain. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until lightly smoking, then reduce the heat. Add 2 medium onions, finely sliced, and fry slowly until deep golden brown.

Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and sauté until fragrant. Stir in ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and 1 teaspoon salt. Add a splash of water to prevent burning and cook the spices until oil begins to separate.

Add the banana pieces and mix thoroughly so they are well coated with the spice mixture. Cook on medium heat for 5–7 minutes, gently stirring. Add ½ cup hot water, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes until the bananas are tender but hold their shape.

Uncover and bhuna on low heat, stirring carefully, until the gravy thickens and clings to the bananas with a glossy finish. Finish with ½ teaspoon garam masala and 1 teaspoon ghee for a Dhaka-style aroma.

Serve hot with steamed rice or luchi, often alongside simple dal or fried green chilies.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut them into thick chunks. Rinse and lightly rub with ½ teaspoon turmeric and ½ teaspoon salt. In a pan or earthen wok, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil or local forest oil until warm (not smoking). Add 2–3 dried red chilies and 1 lightly crushed green chili, letting them release aroma.

Add 1 small onion, thinly sliced (optional in some tribal kitchens), and sauté briefly until soft, not browned. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste and cook gently. Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and a pinch of coriander powder—no heavy spice layering.

Add the banana pieces and toss to coat. Sprinkle ¼–½ cup water, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes until tender. Uncover and bhuna slowly, stirring carefully, until the water evaporates and the bananas pick up a light smoky crust.

Finish with a few drops of mustard oil or crushed wild herbs if available. No garam masala is used. Salt is adjusted at the end.

Serve hot with plain rice or sticky rice, often accompanied by mashed chilies or simple boiled greens.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut them into medium wedges. Rinse and rub lightly with ½ teaspoon turmeric and ½ teaspoon salt. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until it reaches smoking point, then lower the heat. Add 2 dried red chilies and ½ teaspoon nigella seeds (kalojira), letting them crackle.

Add 2 medium onions, thinly sliced, and fry until light golden. Stir in 1 tablespoon ginger paste and ½ teaspoon garlic paste, cooking until aromatic. Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1–1½ teaspoons red chili powder (Khulna style is hotter), ½ teaspoon coriander powder, and 1 teaspoon salt. Splash in a little water and bhuna the spices until oil separates.

Add the banana pieces and toss well to coat. Cook uncovered for 5 minutes so they absorb the spices. Add ½ cup hot water, cover, and cook on low heat for 12–15 minutes until tender.

Uncover and bhuna on low heat until the gravy dries and clings tightly to the bananas with a sharp mustard aroma. Finish with ½ teaspoon mustard paste or a squeeze of lemon for Khulna’s characteristic tang.

Serve hot with steamed rice, often alongside dried fish bhorta or simple lentils.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut them into medium chunks. Rinse and lightly rub with ½ teaspoon turmeric and ½ teaspoon salt. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until just warm, not smoking. Add 1 teaspoon nigella seeds (kalojira) and 2 dried red chilies, letting them release aroma.

Add 1 medium onion, finely sliced, and sauté gently until soft and lightly translucent—no deep browning. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste and cook briefly. Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder (mild), ¼ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Sprinkle a little water and cook until the spices blend smoothly.

Add the banana pieces and toss well. Cover and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes, adding a few tablespoons of water only if needed, until the bananas are tender. Uncover and bhuna slowly until the moisture evaporates and the bananas are lightly coated in spice, without becoming dry or oily.

Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and 1–2 slit green chilies for aroma. No garam masala is used.

Serve hot with plain rice and thin lentil dal, sometimes alongside mashed pumpkin or greens.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut them into medium chunks. Rinse and lightly rub with ½ teaspoon turmeric and ½ teaspoon salt. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until warm.

Add 1 medium onion, finely sliced, and sauté gently until soft and lightly golden. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste and cook briefly. Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, ¼ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add a splash of water and cook the spices until aromatic.

Add the banana pieces and toss gently. Cover and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the bananas are tender. Uncover and bhuna carefully until the liquid evaporates and the bananas are coated lightly with the spiced oil.

Finish with a few drops of mustard oil for aroma and optionally a pinch of sugar for Rajshahi’s subtle sweetness.

Serve hot with plain rice or roti, often accompanied by simple lentils or mashed vegetables.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and lightly rub with ½ teaspoon turmeric and ½ teaspoon salt.

In a clay pot or heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil or local forest oil until warm (not smoking). Add 2–3 dried red chilies or wild chili peppers, letting them release aroma. In some tribal preparations, small leaves or wild herbs are also added for earthy flavor.

Add 1 small onion, sliced thinly (optional), and sauté briefly until softened. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste. Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and a pinch of salt. No heavy spice powders are typically used.

Add the banana pieces and toss gently. Cover and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes, adding a little water only if necessary, until the bananas are tender. Uncover and bhuna carefully so the moisture evaporates and the bananas are lightly coated with spiced oil.

Finish with a few drops of mustard oil or crushed local herbs for aroma. Serve hot with plain rice or sticky rice, often accompanied by green chilies or simple forest vegetables.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and lightly rub with ½ teaspoon turmeric and ½ teaspoon salt.

Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until slightly smoky. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste until aromatic.

Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Mix well. Add the banana pieces and toss to coat evenly with the spices.

Cook uncovered on medium-low heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the bananas are tender but still hold their shape. For Barisal style, keep the dish relatively dry—most of the water should evaporate, leaving a lightly spiced coating on the bananas.

Finish with a few drops of mustard oil and optionally garnish with fried onions or green chilies. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Dhaka-style Kacha Kola Dry, peel 4–5 green bananas, cut them into thin cubes, and boil lightly in salted water for 3–4 minutes before draining. In a pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil, add ½ teaspoon of nigella seeds, 2 dried red chilies, and a few crushed garlic cloves, frying until fragrant, then add the parboiled green banana pieces and stir well. Sprinkle with 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste, cooking on medium heat while stirring gently so the pieces remain whole. Cover and cook for another 8–10 minutes on low heat until tender and coated with spices, finishing with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and fresh green chilies for aroma. Serve hot with plain rice and dal.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and lightly rub with ½ teaspoon turmeric and ½ teaspoon salt.

In a clay pot or heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil or local forest oil until warm. Add 2–3 dried red chilies (or local wild chilies) and sauté briefly for aroma.

Add 1 small onion, thinly sliced (optional) and sauté until soft. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste. Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and ½ teaspoon salt. Mix well.

Add the banana pieces and toss gently. Cover and cook on low heat for 12–15 minutes, adding a few tablespoons of water only if necessary, until the bananas are tender. Uncover and cook briefly until the dish is dry, leaving the bananas lightly coated with oil and spices.

Finish with a few drops of mustard oil or crushed local herbs for aroma. Serve hot with plain rice or sticky rice.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and lightly rub with ½ teaspoon turmeric and ½ teaspoon salt.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until warm and slightly smoky. Add 2 dried red chilies and ½ teaspoon nigella seeds (kalojira), letting them crackle briefly.

Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste. Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1–1½ teaspoons red chili powder, and salt to taste. Mix well.

Add the banana pieces and toss gently to coat with spices. Cover and cook on low heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the bananas are tender. Uncover and bhuna lightly until the dish is dry, leaving the bananas coated in aromatic oil.

Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil for fragrance. Serve hot with plain rice or dal.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and lightly rub with ½ teaspoon turmeric and ½ teaspoon salt.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until soft and light golden. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder (mild), and salt to taste. Mix well.

Add the banana pieces and toss gently to coat with the spices. Cover and cook on low heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the bananas are tender. Uncover and cook briefly until most moisture evaporates, leaving the bananas lightly coated in aromatic oil.

Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil for fragrance. Serve hot with plain rice or lentils.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and pat dry.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil or coconut oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking briefly until aromatic.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Mix well.

Add the banana pieces and stir-fry on medium heat for 12–15 minutes, turning occasionally, until the bananas are tender but slightly crisp on the edges. For Chattogram style, the dish may include a few drops of coconut milk for subtle aroma and richness.

Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil or coconut oil and optionally garnish with slit green chilies. Serve hot with plain rice or as a side dish.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and pat dry.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil until smoking point to remove rawness. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, stirring briefly.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Mix well.

Add the banana pieces and stir-fry on medium heat for 12–15 minutes, turning occasionally, until the bananas are tender but slightly crisp on the outside. For Dhaka style, keep the dish moderately dry with just enough oil to coat the bananas and spices.

Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and optionally garnish with slit green chilies. Serve hot with plain rice or as a side dish.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and pat dry.

Add the banana pieces and stir-fry on low-medium heat for 12–15 minutes, turning occasionally, until the bananas are tender but slightly firm. Avoid excessive oil; the dish should remain lightly coated and dry.

Finish with a few drops of mustard oil or crushed local herbs for aroma. Serve hot with plain rice or sticky rice.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and pat dry.

Prepare a marinade with 1 teaspoon mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon ginger paste. Coat the banana pieces evenly with this mixture.

Wrap each banana piece in banana leaves or keep unwrapped for direct grilling.

Grill the bananas over medium heat on a charcoal grill, tandoor, or stovetop grill pan for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally, until lightly charred, tender, and aromatic. If using banana leaves, steam lightly while grilling to prevent burning.

Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and optionally sprinkle with crushed green chilies or chopped coriander. Serve hot with plain rice or as a snack.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and pat dry.

Prepare a simple marinade with 1 teaspoon mustard oil, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon salt, and optionally a few crushed local chilies. Coat the banana pieces evenly with the mixture.

Wrap each banana piece in banana leaves (optional) or keep unwrapped for direct grilling.

Grill the bananas over medium heat on a charcoal grill, stovetop grill pan, or over an open flame for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally, until tender and slightly charred. If using banana leaves, lightly steam while grilling to prevent burning.

Finish with a few drops of mustard oil or crushed local herbs for aroma. Serve hot with plain rice or sticky rice.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and pat dry.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and set aside.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking briefly until aromatic.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Stir well.

Add the banana pieces and toss gently to coat with the spices. Pour in 2–2.5 cups hot water to make a thin curry (jhol) consistency. Cover and simmer on low heat for 12–15 minutes, until the bananas are tender.

Optionally, finish with a few drops of mustard oil and garnish with slit green chilies or chopped coriander. Serve hot with steamed rice.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and set aside.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until soft and lightly golden. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, stirring briefly until aromatic.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½–1 teaspoon red chili powder (mild), and salt to taste. Mix well.

Add the banana pieces and toss gently to coat with the spices. Pour in 2–2.5 cups hot water for a thin curry (jhol) consistency. Cover and simmer on low heat for 12–15 minutes, until the bananas are tender but intact.

Optionally, finish with a few drops of mustard oil and garnish with slit green chilies or chopped coriander. Serve hot with plain rice.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and set aside.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Wash 1 cup rice (preferably kalijira or basmati) and ½ cup lentils (moong dal) thoroughly and soak for 15–20 minutes.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking briefly until aromatic.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½–1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Mix well.

Add the banana pieces, soaked rice, and lentils. Pour in 3 cups hot water. Stir gently and bring to a boil. Reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer for 20–25 minutes, until the rice, lentils, and bananas are tender and slightly mushy, forming a creamy khichuri consistency.

Optionally, finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and garnish with fried onions or chopped coriander. Serve hot as a main dish, ideal for rainy days or festive occasions.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Wash 1 cup rice (local or kalijira) and ½ cup lentils (moong dal) thoroughly and soak for 15–20 minutes.

In a clay pot or heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil or local forest oil until warm. Add 1 small onion, thinly sliced (optional) and sauté lightly until soft. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and ½ teaspoon salt. Mix well.

Add the banana pieces, soaked rice, and lentils. Pour in 2.5–3 cups hot water. Cover and cook on low heat for 20–25 minutes, until the rice, lentils, and bananas are tender, forming a lightly creamy khichuri.

Finish with a few drops of mustard oil or crushed local herbs for aroma. Serve hot with plain rice or sticky rice, as a simple, hearty meal.

To prepare a delicious Mymensingh-style Kacha Kola Khichuri, a hearty and savory rice and lentil dish with raw bananas, begin by washing 1 cup of fragrant rice and ½ cup of moong dal (yellow split lentils); set them aside. Peel and chop 2 large raw bananas into small cubes and keep them in water to prevent discoloration. In a large pot, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil and fry the banana cubes until they are a light golden color, then remove them and set them aside. In the same oil, add 1 tablespoon of ginger-garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of cumin powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste, stirring until fragrant. Now, add the washed rice and moong dal to the pot and stir-fry for 2-3 minutes. Pour in 3.5 cups of hot water and bring the mixture to a boil. Reduce the heat to a low simmer, add the fried raw banana pieces, cover the pot tightly, and let it cook for 20-25 minutes, or until all the water is absorbed and the khichuri is tender. Serve this comforting and flavorful dish hot with a drizzle of ghee.

Peel 4–5 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Wash 1 cup of basmati or kalijira rice and soak for 20 minutes, then drain.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until soft. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, stirring briefly until aromatic.

Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Stir well. Add the banana pieces and sauté for 3–4 minutes.

Add the soaked rice and 2 cups hot water or light stock. Cover and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes until the rice and bananas are tender and the water is absorbed. For Rangpur style, keep the dish lightly spiced, with a subtle aromatic flavor rather than heavy masala.

Optional garnish: sprinkle fried onions or slit green chilies for aroma. Serve hot as a simple, comforting meal.

Peel 4–5 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Wash 1 cup basmati or kalijira rice and soak for 20 minutes, then drain.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until soft and lightly golden. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking briefly until aromatic.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Mix well, then add the banana pieces and sauté for 3–4 minutes.

Add the soaked rice and 2 cups hot water or light stock. For Sylhet style, optionally add 1–2 tablespoons yogurt or a few drops of lime juice for a gentle tang. Cover and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes, until the rice and bananas are tender and the liquid is absorbed.

Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and optionally garnish with fried onions or green chilies. Serve hot as a comforting meal with plain rice or light accompaniments.

Peel 4–5 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Wash 1 cup rice (preferably kalijira or local hill rice) and soak for 15–20 minutes, then drain.

In a heavy-bottomed clay pot or pan, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil or local forest oil until warm. Add 1 small onion, finely sliced (optional in tribal style) and sauté gently until soft. Add 1 teaspoon crushed garlic and 1 teaspoon grated ginger, stirring briefly.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and ½ teaspoon salt. Mix well, then add the banana pieces and sauté for 2–3 minutes.

Add the soaked rice and 2 cups hot water, or enough to just cover the rice and bananas. Cover and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes, stirring occasionally if needed, until the rice and bananas are tender and all water is absorbed.

Finish with a few drops of mustard oil or crushed local herbs for aroma. Serve hot, traditionally with plain rice or sticky rice, letting the natural flavor of banana and rice shine.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and set aside.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 tablespoon garlic paste, cooking briefly until fragrant.

Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Stir well.

Add ½ cup plain yogurt or coconut milk for creaminess, then gently fold in the banana pieces. Cover and cook on low heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the bananas are tender and coated in a rich, aromatic gravy.

Finish with ½ teaspoon garam masala and a drizzle of mustard oil for aroma. Serve hot with plain rice or paratha.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and set aside.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil until slightly smoky. Add 2 medium onions, thinly sliced, and sauté until deep golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 tablespoon garlic paste, cooking briefly until aromatic.

Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Stir well and lightly fry the spice mixture until fragrant.

Add ½ cup plain yogurt or a mixture of yogurt and cream for richness, then gently fold in the banana pieces. Cover and cook on low heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the bananas are soft and coated in the thick, flavorful gravy.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and set aside.

In a clay pot or heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil or local forest oil until warm (not smoking). Add 1 small onion, thinly sliced (optional in tribal cooking) and sauté lightly until soft. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, stirring briefly.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks. Rinse and set aside.

To prepare a traditional Barisal-style Kacha Kola Paturi, a delicious steamed parcel of raw banana, start by peeling and slicing 2 large raw bananas thinly; keep them in water to prevent discoloration. For the flavorful paste, grind 2 tablespoons of yellow mustard seeds, 1 tablespoon of grated coconut, 4-5 green chilies, and a pinch of salt, adding a little water to create a smooth paste. In a bowl, mix the sliced raw bananas thoroughly with the prepared mustard-coconut paste, along with a drizzle of mustard oil and a pinch of turmeric. For the authentic paturi method, place a generous portion of this mixture onto a large banana or pumpkin leaf, fold it carefully into a sealed parcel, and secure it with a string. Steam the parcels for 15-20 minutes over a pot of boiling water, or until the raw bananas are tender and the flavors have melded together. If you don't have a leaf, you can steam the mixture directly in a small covered bowl inside a steamer. Serve this pungent and wholesome side dish hot with rice.

To prepare Kacha Kola Paturi (Chattogram), start by peeling 4–5 raw green bananas and slicing them lengthwise into thick strips. In a bowl, mix 2 tablespoons of mustard oil, 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds paste, 2–3 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste. Coat the banana slices evenly with this spicy mustard mixture. Take banana leaves, lightly warm them to make them pliable, and wrap the seasoned banana slices tightly in the leaves, securing the edges with kitchen twine or toothpicks. Steam the wrapped parcels over medium heat for 20–25 minutes until the bananas are tender and infused with the aromatic spices. Serve hot as a traditional Chattogram-style mustard-flavored steamed banana dish.

To prepare Kacha Kola Paturi, a traditional Dhaka-style delicacy made with green bananas, start by peeling 3–4 medium-sized kacha kola (green bananas) and cutting them into thin slices or small cubes, then steaming or boiling them until just tender. Mash them coarsely and set aside. In a mixing bowl, combine the mashed green bananas with 3–4 tablespoons of mustard paste (made from soaked mustard seeds, green chilies, and a little salt), 2 tablespoons of grated coconut, 2 finely chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, salt to taste, and 2 tablespoons of mustard oil for aroma, mixing thoroughly into a spiced mash. Take cleaned banana leaves, cut into square pieces, and briefly heat them over an open flame or hot pan to make them pliable. Place portions of the mixture in the center of each leaf, fold into parcels, and secure with thread or toothpicks. Heat a flat pan or tawa, brush lightly with oil, and place the parcels on low heat, cooking covered for 10–12 minutes on each side until the flavors infuse and the paturi is aromatic. Serve hot with plain bhaat as a rustic and authentic side.

Peel 6–7 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and cut into medium chunks.

Wrap each banana piece individually in banana leaves, securing with kitchen twine or toothpicks.

Steam the wrapped bananas over medium heat for 12–15 minutes until tender. Optionally, for a smoky aroma, grill lightly over a low flame for 2–3 minutes after steaming.

Serve hot, directly in the banana leaves, with plain rice or as a side dish.

Peel 5–6 raw green bananas (kacha kola). Slit each banana lengthwise carefully, keeping one side intact to form a pocket. Lightly boil them in salted water for 5–6 minutes until slightly soft, then drain and set aside.

In a bowl, mix 2 tablespoons mashed banana pulp (from the inner part), 1 tablespoon mustard oil, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add 1 tablespoon crushed onion and a little fresh coriander if desired. Mix into a thick stuffing paste.

Stuff this mixture gently inside each slit banana.

In a pan, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil. Place the stuffed bananas carefully in the pan and shallow-fry on low heat, turning gently, for 10–12 minutes, until lightly golden on all sides and fully tender.

Optionally, sprinkle a little hot water and cover for 2–3 minutes to steam-finish the inside.

Finish with a few drops of mustard oil and garnish with slit green chilies or coriander. Serve hot with plain rice and dal.

Peel 5–6 raw green bananas (kacha kola) and slit each lengthwise, keeping one side intact to create a pocket. Parboil them in lightly salted water for 5–6 minutes until just tender, then drain and let cool.

In a bowl, mix 2 tablespoons mashed banana, 1½ tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, ½ teaspoon garlic paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste.
Add 1 tablespoon finely chopped onion, ½ teaspoon crushed mustard seeds, and 1–2 teaspoons lime juice or tok doi (sour yogurt) for the characteristic Sylheti tang.

Stuff the mixture gently into each banana slit.

Heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil in a wide pan. Place the stuffed bananas carefully and cook on low heat, turning gently, for 10–12 minutes until lightly golden and aromatic. Sprinkle 2–3 tablespoons hot water, cover, and let steam for 3–4 minutes so the stuffing flavors fully infuse the bananas.

Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and garnish with slit green chilies. Serve hot with plain rice or soft bhaat, ideally with a light dal.

Peel 5–6 raw green bananas and make a deep lengthwise slit in each, keeping one side intact; parboil in lightly salted water for 4–5 minutes until just tender, then drain and cool. Prepare the stuffing by mixing mashed banana with mustard or sesame oil, crushed garlic and ginger, salt, finely chopped wild or spring onion, crushed green chilies, and a small amount of roasted sesame seeds or ground peanuts for a nutty, earthy flavor. Stuff the mixture into the banana slits, wrap tightly in banana leaves, and traditionally roast over charcoal or an open flame for 12–15 minutes until lightly charred and soft inside; alternatively, shallow-fry gently in oil, sprinkle a little water, cover, and steam-finish for a few minutes. Finish with a few drops of mustard oil and serve hot with plain rice or boiled tubers, yielding a minimally spiced, smoky tribal-style dish.

Peel and cut 5–6 raw green bananas into medium chunks and parboil them in lightly salted water until just tender, then drain. In a pan, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil and sauté chopped onion until soft, adding slit green chilies and a pinch of turmeric with minimal red chili for mild heat. Add the boiled banana pieces and stir gently so they absorb the oil and spices. Pour in water to make a light, thin gravy and season with salt. The signature Barisal sourness is added using tamarind water or raw mango pieces, sometimes finished with a splash of lime juice, giving the dish its refreshing tang. Let it simmer briefly until the flavors balance—soft banana, gentle heat, and sharp sourness—then finish with a drizzle of mustard oil. Serve hot with plain steamed rice as a light, palate-cleansing tok.

Peel and cut 5–6 raw green bananas into medium pieces and parboil them in lightly salted water until just tender, then drain. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan and sauté sliced onion with crushed garlic and slit green chilies until aromatic, adding a pinch of turmeric and a little red chili for moderate heat. Add the boiled banana pieces and toss gently so they coat with the spices, then pour in enough water to form a light, soupy gravy. The Chattogram-style sourness comes from tamarind water or dried sour plums, sometimes balanced with a touch of sugar for a subtle sweet-sour note. Simmer briefly until the bananas soften and the broth turns tangy and fragrant, finish with a drizzle of mustard oil, and serve hot with plain rice as a sharp, comforting tok.

Peel and cut 5–6 raw green bananas into medium pieces and parboil them in lightly salted water until just tender, then drain. Heat mustard oil in a pan and sauté sliced onion until lightly browned, adding crushed garlic, slit green chilies, and a pinch of turmeric with very little red chili. Add the boiled banana pieces and gently bhuna them so they absorb the mustard oil aroma, then pour in enough water to create a thin, clear gravy. The Khulna-style sourness comes mainly from tamarind water or dried tamarind, sometimes reinforced with a touch of green mango, giving a deep, lingering tang rather than sharp acidity. Simmer briefly until the flavors balance, finish with a final drizzle of mustard oil, and serve hot with plain rice as a light yet bold tok.

Peel and cut 5–6 green bananas into chunks and boil them in lightly salted water until soft but intact, then set aside. In a pan, heat a small amount of mustard oil and add dried red chilies and a pinch of panch phoron or kalojeera for aroma, followed by sliced onion sautéed until just translucent. Add turmeric and very mild chili, keeping spices minimal, then mix in the boiled bananas and enough water to make a thin, homely gravy. The sourness in Rangpur-style tok traditionally comes from tok doi (sour yogurt) or sometimes a splash of fermented rice water, giving a gentle, creamy tang rather than sharp acidity. To prepare a traditional Rajshahi-style Lau Dry or Lau Bhaji, a simple yet flavorful bottle gourd stir-fry, start by peeling and finely chopping a small bottle gourd (about 500g). In a pan, heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil and add ½ teaspoon of kalojeera (black cumin seeds) and 2-3 green chilies, letting them splutter for a few seconds. Add 1 small finely chopped onion and sauté until it becomes soft. Now, add the chopped bottle gourd, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, and salt to taste. Stir everything well, cover the pan, and cook on medium-low heat for 15-20 minutes. The bottle gourd will release its own water, which will help it cook. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking. Once the gourd is tender and the water has evaporated, creating a dry consistency, add a pinch of sugar or grated jaggery for a classic Rajshahi sweet-savory balance. Serve this light and delicious side dish hot with rice or roti.

Mix in 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, 1/2 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the bottle gourd and cook on medium heat for 5–7 minutes until soft and well-coated with the spices. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

Cover and cook on low heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lau softens and the water evaporates, leaving a light, dry texture. Add the lau cubes and pour in 2–2.5 cups of water or light stock to create a thin, flavorful gravy. Simmer on low heat until the lau is tender and infused with the nutty aroma of kalojeera. The Khulna-style lau jhol emphasizes bold mustard oil pungency and earthy, aromatic flavors while keeping the dish light and comforting. Serve hot with plain rice.

Peel and cube 500 g of bottle gourd (lau). Rinse 1 cup of rice and ½ cup of moong dal (split yellow lentils) and soak for 15–20 minutes. Heat mustard oil in a pan and lightly toast 2–3 teaspoons of kalojeera (black cumin) until fragrant. Add sliced onions, crushed garlic, and ginger, sautéing until soft and aromatic. Stir in turmeric, salt, and a few slit green chilies. Add the lau cubes, then drain and add the soaked rice and dal along with 3 cups of water or light stock. Cover and cook on low heat until the rice, dal, and lau are soft and creamy. The Barisal-style lau khichuri emphasizes mild, aromatic flavors with subtle nuttiness from kalojeera and the gentle pungency of mustard oil. Serve hot with fried or steamed vegetables.

Peel and dice fresh bottle gourd (lau), then rinse 1 cup of rice and ½ cup of moong dal and soak briefly. Heat mustard or coconut oil in a pan and temper with a little kalojeera, then add sliced onions, crushed garlic, and ginger, sautéing until soft and aromatic. Add the lau pieces, a pinch of turmeric, salt, and a few slit green chilies, stirring gently so the vegetables absorb the flavors. Drain the rice and dal, add them to the pan, and pour in 3–3½ cups of water or light stock. Cover and cook on low heat until the rice, dal, and lau are soft and creamy. The Chattogram-style lau khichuri is mildly spiced and soothing, highlighting the natural sweetness of bottle gourd with a light coastal aroma from the oil. Serve hot with fried vegetables or a simple bharta.
