Peel and cube 500 g of bottle gourd (lau) and set aside. Heat mustard or sesame oil in a pan and lightly toast 1–2 teaspoons of kalojeera (black cumin) until aromatic. Add sliced onions, crushed garlic, and ginger, sautéing gently until soft. Sprinkle a pinch of turmeric and salt, then add the bottle gourd cubes and stir to coat with the spices and oil. Pour in a small amount of water or light stock along with a few tablespoons of ground roasted nuts or coconut to create a mildly thickened, creamy gravy. Cover and simmer on low heat until the lau is tender and infused with the earthy, nutty aroma of kalojeera. The Tribal-style lau korma emphasizes simple, natural flavors with minimal spices, allowing the bottle gourd and kalojeera to shine. Serve hot with plain rice or steamed tubers.

Take 500 grams bottle gourd (lau), peel and cut into medium slices. Lightly rub with ½ teaspoon salt and set aside.

Prepare a spice paste with 1 tablespoon mustard seeds, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and 1 teaspoon mustard oil. Mix into a smooth paste.

Take banana leaves and warm them slightly over flame to make them pliable. Place a few bottle gourd slices on each leaf and spread the spice paste evenly over the pieces. Fold the banana leaves to seal the parcels tightly.

Steam the parcels over medium heat for 12–15 minutes, or until the bottle gourd is tender and infused with the aromatic spices.

Serve hot directly in the banana leaves with plain rice, optionally garnished with green chilies or a drizzle of mustard oil.

Take 500 grams bottle gourd (lau), peel and cut into medium slices. Lightly sprinkle ½ teaspoon salt and set aside.

Prepare a simple paste with 1 tablespoon mustard seeds, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, and a few crushed local chili peppers if available. Mix well with 1 teaspoon mustard oil.

Warm banana leaves lightly over flame to make them pliable. Place the bottle gourd slices on each leaf and spread the spice paste evenly. Fold the leaves to seal the parcels tightly.

Steam the parcels in a bamboo steamer or on a raised rack in a covered pot with minimal water for 12–15 minutes, until the bottle gourd is tender and aromatic.

Serve hot in the banana leaves with plain rice. Tribal style emphasizes the natural flavor of the gourd, so the spice paste is kept minimal.

Peel and grate 400 grams bottle gourd (lau). Wash 2 cups basmati or kalijira rice and soak for 20 minutes, then drain.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and fry until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking briefly until aromatic.

Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Mix well.

Add the grated bottle gourd and sauté for 5 minutes, letting it soften slightly. Then add the soaked rice and 3 cups hot water. Stir gently to combine.

Cover and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes, or until the rice is tender and the water is absorbed. Fluff gently with a fork before serving.

Serve hot with plain fried or steamed fish, or enjoy on its own as a light, aromatic meal.

Peel and grate 400 grams bottle gourd (lau). Wash 2 cups basmati or kalijira rice and soak for 20 minutes, then drain.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil or coconut oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and fry until light golden. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking briefly until aromatic.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Mix well.

Add the grated bottle gourd and sauté for 5–6 minutes until slightly softened. Then add the soaked rice and 3 cups hot water or light stock. For Chattogram style, optionally add 2 tablespoons coconut milk for subtle richness.

Cover and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes, or until the rice is tender and the water is absorbed. Fluff gently before serving.

Serve hot with fried fish or simple dal, or enjoy as a standalone aromatic meal.

Peel and grate 400 grams bottle gourd (lau). Wash 2 cups rice (preferably local hill rice or kalijira) and soak for 15–20 minutes, then drain.

In a clay pot or heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil or local forest oil until warm. Add 1 small onion, thinly sliced (optional), and sauté lightly until soft. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, cooking briefly.

Sprinkle ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and ½ teaspoon salt. Stir well. Add the grated bottle gourd and sauté for 3–5 minutes until slightly softened.

Add the soaked rice and 2–2.5 cups hot water, just enough to cook the rice fully. Cover and cook on low heat for 15–18 minutes, until the rice is tender and fluffy. Fluff gently before serving.

Serve hot with plain rice or sticky rice, letting the natural flavor of bottle gourd dominate. Tribal style emphasizes simplicity and minimal spices.

Serve hot with fried fish, dal, or plain rice, letting the slightly tangy mustard aroma shine.

Peel and grate 400 grams bottle gourd (lau). Wash 2 cups basmati or kalijira rice and soak for 15–20 minutes, then drain.

Serve hot with plain rice or simple lentils, letting the natural flavor of bottle gourd shine.

To prepare a traditional Chattogram-style Lau Steamed, start with 1 small lauki (bottle gourd), weighing about 500g. Peel the lauki and cut it into thin, small pieces. In a bowl, prepare a mixture by adding 1 tablespoon of finely chopped onion, 1 teaspoon of ginger-garlic paste, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, ½ teaspoon of red chili powder, 2-3 green chilies (slit), and salt to taste. Add the lauki pieces to this mixture and mix everything thoroughly to ensure the lauki is well-coated with the spices. In a steamer or a large pot with a steamer basket, place the spiced lauki. You can also add 2-3 small pieces of dried fish (shutki), if desired, for an authentic Chattogram flavor. Cover the pot and steam the lauki on medium heat for 20-25 minutes, or until it becomes tender. Once cooked, drizzle with 1 tablespoon of mustard oil for a final touch. Serve hot as a side dish with rice.

To prepare Lau Steamed (Dhaka style), begin by peeling and cutting 1 medium bottle gourd (lau) into medium-sized pieces. Lightly season with a pinch of salt and ½ teaspoon turmeric. Arrange the lau pieces in a steaming basket or a heatproof plate placed over boiling water. Steam on medium heat for 10–12 minutes, or until the lau becomes tender but still holds its shape. Optionally, drizzle 1 teaspoon mustard oil and sprinkle 1–2 chopped green chilies or fresh coriander on top before serving to enhance flavor. Serve hot as a light side dish with plain rice or dal.

To prepare Lau Steamed (Khulna style), begin by peeling and cutting 1 medium bottle gourd (lau) into medium-sized pieces. Lightly season with a pinch of salt and ½ teaspoon turmeric. Arrange the lau pieces in a steaming basket or on a heatproof plate over boiling water. Steam on medium heat for 10–12 minutes, or until the lau becomes tender while retaining its shape. For added Khulna-style flavor, drizzle 1 teaspoon mustard oil and sprinkle 1–2 chopped green chilies or fresh coriander on top before serving. Serve hot as a light side dish with plain rice or dal.

To prepare Lau Steamed (Mymensingh style), begin by peeling and cutting 1 medium bottle gourd (lau) into medium-sized pieces. Lightly season with a pinch of salt and ½ teaspoon turmeric. Arrange the lau pieces in a steaming basket or on a heatproof plate over boiling water. Steam on medium heat for 10–12 minutes, or until the lau is tender but still firm. For added Mymensingh-style flavor, drizzle 1 teaspoon mustard oil and sprinkle 1–2 chopped green chilies or fresh coriander on top before serving. Serve hot as a light side dish with plain rice or dal.

To prepare Lau Stuffed (Khulna style), begin by peeling and halving 1 medium bottle gourd (lau) lengthwise, then scoop out the seeds to create hollow boats. Prepare a stuffing with 2–3 tablespoons cooked moong dal, 1 small chopped onion, 1 teaspoon mustard paste, 1 teaspoon ginger-garlic paste, 1–2 chopped green chilies, a pinch of turmeric, and salt to taste. Fill the hollowed lau halves with the prepared stuffing. Heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil in a pan, place the stuffed lau carefully, cover, and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes, turning occasionally, until the lau is tender and the stuffing is infused with flavor. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare a unique Sylhet-style Lau Bhorta that serves as a rich, "stuffed" dish, start by peeling and finely chopping a small bottle gourd (about 500g). For the savory filling, heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan and add a handful of dried shrimp (chingri shutki), frying them for a minute. Now, add 1 large finely chopped onion, 1 tablespoon of ginger-garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste, stirring well. Add the chopped bottle gourd to this spicy mix, cover the pan, and cook on medium-low heat for 15-20 minutes. The gourd will release its own water and cook, absorbing the flavors of the shutki and spices. Stir occasionally until the water evaporates and the mixture becomes a thick, dry bhorta. Serve this intensely flavorful and savory "stuffed" dish hot with plain rice for an authentic taste of Sylhet.

To prepare Lau Stuffed (Tribal style), begin by peeling and cutting 1 medium bottle gourd (lau) into thick round or lengthwise pieces and scooping out a small portion from the center. Prepare a simple stuffing by mixing finely chopped onions, crushed garlic, green chilies, turmeric, a little red chili powder, salt, and 1–2 tablespoons mustard or local vegetable oil, keeping the flavors earthy and mild as typical of Tribal cuisine. Fill the hollowed lau pieces with the stuffing. Heat a little oil in a pan, place the stuffed lau pieces gently, cover, and cook on low heat, turning occasionally until the lau becomes tender and lightly caramelized and the stuffing is cooked through. Serve hot with plain rice as a light, wholesome dish.

To prepare Lau Tok (Mymensingh style), begin by peeling and cutting 1 medium bottle gourd (lau) into medium-sized cubes and rinsing them well. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1–2 chopped green chilies and a pinch of turmeric, and sauté briefly until aromatic. Add the lau pieces along with salt to taste and stir well, then pour in a small amount of water to help them soften. Cook covered on low to medium heat until the lau becomes tender. Finish by adding a mild souring agent such as tamarind water or a squeeze of lemon juice, adjust seasoning, and simmer for another minute to balance the sweet–sour flavor typical of Mymensingh-style tok. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Lau Tok (Rajshahi style), begin by peeling and cutting 1 medium bottle gourd (lau) into medium cubes and washing them well. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1–2 chopped green chilies and a pinch of turmeric, and sauté briefly until fragrant. Add the lau pieces with salt to taste and stir well, then add a small amount of water and cook covered on low heat until the lau becomes soft but still holds its shape. Finish by adding a mild souring agent such as tamarind water or lemon juice, adjust the seasoning, and simmer briefly to create the gentle sweet–sour balance characteristic of Rajshahi cuisine. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Lau Tok (Rangpur style), begin by peeling and cutting 1 medium bottle gourd (lau) into medium-sized cubes and rinsing them well. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1–2 chopped green chilies and a pinch of turmeric, and sauté lightly until aromatic. Add the lau pieces with salt to taste, stir well, and add a small amount of water, then cook covered on low heat until the lau becomes tender and slightly translucent. Finish by adding a gentle souring agent such as tamarind water or lemon juice, adjust seasoning, and simmer briefly to achieve the light, refreshing sourness typical of Rangpur-style tok. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Lau Tok (Sylhet style), begin by peeling and cutting 1 medium bottle gourd (lau) into medium-sized pieces and washing them well. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, and a pinch of turmeric, sautéing lightly until aromatic. Add the lau pieces with salt to taste, stir gently, and add a small amount of water, then cook covered on low heat until the lau becomes soft and tender. Finish by adding a mild souring agent such as tamarind water or lemon juice, adjust the seasoning, and simmer briefly to achieve the balanced, slightly tangy flavor typical of Sylhet cuisine. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Morog Polao, a signature Bangladeshi festive dish, start by washing 1 kilogram of chicken pieces and marinating them with ½ cup of yogurt, 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 2 teaspoons of roasted cumin powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 teaspoon of garam masala, 1 teaspoon of black pepper, 2 teaspoons of salt, and 2 tablespoons of mustard oil, leaving it for at least 1 hour. Meanwhile, wash and soak 4 cups of aromatic kalijira or basmati rice for 30 minutes. In a large heavy-bottomed pot, heat ½ cup of ghee and fry 2 medium-sized onions until golden brown, then add the marinated chicken and cook until lightly browned and fragrant. Remove the chicken pieces and in the same pot add the drained rice, frying gently in the remaining ghee and oil for 5–6 minutes. Return the chicken to the pot, then pour in about 8 cups of warm chicken stock or water, add whole spices like cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and bay leaves, and adjust salt to taste. Once it begins to boil, reduce heat to low, cover tightly, and cook for 20–25 minutes until the rice is fluffy and the chicken tender. Rest for 10 minutes, then gently fluff and serve hot with salad, cucumber raita, or borhani.

To prepare authentic Chattogram-style Mutton Bhuna, take 1 kilogram of mutton with bone and wash it thoroughly, then marinate it for at least 30 minutes with 3 tablespoons of ginger paste, 2 tablespoons of garlic paste, 2 teaspoons of Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1½ teaspoons of ground cumin, 1½ teaspoons of ground coriander, salt to taste, and ½ cup of thick yogurt so the meat absorbs the spices deeply; heat ½ cup of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until it reaches smoking point, reduce the heat slightly, and add 3–4 crushed dried red chilies and 2 bay leaves, followed by 3 large finely sliced onions, frying them slowly until they turn deep golden brown and aromatic, then add the marinated mutton and cook on high heat for 10–12 minutes while stirring continuously so the meat sears properly and releases its moisture, after which lower the heat and continue bhuna-style cooking by stirring and scraping the bottom of the pan until the oil separates clearly from the thick spice paste; add 1 teaspoon of freshly ground black pepper, 1 teaspoon of garam masala, and ½ teaspoon of mace–nutmeg powder, then splash in about ½ cup of hot water, cover, and simmer on low heat for 30–40 minutes until the mutton becomes tender and the gravy reduces to a rich, clinging masala, stirring occasionally to prevent burning; finish by adding 6–8 whole green chilies, a drizzle of extra mustard oil for the signature Chattogram aroma, and bhuna once more uncovered for 5–7 minutes until the meat is glossy, spicy, and intensely flavored, then rest for a few minutes before serving hot with rice or paratha.

To make traditional Mymensingh-style Mutton Bhuna, start with 1 kilogram of mutton, washed and cut into medium pieces, and marinate it for 30–45 minutes with 3 tablespoons of yogurt, 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1½ tablespoons of garlic paste, 2 teaspoons of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1½ teaspoons cumin powder, 1½ teaspoons coriander powder, and salt to taste so the flavors penetrate the meat; heat ½ cup of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until it smokes lightly, then add 3 finely sliced onions and fry slowly on medium heat until deep golden brown and caramelized, releasing a rich aroma, after which add the marinated mutton and stir on high heat for 10 minutes to sear the meat and lock in the juices; reduce the heat, cover partially, and continue cooking in bhuna style by stirring occasionally so the oil separates from the thick masala, then mix in ½ teaspoon of garam masala, 1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, and 4–5 whole green chilies, adding a splash of hot water if needed to prevent sticking, and simmer gently for 35–40 minutes until the meat is tender and the gravy thick, clinging to each piece, finally giving a final stir with a drizzle of mustard oil for the authentic Mymensingh aroma, and serve hot with plain rice or traditional flatbreads.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Mutton Bhuna, begin with 1 kilogram of mutton, cleaned and cut into medium pieces, and marinate it for 30–40 minutes with 3 tablespoons of yogurt, 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1½ tablespoons of garlic paste, 2 teaspoons of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1½ teaspoons cumin powder, 1½ teaspoons coriander powder, 1 teaspoon sugar, and salt to taste, allowing the spices and yogurt to tenderize and flavor the meat; heat ½ cup of mustard or vegetable oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until hot, add 3 sliced onions, and fry on medium heat until golden brown and aromatic, then add the marinated mutton and sauté on high heat for 10–12 minutes so the meat sears and moisture starts to release, lowering the heat afterward and cooking in true bhuna style by stirring frequently so the oil separates from the thick masala, then incorporate ½ teaspoon of garam masala, 1 teaspoon of black pepper, 4–5 whole green chilies, and a splash of hot water if needed, covering partially and simmering gently for 35–40 minutes until the meat is tender and the gravy becomes rich and clings to each piece, finishing with a drizzle of mustard oil and a few chopped fresh coriander leaves for the authentic Rajshahi aroma, served best with steamed rice or parathas.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Mutton Khichuri, take 500 grams of mutton, washed and cut into medium pieces, and marinate it for 20–30 minutes with 1½ tablespoons of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, ½ teaspoon garam masala, a pinch of sugar, and salt to taste so the spices fully penetrate the meat; heat ¼ cup of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until lightly smoking, add 2 sliced onions, and sauté on medium heat until golden brown and aromatic, then add the marinated mutton and sauté on high heat for 8–10 minutes to sear the meat and lock in its juices; add 1½ cups of washed basmati or long-grain rice and stir gently for 2–3 minutes so the rice is coated with the spices and oil, then pour in 4–5 cups of hot water or stock, 2–3 chopped tomatoes, 4–5 whole green chilies, and a handful of chopped coriander leaves, bring to a boil, reduce the heat, cover, and simmer gently for 25–30 minutes until the rice is cooked, the mutton is tender, and the dish has a slightly soupy, aromatic consistency characteristic of Mymensingh khichuri; serve hot with fried eggplant, papad, or pickles.

To prepare Rangpur-style Mutton Khichuri, take 500 grams of mutton, washed and cut into medium pieces, and marinate it for 20–30 minutes with 1½ tablespoons of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, ½ teaspoon garam masala, a pinch of sugar, and salt to taste so the spices penetrate the meat thoroughly; heat ¼ cup of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until lightly smoking, add 2 sliced onions, and sauté on medium heat until golden brown and aromatic, then add the marinated mutton and sauté on high heat for 8–10 minutes to sear the meat and lock in its juices; add 1½ cups of washed basmati or long-grain rice and stir gently for 2–3 minutes so the rice is coated with the spices and oil, then pour in 4–5 cups of hot water or stock, 2–3 chopped tomatoes, 4–5 whole green chilies, and a handful of chopped coriander leaves, bring to a boil, reduce the heat, cover, and simmer gently for 25–30 minutes until the rice is cooked, the mutton is tender, and the dish has a slightly soupy, aromatic consistency typical of Rangpur khichuri; serve hot with fried eggplant, papad, or pickles

To prepare Sylhet-style Mutton Khichuri, take 500 grams of mutton, washed and cut into medium pieces, and marinate it for 20–30 minutes with 1½ tablespoons of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, ½ teaspoon fennel powder, ½ teaspoon garam masala, a pinch of sugar, and salt to taste so the spices penetrate deeply into the meat; heat ¼ cup of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until lightly smoking, add 2 sliced onions, and sauté on medium heat until golden brown and aromatic, then add the marinated mutton and sauté on high heat for 8–10 minutes to sear the meat and lock in its juices; add 1½ cups of washed basmati or long-grain rice and stir gently for 2–3 minutes so the rice is coated with the spices and oil, then pour in 4–5 cups of hot water or stock, 2–3 chopped tomatoes, 4–5 whole green chilies, and a handful of chopped coriander and mint leaves, bring to a boil, reduce the heat, cover, and simmer gently for 25–30 minutes until the rice is tender, the mutton is cooked through, and the dish has a slightly soupy, aromatic consistency characteristic of Sylheti khichuri; serve hot with fried eggplant, papad, or pickles.

To prepare Tribal-style Mutton Khichuri, take 500 grams of mutton, washed and cut into medium pieces, and marinate it for 20–30 minutes with 1½ tablespoons of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon roasted cumin powder, 1 teaspoon roasted coriander powder, ½ teaspoon garam masala, a pinch of crushed black cardamom, and salt to taste so the meat absorbs the deep, earthy flavors; heat ¼ cup of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until lightly smoking, add 2 sliced onions, and sauté slowly on medium heat until golden brown and aromatic, then add the marinated mutton and sauté on high heat for 8–10 minutes to sear the meat and lock in its juices; add 1½ cups of washed long-grain or aromatic rice and stir gently for 2–3 minutes so the rice is coated with the spices and oil, then pour in 4–5 cups of hot water or stock, 2–3 chopped tomatoes, 4–5 whole green chilies, and a handful of chopped coriander leaves, bring to a boil, reduce the heat, cover, and simmer gently for 25–30 minutes until the rice is cooked, the mutton is tender, and the dish has a slightly soupy yet deeply aromatic consistency typical of Tribal khichuri; serve hot with fried eggplant, papad, or pickles.

To prepare Chattogram-style Mutton Korma, take 1 kilogram of mutton, washed and cut into medium pieces, and marinate it for at least 30 minutes with 3 tablespoons of thick yogurt, 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1½ tablespoons of garlic paste, 2 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1½ teaspoons cumin powder, 1½ teaspoons coriander powder, ½ teaspoon garam masala, a pinch of sugar, and salt to taste so the meat absorbs the rich spices; heat ½ cup of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until it begins to smoke lightly, add 3 finely sliced onions, and fry slowly on medium heat until golden brown and aromatic, then add the marinated mutton and sauté on high heat for 10–12 minutes to sear the meat and lock in the juices, reduce the heat, cover partially, and cook gently for 35–40 minutes, adding ½ cup of warm water or stock as needed to maintain a slightly thick, creamy consistency; toward the end, stir in ½ teaspoon garam masala, 1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, 1 tablespoon crushed roasted cashews for richness, and 4–5 whole green chilies, simmer for 5–7 minutes so the flavors meld, finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and a sprinkle of freshly chopped coriander for the signature Chattogram aroma, and serve hot with steamed rice or flatbreads.

To prepare Dhaka-style Mutton Korma, start with 1 kilogram of mutton, washed and cut into medium pieces, and marinate it for 30–40 minutes with 3 tablespoons of yogurt, 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1½ tablespoons of garlic paste, 2 teaspoons of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1½ teaspoons cumin powder, 1½ teaspoons coriander powder, ½ teaspoon garam masala, a pinch of cardamom powder, and salt to taste so the flavors penetrate the meat; heat ½ cup of mustard oil or ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan until hot, add 3 finely sliced onions, and fry on medium heat until deep golden brown and aromatic, then add the marinated mutton and sauté on high heat for 10–12 minutes to sear the meat and lock in the juices, after which reduce the heat, cover partially, and cook gently in its own masala for 35–40 minutes while stirring occasionally, adding ½ cup of warm water or stock as needed to maintain a rich, slightly creamy consistency; toward the end, stir in ½ teaspoon garam masala, 1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, 1 tablespoon crushed almonds or cashews for added richness, and 4–5 whole green chilies, simmer for 5–7 minutes so the flavors blend, finishing with a drizzle of ghee and a sprinkle of fresh coriander leaves for the signature Dhaka aroma, and serve hot with plain rice or parathas.

To make Hill Tracts–style Mutton Korma, begin with 1 kilogram of mutton, washed and cut into medium pieces, and marinate it for at least 30 minutes with 3 tablespoons of thick yogurt, 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1½ tablespoons of garlic paste, 2 teaspoons of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1½ teaspoons ground cumin, 1½ teaspoons ground coriander, a pinch of garam masala, and salt to taste so the meat absorbs the spices fully; heat ½ cup of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until smoking lightly, add 3 finely sliced onions, and fry slowly on medium heat until golden brown and deeply aromatic, then add the marinated mutton and sauté on high heat for 10–12 minutes so the meat sears and releases its natural juices, reduce the heat, cover partially, and cook gently in its own masala for 35–40 minutes while stirring occasionally, adding ½ cup of warm water or stock to maintain a slightly thick, creamy consistency; toward the end, mix in ½ teaspoon garam masala, 1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, 4–5 whole green chilies, and a handful of crushed roasted cashews for richness, simmer for 5–7 minutes to meld the flavors, and finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and a sprinkle of fresh coriander leaves for the signature Hill Tracts aroma, serving hot with steamed rice or flatbreads.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Mutton Korma, take 1 kilogram of mutton, washed and cut into medium pieces, and marinate it for 30–40 minutes with 3 tablespoons of yogurt, 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1½ tablespoons of garlic paste, 2 teaspoons of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1½ teaspoons cumin powder, 1½ teaspoons coriander powder, ¼ teaspoon nutmeg powder, ¼ teaspoon cardamom powder, and salt to taste so the spices deeply penetrate the meat; heat ½ cup of mustard oil or ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan until hot, add 3 finely sliced onions, and fry slowly until golden brown and fragrant, then add the marinated mutton and sauté on high heat for 10 minutes to sear the meat and seal in the juices, after which lower the heat, cover partially, and cook gently in its own gravy for 35–40 minutes while stirring occasionally, adding ½ cup of water or stock as needed to maintain a thick but creamy consistency; once the mutton is tender, stir in ½ teaspoon of garam masala, 1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, 1 tablespoon crushed cashews or almonds for richness, and 4–5 whole green chilies, simmer for another 5–7 minutes so the flavors meld, finishing with a drizzle of ghee and a sprinkle of chopped fresh coriander for the signature Mymensingh aroma, and serve hot with steamed rice or parathas.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, turmeric, ginger–garlic paste, and a touch of mustard oil. Heat mustard oil in a pan and lightly toast 2–3 teaspoons of kalojeera (black cumin) until aromatic. Add sliced onions, crushed garlic, and ginger, sautéing until soft and golden. Add the marinated mutton and cook on medium heat until lightly browned. Pour in a small amount of water or light stock along with ground roasted nuts or coconut to form a mildly thick, creamy gravy. Simmer gently on low heat until the mutton is tender and infused with the nutty, earthy aroma of kalojeera. The Rajshahi-style mutton korma emphasizes mild, homely flavors with gentle nuttiness from kalojeera and subtle mustard oil pungency. Serve hot with plain rice or polao.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, turmeric, ginger–garlic paste, and a touch of mustard oil. Heat mustard oil in a pan and lightly toast 2–3 teaspoons of kalojeera (black cumin) until aromatic. Add sliced onions, crushed garlic, and ginger, sautéing until soft and golden. Add the marinated mutton and cook on medium heat until lightly browned. Pour in a small amount of water or light stock along with ground roasted nuts or coconut to form a mildly thick, creamy gravy. Simmer gently on low heat until the mutton is tender and infused with the nutty, earthy aroma of kalojeera. The Sylhet-style mutton korma emphasizes aromatic depth with gentle pungency, producing a rich yet balanced dish. Serve hot with plain rice or polao.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, turmeric, ginger–garlic paste, and a touch of mustard or sesame oil. Heat oil in a pan and lightly toast 2–3 teaspoons of kalojeera (black cumin) until aromatic. Add sliced onions, crushed garlic, and ginger, sautéing until soft and golden. Add the marinated mutton and cook on medium heat until lightly browned. Pour in a small amount of water or light stock along with ground roasted nuts or coconut to form a creamy, lightly thickened gravy. Simmer gently on low heat until the mutton is tender and infused with the earthy, nutty aroma of kalojeera. The Tribal-style mutton korma emphasizes rustic, natural flavors with minimal spices, allowing the mutton and kalojeera to shine. Serve hot with plain rice.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, turmeric, ginger–garlic paste, and a touch of mustard oil for subtle flavor. Prepare a paste by lightly crushing 2–3 teaspoons of kalojeera (black cumin) and mixing it with sliced onions, green chilies, and a little mustard oil. Spread this aromatic mixture evenly over the mutton pieces, then wrap tightly in banana leaves and secure with string. Steam or shallow-grill the parcels over low heat for 25–30 minutes, allowing the mutton to cook gently while absorbing the earthy, nutty aroma of kalojeera. The Mymensingh-style paturi emphasizes mild, aromatic flavors with a gentle smokiness from the leaves. Serve hot with plain rice or soft khichuri.

Select small, tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, crushed garlic, ginger, turmeric, and a touch of mustard oil. Prepare a paste by lightly crushing 2–3 teaspoons of kalojeera (black cumin) and mixing it with sliced onions, green chilies, and a little mustard oil. Spread this paste evenly over the mutton pieces, then wrap tightly in banana leaves and secure with string. Steam or shallow-grill the parcels over low heat for 25–30 minutes, allowing the mutton to cook gently while absorbing the earthy, nutty aroma of kalojeera and the pungency of mustard oil. The Sylhet-style paturi emphasizes aromatic, balanced flavors with minimal spices, producing a tender, flavorful dish. Serve hot with plain rice or soft khichuri.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, turmeric, ginger–garlic paste, and a touch of mustard oil. Heat mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot and sauté sliced onions until golden brown, then add the marinated mutton and cook until lightly browned and aromatic. Add whole spices such as cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves to enhance the flavor. Drain and soak 1 cup of basmati rice for 20 minutes, then add it to the pot. Pour in 2–2.5 cups of hot water or stock, adjust salt, and cook on low heat until the rice is fluffy and the mutton is tender. The Barisal-style polao emphasizes aromatic richness and mild, balanced spices, letting the natural flavor of the mutton shine. Garnish with fried onions and coriander, and serve hot with raita or salad.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, turmeric, ginger–garlic paste, and a touch of mustard or sesame oil for a subtle earthy flavor. Heat oil in a heavy-bottomed pot and sauté sliced onions until golden brown, then add the marinated mutton and cook until lightly browned and aromatic. Add whole spices such as cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves for depth. Drain and soak 1 cup of basmati rice for 20 minutes, then add it to the pot. Pour in 2–2.5 cups of hot water or stock, adjust salt, and cook on low heat until the rice is fluffy and the mutton is tender. The Hill Tracts-style polao emphasizes rustic, earthy flavors with a gentle smokiness from the oil and aromatic depth from the spices. Garnish with fried onions and serve hot with plain rice or light accompaniments.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, turmeric, ginger–garlic paste, and a little yogurt for tenderness. Heat mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot and sauté sliced onions until golden brown, then add the marinated mutton and cook until lightly browned and aromatic. Garnish with fried onions and fresh coriander, and serve hot with raita or salad.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, turmeric, ginger–garlic paste, and a touch of yogurt for softness. Heat mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot and sauté sliced onions until golden brown, then add the marinated mutton and cook until lightly browned and aromatic. Add whole spices such as cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves for depth. Drain and soak 1 cup of basmati rice for 20 minutes, then add it to the pot. Pour in 2–2.5 cups of hot water or stock, adjust salt, and cook on low heat until the rice is fluffy and the mutton is tender. Garnish with fried onions and fresh coriander, and serve hot with raita or salad.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate with salt, turmeric, mild red chili, ginger–garlic paste, and a touch of yogurt for softness. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat mustard oil and sauté sliced onions until golden brown, then add the marinated mutton and cook on medium heat until lightly browned and aromatic. Add a pinch of whole spices such as cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves, then rinse and soak 1 cup of basmati rice for 20 minutes before adding it to the pot. Pour in 2–2.5 cups hot water or stock, adjust salt, and cook on low heat until the rice is fluffy and the mutton tender. The Rangpur-style polao emphasizes mild, balanced spices with a subtle earthiness from mustard oil, letting the mutton’s natural flavor shine. Garnish with fried onions and chopped coriander, and serve hot with raita or salad.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate with salt, turmeric, ginger–garlic paste, and a little yogurt to tenderize. In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat mustard oil and sauté sliced onions until golden brown, then add the marinated mutton and cook until lightly browned and aromatic. Add whole spices such as cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and bay leaf, then rinse and soak 1 cup of basmati rice for 20 minutes before adding it to the pot. Pour in 2–2.5 cups hot water or stock, adjust salt, and cook on low heat until the rice is fluffy and the mutton is tender. The Sylhet-style polao emphasizes a subtle tangy aroma by optionally adding a few drops of lime juice or a small spoon of tok doi (sour yogurt) to the rice, giving it a delicate, slightly sour fragrance. Garnish with fried onions and fresh coriander, and serve hot with raita or salad.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, crushed garlic, ginger, and a pinch of turmeric or mild red chili for flavor. Arrange the meat in a steamer or wrap in banana leaves, optionally layering with sliced onions, green chilies, and whole spices like black pepper or cumin seeds to impart subtle aroma. Steam over medium heat for 30–40 minutes, until the mutton is fully tender and infused with gentle spice and smoky leaf flavors. The Chattogram-style steaming emphasizes simplicity with aromatic depth, allowing the natural richness of the mutton to stand out. Finish with a drizzle of mustard or coconut oil before serving. Serve hot with plain rice or paratha as a fragrant, lightly spiced dish.

Select tender mutton pieces and lightly marinate with salt, crushed garlic, ginger, and a pinch of turmeric or garam masala for mild aroma. Arrange the meat in a steamer or on a banana leaf, optionally layering with sliced onions, green chilies, and whole spices like black pepper or cardamom for added fragrance. Steam over medium heat for 30–40 minutes, until the mutton is fully cooked, tender, and infused with the gentle spice flavors. The Dhaka-style steaming emphasizes a balanced, aromatic profile that highlights the richness of the mutton without overpowering it. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil or ghee for extra fragrance. Serve hot with plain rice or soft khichuri.

Select tender mutton pieces and marinate lightly with salt, crushed garlic, ginger, and optional local herbs or wild spices for an earthy flavor. Arrange the meat in a banana leaf or bamboo steamer, adding sliced onions, green chilies, and a pinch of turmeric for aroma. Steam over medium heat for 30–40 minutes, until the meat is fully tender and infused with subtle, smoky herbal notes from the leaves. The Hill Tracts-style steaming emphasizes simplicity and natural flavors, highlighting the richness of the mutton with minimal spices. Finish with a drizzle of mustard or sesame oil. Serve hot with plain rice, boiled tubers, or sticky rice as a wholesome, aromatic dish.

Select tender mutton pieces and lightly marinate with salt, crushed garlic, ginger, and a pinch of turmeric. Arrange the mutton in a steamer or on a banana leaf, optionally adding sliced onions, green chilies, and whole spices like black pepper or cumin for subtle aroma. Steam over medium heat for 30–40 minutes, until the meat is fully tender and infused with the delicate flavors of the spices. The Mymensingh-style steaming emphasizes simplicity, allowing the natural richness of the mutton to shine while keeping the dish lightly spiced and aromatic. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil or ghee for extra fragrance. Serve hot with plain rice or soft khichuri.

Select small, tender pieces of mutton and marinate lightly with salt, crushed garlic, ginger, and a few local herbs or wild spices for earthy flavor. Place the mutton pieces in a banana leaf or bamboo steamer basket, optionally layering with slices of onion, green chilies, and turmeric for aroma. Steam over medium heat for 30–40 minutes, until the meat is tender and infused with the smoky, herbal aroma from the leaves and spices. The Tribal-style steaming emphasizes simplicity and natural flavors, using minimal spices to highlight the meat’s richness. Finish with a drizzle of mustard or sesame oil before serving. Serve hot with plain rice or boiled tubers as a wholesome, aromatic tribal-style dish.

Select small tender mutton cuts or boneless pieces, and make a deep slit in each to form a pocket. Prepare the stuffing by mixing finely minced onions, garlic, ginger, green chilies, turmeric, red chili powder, garam masala, and salt, along with a tablespoon of mustard oil or ghee for richness. Stuff each mutton piece generously with this mixture. Heat mustard oil or ghee in a heavy pan, sear the stuffed mutton on all sides until lightly browned, then cover and cook on low heat, adding a splash of water or broth to maintain moisture. Simmer until the mutton is fully tender and infused with the aromatic spices, then finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and fresh coriander for fragrance. Serve hot with plain rice or paratha as a rich, aromatic Dhaka-style stuffed mutton dish.

Take 500 grams mutton pieces (preferably bone-in shoulder or leg cuts). Clean and pat dry. Make small slits in the meat to hold the stuffing.

For the stuffing: Mix 2 tablespoons ginger paste, 2 tablespoons garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon garam masala, 1 tablespoon mustard seeds, 2 tablespoons finely chopped onion, and 2 tablespoons yogurt into a smooth paste. Optionally, add a few crushed green chilies for mild heat.

Stuff this mixture into the slits of the mutton pieces and let marinate for 30–45 minutes.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil until warm. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and fry until golden brown. Gently place the stuffed mutton pieces in the pan, sear lightly on all sides for 5–7 minutes.

Add ½ cup plain yogurt, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1 cup hot water. Cover and cook on low heat for 45–50 minutes, or until the mutton is tender and the flavors have infused the meat. Occasionally baste the meat with the cooking juices.

Finish with a sprinkle of garam masala and a drizzle of mustard oil for aroma. Serve hot with steamed rice, paratha, or pulao.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Mutton Stuffed dish, wash 1 kilogram of boneless mutton and mince it finely, then marinate with 3 tablespoons of yogurt, 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons of roasted cumin and coriander powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, salt, and 2 tablespoons of mustard oil, leaving it to rest for 1 hour. Heat 4 tablespoons of ghee in a pan, fry 2 finely sliced onions until golden, add the marinated mutton, and cook until the mixture is dry, aromatic, and well browned; finish with garam masala and chopped coriander leaves. For the stuffing, take medium-sized vegetables such as gourds, pumpkins, or large eggplants, hollow them carefully, fill with the spiced mutton mixture, and secure the openings with a little flour paste. Place the stuffed vegetables in a heavy-bottomed pot, drizzle with ghee, add a splash of water, cover tightly, and cook on low heat for 30–40 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the stuffing inside is juicy and flavorful. Serve hot, cut into thick slices, with plain rice or polao.

To prepare Mutton Stuffed (Rangpur), start by cleaning 500 grams of boneless mutton and cutting it into medium-sized pieces. Prepare a stuffing by mixing 100 grams of minced mutton with 1 finely chopped onion, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, salt to taste, and a handful of chopped coriander leaves. Make a slit in each mutton piece and fill it with the prepared stuffing. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, sear the stuffed mutton pieces until lightly browned on all sides, then reduce the heat. Cover and cook on low heat for 25–30 minutes until the mutton is tender and the flavors are absorbed. Finish by garnishing with chopped coriander and a few slit green chilies. Serve hot as a spicy, aromatic Rangpuri-style stuffed mutton delicacy.

To prepare Mutton Stuffed (Tribal), start by cleaning 500 grams of boneless mutton and cutting it into medium-sized pieces. Prepare a stuffing by mixing 100 grams of minced mutton with 1 finely chopped onion, 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of crushed red chili, salt to taste, and a handful of chopped local herbs or coriander leaves. Make a slit in each mutton piece and fill it with the prepared stuffing. Heat 3 tablespoons of sesame oil or mustard oil in a pan, sear the stuffed mutton pieces until lightly browned on all sides, then cover and cook on low heat for 25–30 minutes until the mutton is tender and infused with the aromatic spices. Finish by garnishing with freshly chopped herbs or coriander. Serve hot as a smoky, flavorful Tribal-style stuffed mutton dish.

Start with 500 grams of bone-in mutton pieces, preferably from the shoulder or leg. Wash and pat dry. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil until it starts smoking slightly to remove rawness.

Add 2 medium thinly sliced onions and fry until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 tablespoon garlic paste, sautéing briefly. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons red chili powder, 1.5 teaspoons salt, and 1 teaspoon garam masala powder, stirring to coat the onions and spices.

Add the mutton pieces and sauté for 10–12 minutes until the meat browns and releases its juices. Add ½ cup plain yogurt and cook for another 5–7 minutes until the oil separates and the mutton is coated in a thick, rich gravy.

Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, cover the pot, and let the mutton simmer on low heat for 45–50 minutes or until tender and almost all liquid evaporates. For a traditional Barisal “tok” (tangy) flavor, add 2–3 tablespoons of tamarind pulp or a few tablespoons of sour yogurt during the last 10 minutes of cooking.

Before serving, fluff the dish with a spoon and garnish with fried onions and green chilies. Serve hot with plain rice.

Start with 500 grams bone-in mutton pieces, preferably from shoulder or leg. Wash and pat dry. Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until slightly smoky to remove raw flavor.

Add 2 medium thinly sliced onions and fry until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 tablespoon garlic paste, sautéing briefly until aromatic. Sprinkle 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons red chili powder, 1.5 teaspoons salt, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and 1 teaspoon garam masala powder, mixing well to coat the onions.

Add the mutton pieces and sauté for 10–12 minutes, allowing the meat to brown and release its juices. Add ½ cup plain yogurt and cook for another 5–7 minutes until the oil separates and the mutton is coated in a thick, rich gravy.

Add 2.5 cups of hot water, cover the pan, and simmer on low heat for 45–50 minutes or until the mutton is tender. For Khulna-style tanginess, add 1–2 tablespoons of tamarind paste or lemon juice during the last 10 minutes of cooking.

Before serving, garnish with fried onions, green chilies, and a few fresh coriander leaves. Serve hot with plain steamed rice.

Take 500 grams bone-in mutton pieces, preferably from shoulder or leg. Wash and pat dry. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil until slightly smoky to remove the raw flavor of the oil.

Add 2 medium thinly sliced onions and fry until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 tablespoon garlic paste, sautéing briefly. Sprinkle 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons red chili powder, 1.5 teaspoons salt, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and 1 teaspoon garam masala powder, mixing well to coat the onions and spices.

Add the mutton pieces and sauté for 10–12 minutes, allowing the meat to brown and release its juices. Add ½ cup plain yogurt and cook for another 5–7 minutes until the oil separates and the mutton is coated in a thick, rich gravy.

Pour in 2.5 cups of hot water, cover, and simmer on low heat for 45–50 minutes until the mutton is tender and most of the liquid has evaporated. For Rangpur-style tanginess, add 1–2 tablespoons of mustard paste or a few drops of lemon juice toward the end of cooking.

Before serving, garnish with fried onions and sliced green chilies. Serve hot with plain steamed rice.

To prepare Plain Bhaat, also known as boiled rice, begin by taking 1 cup of uncooked white rice—ideally a variety like Bangladeshi atop chaal or kalijira for its aroma—and rinse it thoroughly in cold water 3–4 times until the water runs clear, removing excess starch. In a medium-sized saucepan, add the washed rice along with 2.5 cups of clean water and a pinch of salt, though the salt is optional depending on personal taste. Place the pot over medium heat and bring the water to a gentle boil uncovered; once it begins to boil, reduce the heat to low and cover the pot with a tight-fitting lid to allow the rice to simmer. Let it cook undisturbed for about 15 to 18 minutes, or until the water is fully absorbed and the rice grains are soft, tender, and fluffy. Once done, turn off the heat and let the rice sit covered for another 5 minutes to allow the steam to finish cooking it evenly. Then fluff it gently with a fork and serve hot as a base for curries, bhartas, or lentils.

To prepare traditional Bangladeshi Polao, start by washing 2 cups of kalijira or basmati rice thoroughly and soaking it in water for about 20 minutes, then drain and set aside. In a large heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons of ghee or oil over medium heat and add 1 finely sliced medium onion, frying until golden brown and crisp; remove half the fried onions and reserve them for garnish. To the remaining onions in the pan, add 3 to 4 whole green cardamoms, 2 small cinnamon sticks, 3 to 4 cloves, and 1 bay leaf, sautéing the spices for about a minute until fragrant. Add the drained rice to the pan and gently fry for 2 to 3 minutes, coating the grains evenly in the spiced oil without breaking them. Pour in 3.5 cups of hot water along with 1.5 teaspoons of salt and a teaspoon of sugar for balance, stir once gently, and bring it to a boil. Once it begins to boil, reduce the heat to low, cover the pan with a tight-fitting lid, and let the rice cook for 15 to 18 minutes or until all the water is absorbed and the rice is tender but separate. After turning off the heat, allow the polao to rest, covered, for another 5 minutes to finish steaming, then fluff with a fork and garnish with the reserved fried onions before serving.

To prepare Pui Shak Bhuna (Hill Tracts), a dry stir-fry of Malabar spinach often enriched with shrimp and coconut, begin by thoroughly washing 1.5 lbs of Pui Shak (Malabar spinach), separating the stems from the leaves as stems require longer cooking time. In a wok, heat mustard oil and sauté 1 sliced onion until translucent; add 1 tablespoon of sliced garlic, 1/2 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 2 tablespoons of shredded coconut, and salt to taste, stirring for two minutes. Next, add 5 medium shrimp, cooking for another two minutes until they turn pink. Incorporate the Pui Shak stems first, cooking for a few minutes to soften, then add the leaves and 4 slit green chillies, stirring vigorously until the leaves wilt and shrink. Continue to cook for 5−7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until all the liquid is absorbed and the mixture is semi-dry (bhuna), then remove from heat and serve hot with rice.

Start with 2–3 bunches of fresh pui shak (Malabar spinach), washed thoroughly and chopped into 2–3 inch pieces, keeping the tender stems intact. Lightly blanch in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain and set aside to reduce slime.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until it starts to smoke slightly. Lower the heat and add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, frying until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, and sauté for 1–2 minutes.

Add 400 grams of chicken or small beef pieces (optional; traditionally sometimes cooked without meat), then sprinkle 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Cook on medium heat for 10–12 minutes until the meat is lightly browned and fragrant.

Add the blanched pui shak to the pan, stir gently, and cook over low heat for another 10–12 minutes until the greens are tender and fully coated in the spicy oil. For Mymensingh style, a small splash of yogurt or a few drops of mustard oil at the end is added for extra richness and aroma.

Serve hot, traditionally with plain steamed rice or roti.

Start with 2–3 bunches of fresh pui shak (Malabar spinach), washed thoroughly and chopped into 2–3 inch pieces, keeping tender stems intact. Lightly blanch in boiling water for 1–2 minutes to reduce slime, then drain and set aside.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until slightly smoky. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, sautéing for 1–2 minutes until fragrant.

Add 400 grams small pieces of chicken or beef (optional; can also be vegetarian) along with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Bhuna in Rajshahi style often uses slightly less chili and a hint of sugar to balance the flavors. Cook on medium heat for 10–12 minutes until the meat is lightly browned and aromatic.

Add the blanched pui shak, stir gently, and cook on low heat for another 10–12 minutes until the greens are tender and fully coated in the spiced oil. Finish with a few drops of mustard oil for aroma before serving.

Serve hot with plain rice or roti.

Start with 2–3 bunches of fresh pui shak (Malabar spinach), washed thoroughly and chopped into 2–3 inch pieces, keeping tender stems intact. Lightly blanch in boiling water for 1–2 minutes to reduce slime, then drain and set aside.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until it begins to smoke slightly. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon ginger paste and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, sautéing briefly.

Sprinkle 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon sugar, and salt to taste. Add the blanched pui shak to the pan and stir well. Cook on medium heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the greens are tender and most of the moisture has evaporated, giving a “dry” texture.

For Barisal style, finish with a few drops of mustard oil and a small sprinkle of roasted cumin powder for added aroma. Serve hot with plain rice or as a side to fish or meat dishes.

Take 2–3 bunches of fresh pui shak (Malabar spinach), wash thoroughly, and chop into 2–3 inch pieces, keeping the tender stems intact. Lightly blanch in boiling water for 1–2 minutes to reduce slime, then drain and set aside.

Add the blanched pui shak and stir gently. Cook over medium-low heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the greens are tender and most of the water evaporates, giving a dry texture. Finish with a few drops of mustard oil for aroma.

Serve hot, traditionally with plain rice, sticky rice, or as a side to grilled meats.

Take 2–3 bunches of fresh pui shak (Malabar spinach), wash thoroughly, and trim thick stems while keeping tender stems and leaves intact. Lightly blanch in boiling water for 1–2 minutes to reduce slime, then drain.

Prepare a marinade with 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon crushed garlic, ½ teaspoon salt, and optionally a pinch of sugar to balance flavors. Mix the marinade thoroughly.

Coat the pui shak evenly with the marinade and let it rest for 10–15 minutes. Preheat a grill, tandoor, or heavy skillet. Place the pui shak bundles on the grill and cook over medium heat for 5–7 minutes, turning occasionally, until the leaves are lightly charred, tender, and aromatic.

Serve hot, garnished with a few drops of mustard oil or a sprinkle of fried garlic. Traditionally enjoyed with plain rice or as a side to fish or meat dishes.

Take 2–3 bunches of fresh pui shak (Malabar spinach), wash thoroughly, and trim the thick stems while keeping the tender stems and leaves intact. Lightly blanch in boiling water for 1–2 minutes to reduce slime, then drain.

Prepare a marinade with 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon crushed garlic, ½ teaspoon salt, and optionally a pinch of crushed local herbs (as used traditionally in Hill Tracts tribal cooking). Mix the marinade well.

Coat the pui shak thoroughly with the marinade and allow it to rest for 10–15 minutes. Preheat a grill or tandoor (or use a heavy skillet if a grill is unavailable). Place the pui shak bundles on the grill and cook over medium heat for 5–7 minutes, turning occasionally, until the leaves are slightly charred and aromatic, but still tender.

Serve hot, garnished with a drizzle of mustard oil and optionally a sprinkle of crushed roasted spices or dried chili flakes for added aroma. This dish is traditionally enjoyed with plain rice or as a side to grilled meats.

To prepare Pui Shak Grilled (Khulna style), begin by washing and trimming 250 g of pui shak (malabar spinach) stems and leaves. Lightly toss the leaves with 1 teaspoon mustard oil, a pinch of salt, ½ teaspoon turmeric, and 1 chopped green chili. Preheat a grill or a nonstick pan, and place the seasoned leaves on it. Grill on medium heat for 4–6 minutes, turning occasionally, until the leaves are slightly wilted, smoky, and aromatic. Serve hot as a side dish with plain rice or dal.

To prepare Pui Shak Grilled in the Rajshahi style, wash and clean 1 bunch of Malabar spinach (pui shak) and separate the large leaves. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Add 1 teaspoon garlic paste and 1/2 teaspoon salt, sauté on low heat for 1–2 minutes. Add the spinach leaves and grill on medium heat for 3–4 minutes until the leaves are slightly soft with a little crispiness. Optionally, sprinkle a pinch of red chili powder. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Pui Shak Grilled in the Rangpur style, wash and clean 1 bunch of Malabar spinach (pui shak) and separate the large leaves. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Add 1 teaspoon garlic paste and 1/2 teaspoon salt, sauté on low heat for 1–2 minutes. Add the spinach leaves and grill on medium heat for 3–4 minutes until the leaves are slightly soft with a little crispiness. Optionally, sprinkle a pinch of red chili powder. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Pui Shak Grilled in the Tribal style, wash and clean 1 bunch of Malabar spinach (pui shak) and separate the large leaves. Heat 2 tablespoons local oil or mustard oil in a pan. Add 1 teaspoon garlic paste and 1/2 teaspoon salt, sauté on low heat for 1–2 minutes. Add the spinach leaves and grill on medium heat for 3–4 minutes until the leaves are slightly soft with a little crispiness. Optionally, sprinkle a pinch of red chili powder. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.

To prepare Pui Shak Jhol in the Barisal style, wash and clean 1 bunch of Malabar spinach (pui shak) and separate the large leaves. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until translucent. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Add 1/2 cup water and 1/2 cup coconut milk, and simmer gently for 3–4 minutes. Add the spinach leaves and cook for another 5 minutes until the leaves are tender. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Pui Shak Jhol in the Dhaka style, wash and clean 1 bunch of Malabar spinach (pui shak) and separate the large leaves. Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan. Add 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds and 1/2 teaspoon nigella seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 medium chopped onion and sauté until translucent. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Pui Shak Jhol (Rajshahi), start by washing 2 cups of fresh Pui (Malabar spinach) leaves and removing the tough stems. Heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until hot, then add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, sautéing until aromatic. Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook until golden brown. Stir in ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the Pui shak leaves and sauté for 2–3 minutes until they start to wilt. Pour in 1 cup of water and simmer gently for 5–7 minutes until the leaves are soft and the flavors blend, forming a light, soupy consistency. Finish with 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds paste or a splash of mustard oil for the signature Rajshahi flavor. Serve hot as a tangy, mildly spiced green vegetable jhol.

To prepare Rangpur-style Pui Shak Jhol, take 2 cups of washed and chopped Malabar spinach (pui shak). Heat 2 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan and add 1 teaspoon cumin seeds for tempering. Add 1 chopped onion and 1 teaspoon ginger-garlic paste, sautéing until lightly brown. Stir in 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 teaspoon chili powder. Add the spinach to the spiced mixture and stir for 3–4 minutes. Add 1/2 cup water as needed, cover, and cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes until the spinach is soft and the broth slightly thickens. Serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Barisal-style Pui Shak Khichuri, take 1 cup washed atap rice and 1/2 cup red lentils. Also prepare 2 cups washed and chopped Malabar spinach (pui shak). Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pot, add 2 bay leaves, 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, and 1 chopped onion; sauté until lightly brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, salt to taste, and 1/4 teaspoon chili powder. Add the washed rice and lentils, stir for 2–3 minutes. Then add the spinach and 3 cups hot water, cover, and cook on medium heat until the rice and lentils are soft and cooked. Once the khichuri thickens and the spinach is tender, remove from heat and serve hot.

To prepare Hill Tracts-style Pui Shak Khichuri, take 1 cup washed atap rice and 1/2 cup red lentils. Also prepare 2 cups washed and chopped Malabar spinach (pui shak). Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pot, add 2 bay leaves, 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, and 1 chopped onion; sauté until lightly brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, salt to taste, and 1/4 teaspoon chili powder. Add the washed rice and lentils, stir for 2–3 minutes. Then add the spinach and 3 cups hot water, cover, and cook on medium heat until the rice and lentils are soft and cooked. Once the khichuri thickens and the spinach is tender, remove from heat and serve hot.

Once the khichuri thickens and the spinach is tender, remove from heat and serve hot.

To prepare Hill Tracts-style Pui Shak Korma, take 2 cups washed and chopped Malabar spinach (pui shak). Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, and 1 chopped onion; sauté until lightly brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Once the spices are well cooked, gradually mix in 1/2 cup yogurt. Add the spinach, cover, and cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes. When the gravy thickens and the spinach is tender, remove from heat and serve hot with steamed rice or roti.

To prepare Khulna-style Pui Shak Korma, take 2 cups washed and chopped Malabar spinach (pui shak). Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 2 bay leaves, 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, and 1 chopped onion; sauté until lightly brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1/2 teaspoon garlic paste, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Once the spices are well cooked, gradually mix in 1/2 cup yogurt. Add the spinach, cover, and cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes. When the gravy thickens and the spinach is tender, remove from heat and serve hot with steamed rice or roti.

To prepare traditional Tribal-style Pui Shak Korma, start by thoroughly washing and cutting 2 bunches of fresh pui shak (Malabar spinach) into 2–3 inch pieces, keeping the tender stems intact. Lightly blanch the pui shak in hot water for 2–3 minutes, then drain and set aside to remove excess slime. In a heavy-bottomed pan or clay pot (preferred in tribal cooking), heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil until slightly smoky, then reduce the heat. Add 1 medium onion, thinly sliced, and sauté until soft and lightly golden. Add 400 grams of chicken or beef (small bone-in pieces are traditionally used), along with 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Cook the meat over medium heat for 10–12 minutes until it releases moisture and begins to brown.

Next, add ½ cup of thick coconut milk (or lightly beaten yogurt in inland tribal regions) and stir well, allowing the spices to blend into a creamy base. Cook for another 5–7 minutes until the oil gently separates. Add the blanched pui shak along with 1 cup of warm water, cover the pot, and simmer on low heat for about 20–25 minutes, allowing the greens to soften and absorb the korma flavors. Finish by adding a pinch of garam masala and 1 teaspoon of crushed dried chilies or green chilies for aroma. Stir gently and let it rest for a few minutes before serving. This dish is traditionally enjoyed with plain rice or hand-pounded rice.

To prepare a traditional Barisal-style Pui Shak Paturi, which is a flavorful parcel steamed in a leaf, start by washing and chopping pui shak (Malabar spinach) leaves and stems. For the main flavor base, make a paste in a grinder with 2 tablespoons of yellow mustard seeds, 1 tablespoon of grated coconut, a few green chilies, and a small amount of dried shrimp (chingri shutki), adding a little water to help with grinding. In a bowl, mix the chopped pui shak with this mustard-coconut-shrimp paste, adding salt and a drizzle of mustard oil. For the authentic paturi method, place a generous portion of this mixture onto a banana leaf, fold it carefully into a sealed parcel, and secure it with a string or toothpick. Steam the parcels for 15-20 minutes, or until the pui shak is tender and the flavors have melded together. If you don't have a banana leaf, you can cook the mixture directly in a covered pan over low heat until the liquid evaporates and the spinach is cooked. This dish is rich, pungent, and best served as a side with hot rice.

To prepare Chattogram-style Pui Shak Paturi, take 300 grams of fresh pui shak (pointed gourd leaves or equivalent leafy greens), wash and pat dry. Make a mustard paste by soaking 2 tablespoons mustard seeds in warm water for 10 minutes and grinding with 1–2 green chilies. Mix the mustard paste with 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric, and salt to taste. Spread the paste evenly on the leaves, roll or fold them securely, and wrap in banana leaves. Steam or grill the parcels over low heat for 15–20 minutes until the greens are tender and infused with the mustard flavors. Serve hot with plain rice as a traditional Chattogram-style meal.

To prepare Dhaka-style Pui Shak Paturi, wash and chop 300 grams of fresh Malabar spinach (pui shak) and mix it with 2 tablespoons of mustard paste, 1 tablespoon of poppy seed paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, 2–3 slit green chilies, 1 teaspoon salt, and 2 tablespoons of mustard oil. Wrap the mixture in banana leaves, folding them neatly and securing with thread or toothpicks, then place the parcels on a hot tawa or griddle and cook over low heat for 15–20 minutes, turning occasionally until the leaves are charred outside and the contents inside are soft, aromatic, and mustard-flavored. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Pui Shak Paturi (Hill Tracts), start by thoroughly washing 300–400 grams of pui shak (Malabar spinach) leaves and removing tough stems. Blanch the leaves in lightly salted boiling water for 1–2 minutes, then drain and pat dry. Prepare a stuffing by mixing 50 grams of grated coconut, 1–2 chopped green chilies, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, a pinch of salt, and 1 teaspoon sesame oil. Take one leaf at a time, place a spoonful of the stuffing in the center, and fold or roll the leaf to form a parcel. Lightly grease a steaming tray with sesame oil, place the parcels on it, cover, and steam for 8–10 minutes until cooked and aromatic. Serve hot as a traditional Hill Tracts-style Pui Shak Paturi.

To prepare Pui Shak Paturi (Mymensingh), start by thoroughly washing 300–400 grams of pui shak (Malabar spinach) leaves and removing the tough stems. Blanch the leaves in lightly salted boiling water for 1–2 minutes, then drain and pat dry. Prepare a stuffing by mixing 50 grams of grated coconut, 1–2 chopped green chilies, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, a pinch of salt, and 1 teaspoon ghee or mustard oil. Take one leaf at a time, place a spoonful of the stuffing in the center, and fold or roll the leaf to form a parcel. Lightly grease a steaming tray with ghee, place the parcels on it, cover, and steam for 8–10 minutes until cooked and aromatic. Serve hot as a traditional Mymensingh-style Pui Shak Paturi.

To prepare Pui Shak Paturi (Rajshahi), start by thoroughly washing 300–400 grams of pui shak (Malabar spinach) leaves and removing the tough stems. Blanch the leaves in lightly salted boiling water for 1–2 minutes, then drain and pat dry. Prepare a stuffing by mixing 50 grams of grated coconut, 1–2 chopped green chilies, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, a pinch of salt, and 1 teaspoon mustard oil or ghee. Take one leaf at a time, place a spoonful of the stuffing in the center, and fold or roll the leaf to form a parcel. Lightly grease a steaming tray with mustard oil or ghee, place the parcels on it, cover, and steam for 8–10 minutes until cooked and aromatic. Serve hot as a traditional Rajshahi-style Pui Shak Paturi.

To prepare Pui Shak Polao (Barisal), start by washing 1 cup of rice thoroughly and soaking it for 20 minutes. Drain the rice. Heat 2–3 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, 2–3 slit green chilies, and 1 teaspoon ginger paste, sautéing until aromatic. Add the drained rice and stir gently to coat with the oil and spices. Chop 300–400 grams of pui shak (Malabar spinach) and lightly sauté it separately with a pinch of salt and ½ teaspoon turmeric powder. Heat 2–3 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, 2–3 slit green chilies, and 1 teaspoon ginger paste, sautéing until aromatic. Chop 300–400 grams of pui shak (Malabar spinach) and lightly sauté it separately with a pinch of salt and ½ teaspoon turmeric powder. Add the drained rice to the pan, stir gently to coat with the oil and spices, then mix in the sautéed pui shak. Add 2 cups of water and salt to taste, bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat, cover, and cook until the rice is fully done and fluffy. Finish with a drizzle of ghee before serving hot as a traditional Dhaka-style Pui Shak Polao.

To prepare Pui Shak Steamed (Barisal), start by thoroughly washing 300–400 grams of pui shak (Malabar spinach) leaves and removing the tough stems. Chop the leaves roughly. In a bowl, mix the chopped leaves with 1 teaspoon mustard seeds, 1–2 slit green chilies, a pinch of salt, and 1 teaspoon mustard oil. Transfer the mixture to a heatproof bowl or small steaming dish, cover, and steam over medium heat for 7–10 minutes until the leaves are tender but still bright green. Optionally, drizzle a little mustard oil on top before serving. Serve hot as a light and aromatic Barisal-style Pui Shak Steamed dish.

To prepare Rangpur-style Pui Shak Steamed, wash and roughly chop 300 grams of fresh pui shak (Malabar spinach), then mix it with 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, ½ teaspoon roasted mustard seed paste, 2 minced garlic cloves, 2 slit green chilies, and salt to taste, coating well. Wrap the mixture tightly in a banana leaf parcel and secure with thread, then place it in a steamer or on a hot tawa with a heavy lid on low heat for 15–20 minutes until the shak becomes soft, aromatic, and infused with mustard flavor. Serve hot with plain rice as a light and healthy side dish.

To prepare Pui Shak Stuffed (Barisal), start by thoroughly washing 300–400 grams of pui shak (Malabar spinach) leaves and removing the tough stems. Blanch the leaves in lightly salted boiling water for 1–2 minutes, then drain and pat dry. Prepare a stuffing by mixing 100 grams of grated coconut, 2 tablespoons of roasted peanuts or khoya, 1 teaspoon chopped green chilies, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, and a pinch of salt. Take one leaf at a time, place a spoonful of the stuffing in the center, and carefully roll or fold the leaf to enclose the filling. Lightly grease a steaming tray with mustard oil or ghee, arrange the stuffed leaves, cover, and steam for 8–10 minutes until cooked and fragrant. Serve hot as a traditional Barisal-style Pui Shak Stuffed dish.

To prepare Pui Shak Tok (Chattogram), start by thoroughly washing 300–400 grams of pui shak (Malabar spinach) leaves and removing the tough stems. Chop the leaves roughly. Heat 2–3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds and 1–2 slit green chilies, and sauté briefly until fragrant. Add the chopped pui shak, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and a pinch of salt, stirring well. Cook on medium heat for 5–7 minutes until the leaves are tender but still bright green. Dissolve 1–2 tablespoons of jaggery (gur) in a small splash of water and pour over the cooked leaves, stirring gently to coat. Cook for another 2–3 minutes until the mixture thickens slightly. Serve hot as a flavorful Chattogram-style Pui Shak Tok.
