To prepare Pui Shak Tok (Tribal), begin by washing 2 cups of fresh pui shak (Malabar spinach) leaves and tender stems, then roughly chopping them. Heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil or sesame oil in a pan, add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic and 2–3 chopped green chilies, and sauté until aromatic. Add ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder and salt to taste, then stir in the pui shak and cook for a few minutes until it wilts. Pour in 1 cup of water and simmer gently for 5–7 minutes until the leaves become soft and release their natural slimy texture. Finish the dish by adding 1–2 tablespoons of lemon juice or fermented bamboo shoot water (traditional tribal souring agent), mixing well to create a light, tangy broth. Serve hot as a simple, earthy, and sour Tribal-style vegetable dish.

To prepare Rosh Bhuna (Dhaka), begin by cleaning and cutting 500 grams of mutton or beef into medium-sized pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 1 finely sliced onion, and sauté until deep golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, cooking until fragrant. Lower the heat and mix in ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the meat and bhuna thoroughly until the spices coat it well and oil starts to separate. Pour in 1 cup of warm milk or lightly sweetened milk, cover, and cook on low heat until the meat becomes tender and the gravy turns thick, glossy, and mildly sweet. Finish with ½ teaspoon of garam masala and a drizzle of ghee before serving hot as a rich, aromatic Dhaka-style delicacy.

To prepare Hill Tracts–style Rosh Bhuna, wash and cut 1 kilogram of beef or mutton into medium pieces, then marinate with 3 tablespoons of yogurt, 2 tablespoons of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 2 teaspoons of chili powder, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 2 teaspoons roasted cumin and coriander powder, 1 teaspoon garam masala, 2 tablespoons mustard oil, and salt to taste, leaving it for at least 1 hour. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat ½ cup of mustard oil, add 3 sliced onions and fry until golden brown, then add the marinated meat and cook on medium heat until it releases juices and the spices thicken. Add 2 cups of warm water, cover, and cook slowly for 1.5 to 2 hours until the meat is tender and the gravy reduces to a thick, rich “rosh” clinging to the pieces. Finish with green chilies and a drizzle of raw mustard oil for aroma, then serve hot with plain rice or tribal-style chal fry.

To prepare Khulna-style Rosh Bhuna, take 300 grams of cleaned rohu (or similar local) fish pieces and pat dry. Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, frying until golden and aromatic. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, 1 teaspoon roasted cumin-coriander powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and cook on medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the fish is cooked through and coated with the spices. Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer for another 5 minutes until the bhuna develops a rich, thick, and aromatic texture. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Khulna-style meal.

To prepare Rosh Bhuna, a traditional Mymensingh-style rich and flavorful beef curry, begin by taking 500 grams of beef (preferably with a little fat for extra taste) and washing it well. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 4–5 tablespoons of mustard oil until it smokes lightly to remove rawness, then add 2 finely sliced onions and fry until golden brown. Next, add a paste made from 2 medium onions, 6–8 garlic cloves, and 1.5-inch fresh ginger, stirring until the raw smell disappears. Mix in ground spices: 2 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons coriander powder, and salt to taste, frying the masala until oil begins to separate. Add the beef pieces and coat well with the spice mixture, frying on medium-high heat for about 10–12 minutes to develop deep flavor. Then add 1.5 cups of hot water, cover the pan, and let it simmer on low heat until the beef becomes tender and the gravy thickens into a rich, clinging sauce—this slow cooking process, known as “rosh bhuna,” enhances both taste and texture. Finally, finish with 2–3 slit green chilies and a sprinkle of garam masala, allowing it to rest for a few minutes before serving. This dish pairs beautifully with plain bhaat, khichuri, or parathas.

To prepare Rosh Bhuna (Rajshahi style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces and marinating them with turmeric, red chili powder, and salt for 10 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, lightly fry the fish pieces until golden, then remove and set aside. In the same oil, add finely sliced onions and sauté until deep golden, followed by ginger-garlic paste, green chilies, coriander powder, and a pinch of cumin, cooking until the oil separates and the spices become aromatic. Return the fried fish to the pan, mix gently with the thick masala, and cook on low heat until the gravy reduces and coats the fish well, forming a rich, dry bhuna. Rest briefly and serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Rosh Bhuna (Rangpur style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces and marinating them with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt for 10 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, lightly fry the fish pieces until golden, then remove and set aside. In the same oil, sauté finely sliced onions until deep golden, add 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1–2 crushed garlic cloves, 1–2 chopped green chilies, and a pinch of cumin, cooking until aromatic. Return the fried fish to the pan, mix gently with the thick masala, and cook on low heat until the gravy reduces and coats the fish well, creating a rich, dry bhuna typical of Rangpur cuisine. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Rosh Dry (Dhaka style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces. Marinate the fish with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste for 10–15 minutes. Heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, lightly fry the fish pieces until just golden, then remove and set aside. In the same pan, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. Return the fish to the pan, stir gently, and cook on low heat until the moisture dries up and the fish is well coated with spices, creating a dry, flavorful finish. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Rosh Dry (Hill Tracts style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces. Heat 2–3 tablespoons vegetable or mustard oil in a pan, lightly fry the fish pieces until lightly crisp, then remove and set aside. In the same pan, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until fragrant. Return the fish to the pan and cook on low heat, stirring gently until all moisture evaporates and the fish takes on a dry, earthy, and mildly smoky flavor characteristic of Hill Tracts cooking. Serve hot with plain rice.

Remove the fish and briefly sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves in the same oil to release aromatic flavors. Return the fried fish to the pan, toss gently for a minute to coat with the aromatics, and serve hot with plain rice.

Grill on medium heat for 8–10 minutes on each side, or until the fish is cooked through and has a lightly charred, smoky exterior. To prepare Rosh Grilled (Dhaka), begin by cleaning and cutting 500 grams of mutton or beef into medium-sized pieces and boiling them with salt until just tender, then drain and set aside. Remove the meat pieces, brush them lightly with ghee, and grill on a hot tawa or grill pan until lightly charred and aromatic. Serve hot as a rich, mildly sweet, and smoky Dhaka-style Rosh Grilled dish.

Lightly brush the fish pieces with mustard oil or ghee and place them on the grill. Cook for 5–7 minutes on each side, or until the fish is cooked through, slightly charred, and aromatic. Optionally, sprinkle a few crushed roasted spices like cumin or black pepper for extra flavor. Serve hot as a traditional Sylhet-style Rosh Grilled dish.

To prepare Rosh Jhol (Barisal), start by cleaning 500 grams of rohu fish (rosh) and cutting it into medium pieces. Add the marinated rohu pieces carefully and simmer on low heat for 8–10 minutes until the fish is cooked through and the gravy is flavorful. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and garnish with fresh coriander leaves. Serve hot as a traditional Barisal-style Rosh Jhol.

To prepare Rosh Jhol (Rangpur), start by cleaning 500 grams of rohu fish (rosh) and cutting it into medium pieces. Marinate the fish with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and a pinch of salt for 10–15 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until hot, then add 1 finely sliced onion, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, sautéing until fragrant. Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Pour in 2–2½ cups of water or light fish stock and bring to a gentle boil. Carefully add the marinated rohu pieces and simmer on low heat for 8–10 minutes until the fish is cooked through and the gravy is flavorful. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and garnish with fresh coriander leaves. Serve hot as a traditional Rangpur-style Rosh Jhol.

To prepare Rosh Jhol (Sylhet), start by cleaning 500 grams of rohu fish (rosh) and cutting it into medium-sized pieces. Marinate the fish with ½ teaspoon turmeric powder and a pinch of salt for 10–15 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee in a pan until hot, then add 1 finely sliced onion, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1 teaspoon garlic paste, sautéing until aromatic. Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Pour in 2–2½ cups of water or light fish stock and bring to a gentle boil. Carefully add the marinated rohu pieces and simmer on low heat for 8–10 minutes until the fish is cooked and the gravy is flavorful. Finish with a drizzle of mustard oil and garnish with fresh coriander leaves. Serve hot as a traditional Sylhet-style Rosh Jhol.

To prepare Rosh Khichuri (Dhaka), start by washing 1 cup of rice and ½ cup of moong dal (split yellow lentils) thoroughly and soaking them for 15–20 minutes. Drain well. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil, add 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, 2–3 slit green chilies, and 1 teaspoon ginger paste, sautéing until aromatic. Add the drained rice and dal, stirring gently to coat with the oil and spices. Dissolve 2–3 tablespoons of jaggery (gur) in ½ cup of warm water (optional for a mildly sweet variation) and pour it into the pan. Add 2½ cups of water and salt to taste. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat, cover, and simmer until the rice and dal are fully cooked, soft, and creamy. Finish with a drizzle of ghee before serving hot as a traditional Dhaka-style Rosh Khichuri.

To prepare Rosh Khichuri (Hill Tracts), start by washing 1 cup of rice and ½ cup of moong dal (split yellow lentils) thoroughly and soaking them for 15–20 minutes. Drain well. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 2 tablespoons of sesame oil or mustard oil, add 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, 2–3 chopped green chilies, and 1 teaspoon freshly crushed ginger, sautéing until aromatic. Add the drained rice and dal, stirring gently to coat with the oil and spices. Dissolve 2–3 tablespoons of jaggery (gur) in ½ cup of warm water and pour it into the pan. Add 2½ cups of water and salt to taste. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat, cover, and simmer until the rice and dal are fully cooked, soft, and creamy. Finish with a light drizzle of sesame oil before serving hot as a traditional Hill Tracts-style Rosh Khichuri.

To prepare Rosh Khichuri (Mymensingh), begin by washing 1 cup of rice and ½ cup of moong dal thoroughly and soaking them for about 15–20 minutes. Heat 2 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds, 2–3 slit green chilies, and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, sautéing until fragrant. Add the drained rice and dal, stirring gently to coat them with the oil and spices. Dissolve 2–3 tablespoons of jaggery (gur) in ½ cup of warm water and pour it into the pan, followed by 2½ cups of water and salt to taste. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat, cover, and simmer until the rice and dal are fully cooked, soft, and mildly sweet. Finish with a light drizzle of ghee before serving hot as a comforting Mymensingh-style Rosh Khichuri.

To prepare Rosh Khichuri (Sylhet), begin by washing 1 cup of fragrant rice and ½ cup of moong dal thoroughly and soaking them for about 15–20 minutes. To prepare Rosh Khichuri (Tribal), begin by washing 1 cup of local rice and ½ cup of moong dal thoroughly and soaking them for about 15 minutes. Heat 2 tablespoons of sesame oil or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot, add 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds, 2–3 crushed green chilies, and 1 teaspoon of freshly crushed ginger, sautéing until fragrant. Add the drained rice and dal, stirring gently to coat them with the oil and spices. Dissolve 2–3 tablespoons of jaggery (gur) in ½ cup of warm water and pour it into the pot, followed by 2½ cups of water and salt to taste. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat, cover, and simmer until the rice and dal are fully cooked and the khichuri becomes soft, creamy, and mildly sweet. Finish with a light drizzle of sesame oil before serving hot as a comforting Tribal-style Rosh Khichuri.

To prepare Rosh Korma (Chattogram), start by cleaning and cutting 500 grams of mutton or beef into medium-sized pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee in a pan, add 1 finely sliced onion, and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, cooking until aromatic. Reduce the heat and stir in ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the meat and bhuna well until the spices coat it evenly and the oil begins to separate. Pour in 1½ cups of coconut milk or lightly sweetened milk, a signature Chattogram-style touch, and simmer on low heat until the meat becomes tender and the gravy turns rich, creamy, and mildly sweet. Finish with ½ teaspoon of garam masala and a drizzle of ghee before serving hot as a fragrant Chattogram-style Rosh Korma.

To prepare Rosh Korma (Hill Tracts), begin by cleaning and cutting 500 grams of mutton or beef into medium-sized pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of sesame oil or mustard oil in a heavy pan, add 1 finely sliced onion, and sauté until lightly golden. Add 1 teaspoon of crushed garlic and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, cooking until aromatic. Reduce the heat and stir in ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of crushed dry red chili, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the meat and bhuna well until the spices coat it evenly and oil begins to separate. Pour in 1–1½ cups of coconut milk or lightly sweetened milk, a signature Hill Tracts variation, and simmer on low heat until the meat is tender and the gravy becomes rich, mildly sweet, and creamy. Finish with a drizzle of ghee or sesame oil and serve hot as a fragrant Hill Tracts-style Rosh Korma.

To prepare Rosh Korma (Mymensingh), start by cleaning and cutting 500 grams of mutton or beef into medium-sized pieces. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil or ghee in a pan, add 1 finely sliced onion, and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon of ginger paste and 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, cooking until fragrant. Reduce the heat and stir in ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, ½ teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Pour in 1½ cups of warm milk or lightly sweetened milk (traditional Mymensingh touch) and simmer on low heat until the meat becomes tender and the gravy turns rich, mildly sweet, and glossy. Finish with ½ teaspoon of garam masala and a drizzle of ghee before serving hot.

To prepare Rosh Korma (Rangpur style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (freshwater fish) into medium pieces. In a pan, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until fragrant. Add 2–3 tablespoons yogurt or mustard paste to create a smooth, mildly spiced gravy, then season with ½ teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Gently add the fish pieces, cover, and simmer on low heat for 10–12 minutes until the fish is cooked and the korma thickens slightly, allowing the flavors to meld in typical Rangpur-style richness. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Rosh Korma (Sylhet style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces. In a pan, heat 2–3 tablespoons mustard or vegetable oil, sauté 1 small sliced onion, 1–2 chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, and 1–2 crushed garlic cloves until aromatic. Add 2–3 tablespoons yogurt or mustard paste to create a creamy base, then gently mix in the fish pieces. Season with ½ teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Cover and simmer on low heat for 12–15 minutes until the fish is tender and the korma has thickened with rich, mildly spiced flavors characteristic of Sylheti cuisine. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Rosh Paturi (Barisal style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces. Marinate the fish with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon mustard paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1–2 crushed garlic cloves, and salt to taste for 15–20 minutes. Take large banana leaves, lightly grease them with mustard oil, place the marinated fish in the center, fold the leaves to wrap securely, and tie with kitchen string if needed. Heat a pan or grill and cook the wrapped fish on low to medium heat for 10–15 minutes, turning carefully until the fish is fully cooked and infused with the smoky aroma from the leaves. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Rosh Paturi (Chattogram style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces. Marinate the fish with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon mustard paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1–2 crushed garlic cloves, and salt to taste for 15–20 minutes. Take large banana leaves, lightly grease them with mustard oil, place the marinated fish in the center, fold the leaves to wrap securely, and tie with kitchen string if needed. Heat a pan or grill and cook the wrapped fish on low to medium heat for 10–15 minutes, turning carefully until the fish is fully cooked and infused with the smoky aroma from the leaves. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Rosh Paturi (Khulna style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces. Marinate the fish with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon mustard paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1–2 crushed garlic cloves, and salt to taste for 15–20 minutes. Take large banana leaves, lightly grease them with mustard oil, place the marinated fish in the center, fold the leaves to wrap securely, and tie with kitchen string if needed. Heat a pan or grill and cook the wrapped fish on low to medium heat for 10–15 minutes, turning carefully to avoid burning, until the fish is fully cooked and infused with the smoky aroma from the leaves. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Rosh Paturi (Rajshahi style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces. Marinate the fish with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon mustard paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1–2 crushed garlic cloves, and salt to taste for 15–20 minutes. Take large banana leaves, lightly grease them with mustard oil, place the marinated fish in the center, fold the leaves to wrap securely, and tie with a kitchen string if needed. Heat a pan or grill and cook the wrapped fish on low to medium heat for 10–15 minutes, turning carefully to avoid burning, until the fish is fully cooked and infused with the smoky aroma from the leaves. To prepare Rosh Polao (Hill Tracts style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300–400 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces and lightly marinating them with turmeric and salt. Wash 1 cup fragrant rice (such as kalijira) and soak it for 20 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil or local vegetable oil in a heavy pot, lightly fry the fish pieces until just golden, then remove and set aside. In the same oil, add sliced onions, crushed garlic, ginger, green chilies, and a few whole spices, sautéing gently to keep the flavors mild and earthy. Add the soaked rice, stir carefully, then pour in about 2½ cups of water and salt to taste. Cover and cook on low heat until the rice is nearly done, then place the fried fish on top, cover again, and allow it to steam for a few minutes so the aroma infuses the rice. Serve hot with a light drizzle of oil.

To prepare Rosh Polao (Khulna style), begin by cleaning and cutting 300 g of rosh (local freshwater fish) into medium pieces. Marinate the fish with 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and a pinch of salt for 10–15 minutes. Wash 1 cup basmati or kalijira rice thoroughly and soak for 20 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot, fry the fish pieces lightly until golden, then remove and set aside. In the same oil, sauté 1 sliced onion until golden, add 1 teaspoon ginger-garlic paste, 2–3 whole spices (cardamom, cinnamon, cloves), and the soaked rice, stirring gently to coat the grains. Pour in 2½ cups water, season with salt, cover, and cook on low heat until the rice is fluffy and aromatic. Layer the fried rosh on top before the final steaming for 5 minutes to infuse flavor. Serve hot with a light drizzle of mustard oil.

To prepare Rangpur-style Rosh Polao, begin by washing 2 cups of aromatic rice such as kalijira or basmati and soaking it for 20–30 minutes before draining. Heat 3 tablespoons ghee or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 1 sliced onion and sauté until lightly golden. Stir in 4–5 medium-sized rosh (pointed gourd), peeled and cut into thick pieces, along with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, a pinch of mild red chili powder, and salt to taste, and cook briefly until the vegetables are lightly coated. Add the soaked rice, mix gently, then pour in about 4 cups of hot water. Cover and simmer on low heat until the rice is fully cooked, fluffy, and lightly infused with the subtle sweetness of rosh. Serve hot with a simple curry or lentils.

To prepare Sylheti-style Rosh Polao, begin by washing 2 cups of aromatic rice such as kalijira or basmati and soaking it for 20–30 minutes, then draining well. Heat 3 tablespoons ghee or mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 1 sliced onion and sauté until lightly golden. Add 4–5 medium-sized rosh (pointed gourd), peeled and cut into thick pieces, along with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, a pinch of mild red chili powder, and salt to taste, and cook briefly so the vegetables are lightly coated with oil and spices. Stir in the soaked rice, mix gently, then pour in about 4 cups of hot water. Cover and cook on low heat until the rice is tender, fluffy, and delicately infused with the subtle sweetness of rosh, a hallmark of Sylheti-style polao. Serve hot with a light curry or lentils.

To prepare Tribal-style Rosh Polao, begin by washing 2 cups of aromatic rice such as kalijira thoroughly and soaking it for about 20–30 minutes before draining. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 lightly crushed garlic cloves, and sauté until fragrant and lightly golden. Add 4–5 medium-sized rosh (pointed gourd), peeled and cut into thick pieces, along with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, a pinch of red chili powder, and salt to taste, keeping the seasoning simple and earthy. Stir in the soaked rice, mix gently to coat the grains, then add about 4 cups of hot water. Cover and cook on low heat until the rice is soft, fluffy, and infused with the mild sweetness of rosh and mustard oil. Serve hot with plain lentils or a simple vegetable side.

To prepare Hill Tracts–style Rosh Steamed, begin by taking about 4–5 medium-sized rosh (pointed gourd), wash them thoroughly, lightly scrape the skin, and cut them lengthwise into halves or thick pieces. In a bowl, mix 1 tablespoon mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, a small pinch of red chili powder, and salt to taste, keeping the seasoning very simple and natural, as is common in Hill Tracts cooking. Coat the rosh evenly with this mixture and arrange them in a heatproof dish. Place the dish in a steamer or inside a covered pan with a little water at the bottom, and steam on medium heat for about 10–12 minutes until the rosh becomes soft, tender, and lightly aromatic. Serve hot with plain rice and fresh green chilies for a rustic Hill Tracts–style meal.

To prepare Khulna-style Rosh Steamed, begin by taking about 4–5 medium-sized rosh (pointed gourd), wash them well, lightly scrape the skin, and cut them lengthwise into halves or thick pieces. In a bowl, mix 1 tablespoon mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, a small pinch of red chili powder, and salt to taste, keeping the seasoning mild yet slightly pungent, as preferred in Khulna cuisine. Coat the rosh evenly with this mixture and arrange them in a heatproof dish. Place the dish inside a steamer or a covered pan with a little water at the bottom, and steam on medium heat for about 10–12 minutes until the rosh becomes soft, tender, and lightly infused with the mustard oil aroma. Serve hot with plain rice and green chilies.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Rosh Steamed, begin by taking about 4–5 medium-sized rosh (pointed gourd), wash them thoroughly, lightly scrape the skin, and cut them lengthwise into halves or thick pieces. In a bowl, mix 1 tablespoon mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, a small pinch of red chili powder, and salt to taste, keeping the seasoning gentle and balanced as is common in Mymensingh cooking. Coat the rosh evenly with this mixture and arrange them in a heatproof dish. Place the dish in a steamer or inside a covered pan with a little water at the bottom, and steam on medium heat for about 10–12 minutes until the rosh becomes soft, tender, and lightly aromatic. Serve hot with plain rice and green chilies for a simple, comforting Mymensingh-style meal.

To prepare Rangpur-style Rosh Steamed, begin by taking about 4–5 medium-sized rosh (pointed gourd), wash them well, lightly scrape the skin, and cut them lengthwise into halves or thick pieces. In a bowl, mix 1 tablespoon mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, a pinch of red chili powder, and salt to taste, keeping the seasoning mild and clean as preferred in Rangpur cuisine. Coat the rosh evenly with this mixture and place them in a heatproof dish. Set the dish inside a steamer or a covered pan with a little water at the bottom, and steam on medium heat for 10–12 minutes, or until the rosh becomes soft, tender, and lightly infused with the mustard oil aroma. Once done, remove from heat and serve hot with plain rice and green chilies for a simple Rangpur-style meal.

To prepare Barisal-style Rosh Stuffed, begin by taking about 4–5 medium-sized rosh (pointed gourd), wash them well, lightly scrape the skin, and make a lengthwise slit to carefully remove some of the inner pulp while keeping the gourds intact. In a bowl, prepare the stuffing by mixing the scooped pulp with 1 small finely chopped onion, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, salt to taste, and 1 tablespoon mustard oil, creating a mildly spiced mixture typical of Barisal flavors. Gently stuff this mixture back into the rosh and secure them if needed. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, arrange the stuffed gourds in a single layer, and fry them on low to medium heat, turning carefully, until they become lightly golden on all sides. Add a small splash of water, cover the pan, and let the rosh cook until tender and the stuffing is fully cooked, with the oil lightly coating the vegetables. Serve hot with plain rice as a simple yet flavorful Barisal-style dish.

To prepare Chattogram-style Rosh Stuffed, begin by taking about 4–5 medium-sized rosh (pointed gourd), wash them well, lightly scrape the skin, and make a lengthwise slit to remove some of the inner pulp while keeping the gourds intact. In a bowl, prepare a flavorful stuffing by mixing the scooped pulp with 1 small finely chopped onion, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, salt to taste, and 1 tablespoon mustard oil, reflecting the slightly richer spice profile of Chattogram cuisine. Carefully stuff this mixture back into the rosh. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, place the stuffed gourds gently, and fry on low to medium heat, turning carefully, until they are lightly golden on all sides. Add a small splash of water, cover, and cook until the rosh becomes tender and the stuffing is well cooked, with the spices coating the vegetables evenly. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Chattogram-style meal.

To prepare Dhaka-style Rosh Stuffed, take 6–8 medium-sized green chilies or sweet peppers, slit them lengthwise without cutting fully, and remove the seeds carefully. Prepare a filling by mixing ½ cup grated coconut, 2 tablespoons roasted sesame seeds, 1 teaspoon mustard paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric, ½ teaspoon chili powder, 1 teaspoon sugar, salt to taste, and 2 tablespoons mustard oil, making a moist, spicy-sweet mixture. Stuff this filling into the chilies, pressing gently so they hold shape. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a flat pan, arrange the stuffed chilies, cover, and cook on low flame for 8–10 minutes, turning once until soft, aromatic, and lightly charred but not broken. Serve hot with plain rice as a flavorful side dish.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Rosh Stuffed, take 500 grams of cleaned rohu or similar local fish, slit each piece carefully to create pockets for stuffing. Prepare a stuffing by mixing 2 tablespoons mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon roasted cumin–coriander powder, and salt to taste. Stuff the fish pockets with this mixture. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan and lightly fry the stuffed fish on medium heat for 5–7 minutes on each side until golden and cooked through. Reduce heat, cover, and simmer for another 5 minutes to let the flavors meld. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Mymensingh-style meal.

To prepare Sylhet-style Rosh Stuffed, take 500 grams of cleaned rohu or similar local fish and make slits to create pockets for stuffing. Prepare a stuffing by mixing 2 tablespoons mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 teaspoon roasted cumin–coriander powder, and salt to taste. Fill the fish pockets evenly with the mustard-spice mixture. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan and fry the stuffed fish on medium heat for 5–7 minutes on each side until golden and cooked through. Reduce heat, cover, and simmer for another 5 minutes to allow the flavors to meld. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Sylhet-style meal.

To prepare Barisal-style Rosh Tok, take 300 grams of cleaned rohu or similar local fish pieces and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and cook on medium heat for 8–10 minutes, then pour in ½ cup water and simmer uncovered for another 5 minutes until the fish is tender and coated with a lightly spiced, tangy gravy characteristic of Barisal cuisine. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Chattogram-style Rosh Tok, take 300 grams of cleaned rohu or similar local fish pieces and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and cook on medium heat for 8–10 minutes, then pour in ½ cup water and simmer uncovered for another 5 minutes until the fish is tender and coated with a lightly spiced, tangy gravy typical of Chattogram cuisine. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Dhaka-style Rosh Tok, take 300 grams of cleaned rohu or similar local fish pieces and pat them dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste. To prepare Khulna-style Rosh Tok, take 300 grams of cleaned rohu or similar local fish pieces and pat them dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare an authentic Mymensingh-style Rosh Tok, a light and sour fish curry, start with 500g of freshwater fish, such as rui or shing, cut into small pieces and marinated with a pinch of salt and turmeric. In a pan, heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil and add a few whole green chilies and ½ teaspoon of panch foron (Bengali five-spice mix). As the spices splutter, add 1 large sliced onion and fry until it becomes soft. Add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder and salt to taste, stirring well. Now, carefully add the fish pieces and cook them lightly on both sides. To create the tok or sour broth, mix 1 tablespoon of tamarind paste with 1.5 cups of water and pour it into the pan. Alternatively, you can use thin slices of green mango. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat and let the curry simmer for 10-15 minutes, or until the fish is cooked and the gravy has thinned to a watery consistency. Garnish with chopped fresh coriander before serving this refreshing and tangy dish with hot rice.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Rosh Tok, take 300 grams of cleaned rohu or similar local fish pieces and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and fragrant. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, ½ teaspoon roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and cook on medium heat for 8–10 minutes, then pour in ½ cup water and simmer uncovered for another 5 minutes until the fish is tender and coated with a lightly spiced, tangy gravy typical of Rajshahi cuisine. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Hill Tracts–style Shorshe Bhuna, take 300 grams of cleaned fish pieces such as punti or small freshwater fish, wash and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until hot, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 2 tablespoons smooth mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and cook on medium heat, turning occasionally, until the fish is tender and the spices form a thick, lightly coated bhuna-style layer over the fish. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Hill Tracts-style meal.

To prepare Khulna-style Shorshe Bhuna, take 300 grams of cleaned fish pieces such as rui, katla, or small local freshwater fish, wash them thoroughly, and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until hot, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 2 tablespoons smooth mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and cook on medium heat, turning occasionally, until the fish is tender and the spices form a thick, bhuna-style coating over the fish. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Khulna-style meal.

To prepare Tribal-style Shorshe Bhuna, take 300 grams of small freshwater fish or thick fish slices, wash them thoroughly, and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until hot, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 2 tablespoons freshly ground mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and cook on medium heat, turning occasionally, until the fish is tender and the spices form a thick, bhuna-style coating that clings to the fish. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Tribal-style meal.

To prepare Barisal-style Shorshe Dry, take 300 grams of cleaned fish pieces such as rui, katla, or small freshwater fish, wash them well, and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until hot, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and fragrant. Stir in 2 tablespoons smooth mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and fry on medium heat, turning occasionally, until the fish is fully cooked, slightly crisp on the edges, and coated with a thick, dry mustard-flavored layer. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Barisal-style meal.

To prepare Khulna-style Shorshe Dry, take 300 grams of cleaned fish pieces such as rui, katla, or small local freshwater fish, wash them well, and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until hot, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional meal.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Shorshe Dry, take 300 grams of cleaned fish pieces such as rui, katla, or small freshwater fish, wash them thoroughly, and pat dry. Stir in 2 tablespoons freshly ground mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and fry on medium heat, turning occasionally, until the fish is fully cooked, slightly crisp on the edges, and coated with a thick, dry mustard-flavored layer. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Mymensingh-style meal.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Shorshe Dry, take 300 grams of cleaned fish pieces such as rui, katla, or small local freshwater fish, wash them thoroughly, and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until hot, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 2 tablespoons smooth mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and fry on medium heat, turning occasionally, until the fish is fully cooked, slightly crisp on the edges, and coated with a thick, dry mustard-flavored layer typical of Rajshahi cuisine. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional meal.

To prepare Sylhet-style Shorshe Dry, take 300 grams of fish pieces (such as tengra, pabda, or rui), wash well, and pat dry. Prepare a spice paste with 2 tablespoons mustard seeds soaked and ground into a smooth paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, 2 minced garlic cloves, 2 green chilies, salt to taste, and 2 tablespoons mustard oil. Rub the fish thoroughly with this mixture and let it marinate for 15 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a flat pan, place the fish pieces carefully, and cook on low flame without adding extra water, letting the mustard paste coat and cling to the fish while it cooks slowly. Fry each side until the oil separates and the dish takes on a dry, aromatic texture. Serve hot with plain rice for a sharp, mustard-flavored delicacy.

To prepare Tribal-style Shorshe Dry, take 300 grams of small freshwater fish or thick fish slices, wash them thoroughly, and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until hot, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 2 tablespoons freshly ground mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and fry on medium heat, turning occasionally, until the fish is fully cooked, slightly crisp on the edges, and coated with a thick, dry mustard-flavored layer. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Tribal-style meal.

To prepare Barisal-style Shorshe Fry, take 300 grams of cleaned fish pieces such as rui, katla, or small freshwater fish, wash thoroughly, and pat dry. Heat 3–4 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until hot, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 2 tablespoons smooth mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and fry on medium heat, turning occasionally, until the fish is fully cooked, slightly crisp on the edges, and coated with a mustard-flavored layer. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Barisal-style meal.

To prepare Dhaka-style Shorshe Fry, begin by taking about 300 grams of freshwater fish slices such as rui, katla, or ilish pieces, wash them thoroughly, and pat them dry. Marinate the fish with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder and salt to taste, then set aside for 10 minutes. Prepare a smooth mustard paste by grinding 2 tablespoons yellow mustard seeds with 2 green chilies and a little water, keeping the flavor sharp but refined, as commonly preferred in Dhaka cooking. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until lightly smoky, fry the fish slices gently until golden on both sides, and remove them. Lower the heat and add the mustard paste to the same pan, stirring carefully so it does not turn bitter, then add a small splash of water to lightly cook the paste. Return the fried fish to the pan and cook for another 3–4 minutes, coating the fish evenly with the mustard mixture without making a heavy gravy. Serve hot with plain rice and a wedge of lemon.

To prepare Hill Tracts–style Shorshe Fry, begin by taking about 300 grams of small freshwater fish or thick fish slices, wash them thoroughly, and pat them dry. Marinate the fish lightly with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder and salt to taste, keeping the seasoning simple to highlight the natural flavor of the fish. Prepare a coarse mustard paste by grinding 2 tablespoons mustard seeds with 1–2 green chilies and a little water, maintaining a slightly grainy texture typical of Hill Tracts cooking. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until lightly smoky, gently fry the fish pieces until both sides turn golden and crisp, then remove them from the pan. Reduce the heat and add the mustard paste to the remaining oil, stirring briefly to release its aroma without burning, then add a small splash of water. Return the fried fish to the pan and cook together for 3–4 minutes, allowing the sharp mustard flavor to coat the fish without forming a heavy gravy. Serve hot with plain rice and fresh green chilies for a rustic Hill Tracts–style meal.

To prepare Khulna-style Shorshe Fry, begin by taking about 300 grams of freshwater fish slices such as rui, katla, or small local fish, wash them well, and pat dry. Return the fried fish to the pan and cook for another 3–4 minutes until the mustard flavor fully coats the fish. Serve hot with plain rice, raw onion, and green chilies.

To prepare Sylheti-style Shorshe Fry, begin by taking about 300 grams of freshwater fish slices such as rui, katla, or punti, wash them well, and lightly pat dry. Marinate the fish with 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, salt to taste, and a few drops of lemon juice, then set aside for 10 minutes. In a bowl, prepare a smooth mustard paste using 2 tablespoons yellow mustard seeds soaked and ground with 2–3 green chilies, adding a little water for blending, keeping the flavor sharp and pungent as preferred in Sylhet. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan until lightly smoky, gently fry the fish pieces until golden on both sides, and remove them from the oil. In the same pan, lower the heat and add the prepared mustard paste, stirring carefully to avoid bitterness, then add a splash of water and simmer briefly until the oil begins to separate. Return the fried fish to the pan, coat them well with the mustard sauce, and cook for another 3–4 minutes until the flavors are absorbed. Serve hot with plain rice, fresh green chilies, and a squeeze of lemon if desired.

To prepare Tribal-style Shorshe Fry, begin by taking about 300 grams of small whole fish or thick fish slices, such as punti or koi, and wash them thoroughly before patting them dry. In a bowl, prepare a simple marinade by mixing 2 tablespoons freshly ground mustard paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, salt to taste, and 1–2 tablespoons water to form a coarse but spreadable mixture, keeping the flavors sharp and rustic as is common in tribal cooking. Coat the fish evenly with this mustard mixture and let it rest for about 15–20 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a shallow pan over medium heat until it becomes lightly smoky, then gently place the marinated fish into the oil and fry slowly, turning carefully, until both sides are golden, crisp on the outside, and fully cooked inside, allowing the mustard paste to form a slightly crusted layer on the fish. Once done, remove from the pan and serve hot with plain rice, fresh green chilies, and raw onion slices for a traditional tribal-style meal.

To prepare Dhaka-style Shorshe Grilled, begin by taking 300 grams of firm fish fillets such as rui or ilish and washing them thoroughly, then patting them dry. In a bowl, make a marinade by blending 2 tablespoons mustard paste (yellow mustard preferred), 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 2 tablespoons mustard oil, salt to taste, and 1–2 tablespoons water to form a smooth, thick paste. Coat the fish pieces evenly with this mustard mixture and allow them to marinate for about 20–30 minutes so the sharp mustard flavor penetrates the flesh. Preheat a grill pan or charcoal grill and lightly grease it with mustard oil, then place the marinated fish pieces on the grill and cook on medium heat for about 6–8 minutes per side, turning carefully, until the fish is cooked through, lightly charred on the outside, and aromatic. Once done, remove from heat and drizzle a few drops of raw mustard oil on top before serving hot with plain bhaat, sliced onion, and green chilies, as is traditional in Dhaka-style meals.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Shorshe Jhol, take 500 grams of fish pieces such as rui or katla, wash and pat dry. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 2 tablespoons smooth mustard seed paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add the fish pieces and 1–1.5 cups of water, cover, and simmer on low heat for 15–20 minutes until the fish is tender and the gravy is light, slightly pungent, and aromatic. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Mymensingh-style meal.

To prepare Khulna-style Shorshe Khichuri, wash 1 cup of rice and ½ cup of lentils (moong dal) thoroughly and soak for 20–30 minutes. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot, add 1 sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until golden and aromatic. Stir in 2 tablespoons smooth mustard seed paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon mild red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add 300 grams of fish or chicken pieces and lightly sauté for 5–7 minutes. Drain the soaked rice and lentils, add them to the pot along with 4 cups of hot water, cover, and cook on low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice and lentils are soft and infused with the mustard-flavored protein. Serve hot with a drizzle of ghee for a traditional Khulna-style meal.

To prepare Barisal-style Shorshe Korma, take 500 grams of fresh river fish such as rui or katla, wash and pat dry. Serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare Chattogram-style Shorshe Paturi, take 500 grams of fresh fish pieces such as rui, katla, or local sea fish, wash and pat dry. Coat the fish pieces evenly with this mixture, place them on banana leaves, and wrap tightly into parcels. Steam or grill over low heat for 20–25 minutes until the fish is tender and fully infused with the sharp, aromatic mustard flavor typical of Chattogram cuisine. Serve hot with plain rice for a classic coastal-style meal.

To prepare Dhaka-style Shorshe Polao, wash 2 cups of basmati or fine atop rice thoroughly and soak for 20–30 minutes, then drain. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil and 1 tablespoon ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan, add 1 finely sliced onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 1-inch ginger paste, sautéing until lightly golden and fragrant. Stir in 2 tablespoons smooth mustard seed paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon mild red chili powder, and salt to taste. Add 500 grams of lightly fried fish pieces (such as rui or katla), then gently mix in the soaked rice and 4 cups of hot water. Cover and cook on low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice is fluffy and fully infused with the subtle mustard aroma and fish flavor. Serve hot as a refined Dhaka-style polao with a light mustard finish.

Mix in the soaked rice and 4 cups of hot water, cover, and cook on low heat for 20–25 minutes until the rice is tender and infused with the aromatic mustard-flavored fish. Serve hot garnished with fried onions for a traditional Hill Tracts-style meal.

Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Barisal-style meal.

Serve hot with plain rice as a traditional Rangpur-style dish.

To prepare Chattogram-style Shorshe Stuffed, take 6–8 medium green chilies, slit them lengthwise without cutting through completely, and remove the seeds carefully. Prepare a stuffing by mixing ½ cup grated coconut, 2 tablespoons roasted sesame seeds, 1 teaspoon mustard paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric, ½ teaspoon chili powder, 1 teaspoon sugar, salt to taste, and 2 tablespoons mustard oil, making a moist, aromatic mixture. Stuff this mixture carefully into the chilies, pressing gently so they hold shape. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, place the stuffed chilies, cover, and cook on low flame for 8–10 minutes, turning once until soft, aromatic, and lightly charred. Serve hot with plain rice for a flavorful Chattogram-style side dish.

To make traditional Rangpur-style Shorshe Stuffed Begun (Shorshe Bhora Begun), begin by washing and drying 6–8 small to medium eggplants (begun). Slit each eggplant lengthwise in a cross shape, keeping the stem intact so the vegetable remains whole. Lightly rub the eggplants with a pinch of salt and turmeric powder and set aside for 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, prepare the mustard stuffing by soaking 3 tablespoons of yellow mustard seeds and 1 tablespoon of poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes. Drain and grind them into a thick paste with 2 green chilies, 1 teaspoon of salt, and a small splash of water. Transfer the paste to a bowl and mix in ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon of red chili powder, and 1 tablespoon of mustard oil to enhance the aroma.

Carefully stuff the mustard paste into the slits of each eggplant, pressing gently so the filling goes deep inside. Heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil in a wide pan until it reaches smoking point, then lower the heat. Add the stuffed eggplants gently and fry them on medium-low heat, turning occasionally, until all sides become lightly golden and the skin softens.

Once the eggplants are partially cooked, add any remaining mustard paste to the pan along with ½ cup of warm water. Cover and let it simmer on low heat for 12–15 minutes until the eggplants are fully tender and the gravy thickens, releasing mustard oil on top. Adjust salt if needed and finish with 2–3 slit green chilies for extra pungency.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice, as traditionally enjoyed in Rangpur households.

Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion and 2 minced garlic cloves, frying until aromatic. Add the fish and pour in the mustard paste, stirring gently. Cook on low heat for 10–12 minutes until the fish is tender, the mustard flavor fully infuses, and the curry develops a slightly thick, tangy consistency. Serve hot with plain rice as a traditional Barisal-style meal.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Shorshe Tok, take 300 grams of fish pieces (such as rui, katla, or pabda), wash and pat dry, then rub lightly with ½ teaspoon turmeric and salt. Soak 3 tablespoons mustard seeds in warm water for 10–15 minutes and grind into a smooth paste with 2 green chilies. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion and 2 minced garlic cloves, frying until aromatic. Add the fish and pour in the mustard paste, stirring gently. Cook on low heat for 10–12 minutes until the fish is tender, the mustard flavor is fully infused, and the curry develops a slightly thick, tangy consistency. Serve hot with plain rice as a traditional Mymensingh-style dish.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Shorshe Tok, take 300 grams of fish pieces (such as rui, katla, or pabda), wash and pat dry, then rub lightly with ½ teaspoon turmeric and salt. Soak 3 tablespoons mustard seeds in warm water for 10–15 minutes and grind into a smooth paste with 2 green chilies. Heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion and 2 minced garlic cloves, frying until aromatic. Add the fish and pour in the mustard paste, stirring gently. Cook on low heat for 10–12 minutes until the fish is tender, the mustard flavor infuses fully, and the curry takes on a slightly thick, tangy texture. Serve hot with plain rice as a traditional Rajshahi-style dish.

To prepare Tribal-style Shorshe Tok, soak 3 tablespoons of mustard seeds in warm water for 15 minutes and grind into a smooth paste with 2 green chilies and a pinch of salt, then set aside. In a clay pot or heavy pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil until sharp, add ½ teaspoon nigella seeds and 2 dried red chilies, then stir in 1 chopped tomato and cook until soft and pulpy. Add the mustard paste with ½ teaspoon turmeric and a little water, simmering gently for 5–6 minutes until the rawness disappears and the sauce thickens slightly with a tangy, pungent aroma. Adjust salt and sourness by adding a touch of tamarind pulp or extra tomato if desired, then drizzle with a spoonful of raw mustard oil before serving hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Shutki Bhuna, a spicy and dry preparation of dried fish from the Chittagong region, also known as Loitta Shutki Bhuna when using dried Bombay Duck, begin by taking 8 to 10 pieces of dry fish, cutting them into 1-inch pieces, and soaking them in warm water for 20 to 30 minutes, then wash thoroughly multiple times to remove sand and grit. Heat 1 half cup of mustard oil in a pan, and sauté 1 cup of thinly sliced onions and a generous handful of crushed garlic cloves until the onions are soft and translucent. Stir in 1 tablespoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of ground coriander, and salt to taste, adding a splash of water to prevent burning, and cook the spices until the oil separates. Add the cleaned shutki pieces to the pan and fry the fish with the spices on medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring frequently until the fish is flaky and the spices are well-absorbed. Add 4 to 5 whole green chilies for fragrance and a small amount of water if necessary, continuing to cook until the water dries out and the oil rises to the top, signaling the completion of the bhuna process. Garnish with chopped coriander leaves and serve hot with plain steamed rice.

To prepare Shutki Bhuna, a spicy and intensely flavored dry curry popular in Dhaka, often made with Loitta Shutki (dried Bombay Duck) or Churi Shutki (dried Ribbon Fish), begin by taking 1 cup of dry fish, cutting it into 1-inch pieces, and dry roasting it in a pan for 2 minutes before soaking and washing it thoroughly in warm water 4 to 5 times to remove all traces of sand and dirt. In a pot, heat 1 quarter cup of mustard oil and fry 1 cup of sliced onions and 1 cup of sliced garlic until the onions are translucent and the garlic is lightly browned. Add 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of ground cumin, 1 teaspoon of ground coriander, and salt to taste, adding a splash of water to cook the spices thoroughly until the oil separates. Add the cleaned shutki, along with 1 cup of cubed vegetables like potato and eggplant, and cook the mixture for 10 minutes over medium heat, adding water as needed to keep the mixture moist. Finally, add 5 to 6 whole green chilies, cover, and let it simmer on low heat for 10 minutes, making sure to stir occasionally until the oil rises to the top and the curry is dry and fully bhuna (sautéed). Garnish with fresh coriander leaves and serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare an authentic Chittagong Hill Tracts-style Shutki Bhuna, which is a spicy and flavorful dry curry, start by thoroughly washing 100g of sidol or nappi (fermented fish paste) or dried fish such as churi shutki to remove any sand. For the base, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan and fry 1 finely chopped large onion until it is golden brown. Add a paste made from 1 tablespoon of ginger, 1 tablespoon of garlic, and a generous handful of dani morich (bird's eye chilies) for that authentic Hilly heat. Cook the paste well, then mix in ½ teaspoon of turmeric powder and a pinch of salt. Now, add the cleaned shutki along with about 1 cup of thinly sliced bamboo shoots, and continue to sauté the mixture on medium heat. Pour in a small amount of hot water, cover the pan, and let it simmer for 15-20 minutes until the shutki is soft and has melded with the spices. The dish is complete when the water has evaporated and the gravy has thickened to a rich, dark bhuna consistency. Serve this intensely flavorful dish with plain rice.

To prepare Khulna-style Shutki Bhuna, take 200 grams of dry fish (such as loitta or chhuri shutki), rinse briefly in warm water to remove excess salt, and drain well. Heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 3 minced garlic cloves, and 2 slit green chilies, frying until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, ½ teaspoon roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste, then add the shutki and cook on medium heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally until the fish is dry, slightly crisp, and fully coated with aromatic spices. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and serve hot with plain rice or khichuri for a flavorful Khulna-style meal.

To prepare Mymensingh-style Shutki Bhuna, take 200 grams of dry fish (such as loitta or chhuri shutki), rinse briefly in warm water to remove excess salt, and drain well. Heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan, add 1 sliced onion, 3 minced garlic cloves, and 2 slit green chilies, frying until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, ½ teaspoon roasted cumin powder, and salt to taste, then add the shutki and cook on medium heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally until the fish becomes dry, slightly crisp, and fully coated with the aromatic spices. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and serve hot with plain rice or khichuri as a rich, traditional Mymensingh-style dish.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Shutki Bhuna, start by dry-roasting 150–200 grams of dried fish (commonly loitta or punti shutki) over low heat until fragrant, then rinse briefly in warm water and squeeze to remove excess salt; heat 3–4 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until it reaches smoking point, lower the heat, and add 1 large finely sliced onion, frying until deep golden, followed by 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1½ teaspoons red chili powder, and salt to taste, then add the prepared shutki and bhuna everything together on medium heat for 10–12 minutes until the fish breaks down and absorbs the spices, after which add 2 tablespoons of mustard paste and 2–3 slit green chilies, cooking for another 4–5 minutes until the oil separates and the bhuna becomes rich, spicy, and slightly sharp with mustard flavor; this Rajshahi-style shutki bhuna is drier, bolder, and more pungent than coastal versions.

To prepare Tribal-style Shutki Bhuna, begin by lightly dry-roasting 150–200 grams of mixed dried fish (such as loitta, chepa, or chingri shutki) over low heat until aromatic, then rinse quickly in warm water and squeeze gently to remove excess salt and odor; heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until smoking, reduce the heat, and add 1 medium onion finely sliced, frying until lightly browned, followed by 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 4–5 crushed dried red chilies (or to taste), and ½ teaspoon turmeric, then add the prepared shutki and bhuna everything together over medium-low heat for 10–12 minutes, mashing slightly with the spatula so the fish blends with the spices, and finally stir in 2 tablespoons of chopped garlic and a handful of crushed green chilies, cooking for another 3–5 minutes until the mixture becomes dry, intensely aromatic, and rustic in texture; this tribal-style version avoids heavy spices and emphasizes mustard oil, chili heat, and the natural flavor of dried fish.

To prepare Barisal-style Shutki Dry, take 200 grams of dry fish (such as loitta or chhuri shutki), rinse briefly in warm water to remove excess salt, and drain well. Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, and salt as needed, then add the shutki and cook on medium heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring occasionally until the fish is dry, slightly crisp, and coated with spices. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and serve hot with plain rice or khichuri for a rustic Barisal-style meal.

To prepare traditional Hill Tracts–style Shutki Dry, start with 250 grams of dried fish (shutki), commonly small local varieties. Rinse the shutki well and soak in warm water for 15–20 minutes, then drain and pat dry.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil over medium heat. Add 2–3 crushed garlic cloves and sauté lightly until fragrant. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon crushed dry red chili or chili flakes (adjust to taste), and salt if needed. Stir briefly.

Add the prepared shutki and cook on medium heat, stirring gently, until the fish turns dry, aromatic, and lightly crispy. Hill Tracts cooking typically uses minimal spices, so avoid heavy masala and let the natural flavor of the shutki dominate.

Serve hot with plain boiled rice or traditional hill rice for an authentic Hill Tracts–style Shutki Dry experience.

To prepare traditional Khulna-style Shutki Dry, start with 250 grams of dried fish (shutki). Rinse the shutki well and soak it in warm water for 15–20 minutes to reduce excess saltiness, then drain and pat dry.

Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until hot. Add 1 medium onion thinly sliced and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add the soaked shutki and fry on medium heat for 8–10 minutes, stirring gently, until the fish becomes dry, slightly crispy, and well coated with spices. Add 2–3 slit green chilies toward the end for extra aroma.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Khulna-style Shutki Dry experience.

To prepare traditional Mymensingh-style Shutki Dry, start by washing 200 g of dry fish (such as chhuri, loitta, or shidol shutki) lightly in warm water and draining well. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until it releases aroma, then add 2 medium onions finely sliced and fry until golden brown; remove a small portion for garnish. To the remaining onions, add 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste, frying for 2 minutes with a splash of water until the oil separates. Add the shutki pieces and stir-fry on medium heat for 8–10 minutes, allowing the fish to absorb the spices and dry out completely. Add 3–4 slit green chilies toward the end and cook uncovered for another 2 minutes, stirring gently until the dish is aromatic and slightly crisp. Remove from heat and garnish with the reserved fried onions. Serve hot with plain steamed rice for the most authentic experience.

To prepare Rajshahi-style Shutki Dry, wash 200 grams of dry fish (such as chhuri or loitta shutki) quickly in warm water to soften and remove excess salt, then drain well. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, and salt if needed, then stir in the shutki and cook on medium flame, stirring occasionally, for 10–12 minutes until the fish turns slightly crisp and the spices cling to it. Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and serve hot with plain rice for a bold and rustic Rajshahi-style flavor.

To make traditional Rangpur-style Shutki Dry, begin by lightly rinsing 150 grams of dried fish (shutki—commonly loitta or punti) under running water to remove excess salt and odor. Pat dry completely and set aside.

Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until it reaches smoking point, then reduce the heat. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until golden brown. Add 2–3 dried red chilies and 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, stirring gently for 1–2 minutes until aromatic.

Add the dried fish to the pan and mix carefully. Cook on low heat for 8–10 minutes, turning occasionally, until the shutki becomes slightly crispy and well-coated with the spices. Adjust salt sparingly, as the fish is naturally salty. For a Rangpur touch, add 1–2 slit green chilies and a small sprinkle of crushed roasted mustard seeds or poppy seeds for added flavor.

Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil before serving. Serve hot with plain rice or rice porridge, as traditionally enjoyed in Rangpur households.

To make traditional Tribal-style Shutki Dry, begin by lightly washing 150 grams of dried fish (shutki—such as loitta, chingri, or punti) quickly under running water to remove excess salt and odor. Pat dry completely and set aside. In a dry pan over low heat, lightly roast the shutki for 2–3 minutes to enhance aroma, then remove and keep aside.

Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until it reaches smoking point, then reduce the heat. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until lightly golden. Add 3–4 dried red chilies (broken) and stir briefly until fragrant. Add the roasted shutki to the pan and mix well with the spices. Cook on low to medium heat for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the shutki becomes crispy and well coated. Add salt only if needed (usually minimal, as shutki is naturally salty). For a true tribal touch, add 2–3 crushed green chilies and optionally a small amount of mashed roasted eggplant or smashed tomato (about ¼ cup), mixing thoroughly.

Cook for another 3–5 minutes until everything comes together and the oil separates slightly. Turn off the heat and finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil for a strong, authentic aroma.

Serve hot with plain rice or rice porridge (bhaat or pej), as commonly enjoyed in tribal communities.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Shutki Fry, start with 250 grams of dried fish (shutki). Soak the shutki in warm water for 15–20 minutes to reduce excessive saltiness, then drain and pat dry.

Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until hot. Add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add the soaked shutki pieces and sauté on medium heat for 5–7 minutes until the fish is crisp and coated with spices. Be careful while stirring to prevent the fish from breaking apart. Optionally, garnish with a few chopped green chilies for extra heat.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Barisal-style Shutki Fry experience.

To prepare traditional Dhaka-style Shutki Fry, start with 250 grams of dried fish (shutki), such as dried Ilish, Pabda, or small local dried fish. Wash the dried fish thoroughly to remove excess salt and soak in warm water for 20–30 minutes. Drain and pat dry.

Heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan until hot. Add the dried fish pieces in batches and shallow fry on medium heat until golden brown and crisp, turning occasionally to cook evenly. Remove and drain excess oil on paper towels.

In the same pan, add 1 medium onion finely sliced and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic. Return the fried shutki to the pan and toss gently to coat with the spices. Cook for another 3–5 minutes to let the flavors blend.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Dhaka-style Shutki Fry experience.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice and a side of fresh vegetables for an authentic Barisal-style Shutki Grilled experience.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Shutki Jhol, start with 250 grams of dried fish (shutki), such as dried Ilish or Pabda. Wash the dried fish thoroughly to remove excess salt and soak in warm water for 20–30 minutes. Drain and pat dry.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil until hot. Add 1 medium onion finely chopped and sauté until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, and salt to taste. Fry briefly until aromatic.

Add the soaked dried fish and sauté gently for 5–7 minutes to coat with the spices. Pour in 2 cups of water and simmer on low heat for 15–20 minutes, allowing the flavors to meld and the fish to cook through. Optionally, add 2–3 slit green chilies and a handful of chopped coriander leaves before serving.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice for an authentic Barisal-style Shutki Jhol experience.

Reduce heat to low, cover with a tight-fitting lid, and simmer for 20–22 minutes until the khichuri is cooked, creamy, and the rice and lentils are tender. Cover and cook on medium heat until the rice and dal are soft and the liquid is mostly absorbed, about 15–20 minutes. Reduce heat to low, cover tightly, and steam for another 5–7 minutes for fluffy texture.

Garnish with 2–3 slit green chilies and a handful of chopped coriander leaves. Serve hot with plain yogurt or fried egg for a hearty Chattogram-style meal.
