To prepare Shutki Paturi (Mymensingh-style), begin by selecting 200 grams of cleaned and deboned dry fish—preferably loitta (bombay duck) or chhuri shutki—for its strong flavor and soft texture when steamed. Soak the shutki in warm water for 10–15 minutes to soften and reduce saltiness, then drain and pat dry. In a bowl, mix the shutki with 2 tablespoons of mustard oil, 1 finely chopped onion, 1–2 minced green chilies, 1 teaspoon each of garlic and ginger paste, ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, and salt to taste (sparingly, as shutki is already salty). Add a teaspoon of mustard paste and a few chopped coriander leaves for added aroma. Cut banana leaves into medium rectangles, lightly heat them over an open flame to make them pliable, and place a spoonful of the fish mixture in the center of each leaf. Fold into tight parcels and secure with thread or toothpicks. Steam the parcels in a steamer or place them on a hot tawa (pan) over low heat, covering with a lid, and cook for 15–20 minutes, flipping halfway if using a pan. Once done, serve the aromatic shutki paturi hot with plain bhaat and a squeeze of lemon.

To prepare traditional Rangpur-style Shutki Paturi, start by washing 200 grams of dried fish (commonly punti shutki, mola shutki, or loitta shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to remove excess salt and odor. Soak for 10 minutes, then drain well. Pat the fish dry with a kitchen towel.

In a bowl, prepare the spice paste by mixing 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 tablespoon mustard seeds (ground to a paste), 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, 1 tablespoon finely chopped green chilies, 1 teaspoon garlic paste, salt to taste, and a handful of chopped coriander leaves. Coat the dried fish thoroughly with this spice mixture.

Take banana leaves (or foil if unavailable) and lightly warm them to make them pliable. Place the spiced shutki on the leaf, fold it into a neat parcel, and secure with kitchen twine or toothpicks.

Steam or shallow fry the parcels on low heat for about 15–20 minutes until the fish is cooked through and the spices have infused well. For a smoky aroma, you can slightly char the leaf-wrapped parcels over an open flame for a few seconds before serving.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice, green chilies, and a squeeze of lemon, reflecting the rustic and bold flavors of Rangpur cuisine.

To prepare traditional Sylhet-style Shutki Paturi, begin by washing 200 grams of dried fish (commonly loitta shutki, punti shutki, or chingri shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to remove excess salt and odor. Soak for about 10 minutes, then drain and pat dry.

In a bowl, make a spice paste by mixing 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 tablespoon mustard seeds ground to a paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1–2 teaspoons red chili powder (Sylhet style is moderately spicy), 1 teaspoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon chopped green chilies, and salt to taste. Add a handful of chopped coriander leaves for extra aroma. Coat the dried fish thoroughly with this mixture.

Take banana leaves (or foil as an alternative) and soften them over low heat. Place the spiced fish on the leaf and fold it into a tight parcel, securing the edges. Steam the parcels in a steamer or shallow pan with a little water for about 20–25 minutes until the fish is fully cooked and the flavors are infused. Optionally, lightly char the parcels over an open flame for a smoky aroma just before serving.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice, raw green chilies, and a small side of mashed vegetables (like aloo bharta) to enjoy the authentic Sylhet-style Shutki Paturi.

To prepare traditional Tribal-style Shutki Paturi, commonly found among indigenous communities of the Chittagong Hill Tracts and northern tribal regions, start by washing 200 grams of dried fish (such as punti shutki, mola shutki, or chapila shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to reduce excess salt and strong odor. Soak for about 10 minutes, then drain and pat dry.

In a bowl, prepare a simple spice mixture using 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1–2 finely chopped green chilies, a pinch of salt, and a handful of local wild herbs or coriander leaves. Unlike mainstream Bengali recipes, tribal versions focus on earthy, raw flavors and minimal spices. Coat the fish thoroughly with this mixture.

Take banana leaves or large locally available leaves and soften them over low heat. Place the spiced fish on the leaf and fold it into a tight parcel. Steam the parcels over boiling water in a steamer or covered pot for 20–25 minutes until the fish is tender and aromatic. Tribal methods often avoid frying, keeping the dish lighter and closer to natural flavors.

Serve hot with plain boiled rice, boiled vegetables, or local greens, reflecting the rustic and earthy cuisine of the tribal regions.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Shutki Polao, begin by washing and soaking 2 cups of short-grain rice or kalijira rice for 15–20 minutes, then drain and keep aside. Wash 150–180 grams of dried fish (commonly loitta shutki, chingri shutki, or punti shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to remove excess salt and odor, then soak for 10 minutes and drain well.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until lightly smoking. Add 1 medium onion thinly sliced and sauté until soft and lightly golden. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon ground cumin, and salt to taste. Stir for 2–3 minutes until aromatic.

Add the prepared shutki and sauté gently for 4–5 minutes so the fish is well coated with spices. Unlike other regional polao recipes, Barisal-style polao usually avoids yogurt or ghee, keeping the flavors simple and earthy. Add the drained rice and mix carefully to combine with the fish and spices. Pour in about 3 cups of hot water, add 2–3 slit green chilies, and bring to a boil.

Reduce the heat to low, cover tightly, and cook for 12–15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and aromatic. Let it rest for 5 minutes before fluffing gently with a fork.

Serve hot with mashed vegetables, green chilies, and plain boiled greens for a rustic, authentic Barisal-style meal.

To prepare traditional Chattogram-style Shutki Polao, start by washing 2 cups of kalijira or basmati rice thoroughly and soaking it in water for 20 minutes, then drain and set aside. In a pan, lightly fry 150 g of dry fish (such as loitta shutki or chhuri shutki) without oil for 2–3 minutes to remove excess moisture and smell, then set aside. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat 4 tablespoons of ghee or mustard oil and fry 2 finely sliced medium onions until golden brown; remove half the fried onions and reserve them for garnish. To the remaining onions, add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 3 to 4 green cardamoms, 2 cinnamon sticks, 3 to 4 cloves, and 1 bay leaf, sautéing until fragrant. Stir in ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon red chili powder, and 1 teaspoon cumin powder with a splash of water, cooking until the oil separates. Add the fried shutki and stir well for 4–5 minutes so the fish absorbs the spices. Next, add the drained rice and gently fry for 2–3 minutes, coating each grain with the spiced mixture. Pour in 3.5 cups of hot water, 1.5 teaspoons of salt, and 1 teaspoon of sugar, stir gently, and bring it to a boil. Once it begins to boil, reduce the heat to low, cover the pan with a tight-fitting lid, and cook for 15–18 minutes until the rice is tender and the water is fully absorbed. After turning off the heat, let the polao rest, covered, for another 5 minutes to finish steaming. Fluff gently with a fork and garnish with the reserved fried onions before serving hot.

To prepare traditional Dhaka-style Shutki Polao, begin by washing and soaking 2 cups of kalijira or basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside. Separately, wash 150 grams of small dried fish (such as chingri shutki or punti shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to reduce excess odor, then soak for 10 minutes and drain well.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 4 tablespoons of ghee mixed with 1 tablespoon mustard oil for aroma. Add 2 medium onions thinly sliced and fry until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, 1 teaspoon coriander powder, and salt to taste. Sauté the spices on low heat for 2–3 minutes until fragrant.

Add the prepared shutki to the pot and cook for 5–6 minutes, stirring gently so the fish is well coated with the spice mixture. Add 2 tablespoons plain yogurt and cook until the oil separates. Now add the drained rice and gently mix everything together for 1–2 minutes. Pour in 3.5 cups of hot water, add 2–3 green cardamoms, 1 cinnamon stick, and 2 bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover tightly, and cook for about 15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and fluffy.

Before serving, gently fluff the polao with a fork and drizzle a little ghee on top for rich Dhaka-style aroma. Serve hot with cucumber salad or plain yogurt.

To prepare traditional Hill Tracts–style Shutki Polao, begin by washing and soaking 2 cups of short-grain rice or kalijira rice for 15–20 minutes, then drain and keep aside. Wash 150–180 grams of dried fish (commonly loitta shutki, chapila shutki, or punti shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times and soak for 10 minutes to reduce excess salt and odor. Drain well.

In a heavy pot or clay handi, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil until lightly smoking, then lower the heat. Add 2–3 crushed dried red chilies and 1 tablespoon chopped garlic, frying briefly until aromatic. Add the prepared shutki and sauté on low heat for 4–5 minutes until lightly crisp and fragrant.

Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, salt to taste, and 2–3 slit green chilies. Unlike Dhaka-style polao, no garam masala or ghee is traditionally used. Add the drained rice and gently mix so the grains are coated with oil and shutki flavor. Pour in about 3 cups of hot water (slightly less than regular polao), stir once, and bring to a boil.

Reduce heat to low, cover tightly, and cook for 12–15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and aromatic with distinct grains. Once done, let it rest for 5 minutes before fluffing gently with a fork.

Serve hot with simple boiled vegetables, bamboo shoot bharta, or green leafy bhaji, reflecting the minimal, earthy cuisine of the Hill Tracts.

To prepare traditional Rangpur-style Shutki Polao, begin by washing and soaking 2 cups of kalijira or local short-grain rice for about 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside. Wash 150–180 grams of dried fish (commonly punti shutki, mola shutki, or chapila shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to reduce excess salt and strong odor, then soak for 10 minutes and drain well.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 4 tablespoons mustard oil until lightly smoking, then reduce the heat. Add 2 medium onions thinly sliced and fry until deep golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon garlic paste and 1 teaspoon ginger paste, sautéing briefly until aromatic. Add 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons red chili powder (Rangpur-style is slightly spicier), 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Stir well on low heat for 2–3 minutes.

Add the prepared shutki and cook for 5–6 minutes until the fish is well coated with spices and slightly crisp. Add 1 tablespoon plain yogurt (optional but common in Rangpur homes) and cook until oil separates. Add the soaked rice and gently mix for 1–2 minutes. Pour in about 3 to 3.5 cups of hot water, add 2 bay leaves and 2–3 green chilies, and bring to a boil.

Reduce heat to low, cover the pot tightly, and cook for about 15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and fluffy. Let it rest for 5 minutes, then gently fluff the rice with a fork before serving.

Serve hot with aloo bhorta, green chili, and raw onion slices for an authentic Rangpur-style meal.

To prepare traditional Sylhet-style Shutki Polao, begin by washing and soaking 2 cups of kalijira or aromatic short-grain rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside. Wash 150–180 grams of dried fish (commonly loitta shutki or punti shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times and soak for 10 minutes to reduce excess salt and strong aroma. Drain well.

In a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3 tablespoons mustard oil mixed with 1 tablespoon ghee. Add 2 medium onions finely sliced and fry until golden brown. Add 1 tablespoon ginger paste, 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, 1 teaspoon cumin powder, and salt to taste. Sauté on low heat for 2–3 minutes until fragrant.

Add the prepared shutki and cook for 5–6 minutes, gently stirring so the fish absorbs the spices. Add 2 tablespoons plain yogurt, a common Sylheti touch, and cook until oil separates. Add the soaked rice and mix gently for 1–2 minutes. Pour in about 3.5 cups of hot water. Add 2 green cardamoms, 1 small cinnamon stick, 2 bay leaves, and 1 teaspoon crushed black pepper (distinctive in Sylhet cuisine).

Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover tightly, and cook for about 15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and aromatic. Let it rest for 5 minutes before fluffing lightly with a fork.

Serve hot with lemon wedges, green chilies, and simple vegetable bhaji or salad, as traditionally enjoyed in Sylhet households.

To prepare traditional Barisal-style Steamed Shutki, begin by washing 200 grams of dried fish (commonly chingri shutki, loitta shutki, or punti shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to reduce excess salt and strong odor. Soak for about 10–15 minutes, then drain well. Lightly break the shutki into medium pieces and place them in a bowl.

Add 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 medium onion finely sliced, 4–5 green chilies slit lengthwise, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, salt to taste, and 1 teaspoon crushed mustard seeds. Mix everything well so the fish is evenly coated with spices and oil. No frying is done in this method, which is characteristic of Barisal’s steamed shutki dishes.

Transfer the mixture into a heatproof bowl or traditional covered container. Place it in a steamer or a pot with boiling water, cover tightly, and steam on medium heat for about 20–25 minutes until the fish is soft, aromatic, and fully cooked, and the spices have infused well.

Once done, remove from heat and finish with a drizzle of 1 teaspoon raw mustard oil for authentic Barisal aroma. Serve hot with plain steamed rice, mashed potato (aloo bhorta), and lentils.

To prepare traditional Chattogram-style Steamed Shutki, begin by washing 200 grams of dried fish (commonly loitta shutki, chingri shutki, or faissa shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to reduce excess salt and strong smell. Soak for about 10 minutes, then drain well and break the shutki into medium-sized pieces.

Place the prepared shutki in a bowl and add 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 medium onion thinly sliced, 5–6 green chilies slit lengthwise, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons red chili powder (Chattogram style is spicier), salt to taste, and 1 teaspoon crushed mustard seeds. Add 1 tablespoon garlic paste and mix everything well so the fish is evenly coated with spices and oil.

Transfer the mixture to a heatproof bowl or covered container. Steam it in a steamer or in a pot with boiling water on medium heat for about 25 minutes until the fish becomes soft, aromatic, and fully cooked, and the spices blend into a bold, pungent flavor.

Once done, remove from heat and drizzle 1 teaspoon of raw mustard oil on top for authentic Chattogram aroma. Serve hot with plain steamed rice, mashed vegetables (like aloo or begun bhorta), and fresh green chilies.

To prepare Dhaka-style Shutki Steamed, take 200 grams of dry fish (such as loitta or chhuri shutki), rinse lightly in warm water, and drain well. In a bowl, mix the shutki with 2 tablespoons mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, ½ teaspoon mustard paste, 2 minced garlic cloves, 1 sliced onion, 2 slit green chilies, and salt if needed, coating everything evenly. Wrap the mixture tightly in a banana leaf parcel and secure with thread, then place it in a steamer or on a hot tawa under a heavy lid for 15–20 minutes until the fish becomes soft, aromatic, and infused with mustard flavor. Serve hot with plain rice for a traditional Dhaka-style rustic meal.

To prepare Khulna-style Shutki Steamed, wash 200 grams of dry fish (such as chhuri or loitta shutki) lightly and soak in warm water for 10 minutes to soften, then drain. In a bowl, mix the shutki with 2 tablespoons of mustard oil, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon chili powder, ½ teaspoon mustard seed paste, 2 minced garlic cloves, 1 sliced onion, 2 slit green chilies, and salt to taste, coating everything well. Wrap the mixture in a banana leaf parcel and secure tightly, then steam it for 15–20 minutes or place the parcel on a hot tawa under a heavy lid until the fish is tender and infused with mustard flavor. Serve hot with plain rice for a rustic, flavorful meal.

To prepare Shutki Steamed, a traditional preparation that locks in the strong flavors of dried fish by steaming, often using Loitta Shutki (dried Bombay Duck), begin by taking 12 to 15 pieces of dried fish, cutting them into 1 to 2 inch long pieces, and soaking them in warm water for 20 to 25 minutes, then washing and draining them well to remove all dirt. In a bowl, combine the cleaned shutki with 1 cup of chopped onion, 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, 1 half teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of green chili paste, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 half cup of oil, 1 half cup of chopped coriander leaves, and salt as required, mixing everything thoroughly by hand. Transfer the marinated mixture into a steel container or tiffin box, cover it tightly with a lid, and place the box inside a large pot or steamer containing boiling water, ensuring the water level is below the box. Steam the sealed container for 30 to 40 minutes over a medium flame, or until the fish is tender and fully cooked in its own flavorful juices. Open the box carefully and serve the intensely flavored steamed shutki with hot plain rice.

To prepare Shutki Steamed, a pungent and flavorful preparation from the Rangpur region, typically using Chepa Shutki (semi-fermented small fish) known for its high nutritional value, begin by taking 6 to 8 pieces of Chepa Shutki and thoroughly washing them multiple times in warm water to remove all grit and sand. In a bowl, combine the cleaned Chepa Shutki with 1 cup of chopped onions, 1 tablespoon of crushed garlic, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of salt, and 1 half cup of chopped coriander leaves, mixing the ingredients well with your hands. Add a splash of mustard oil, approximately 2 tablespoons, to the mixture to bind the spices. Transfer the entire mixture to a small, lidded steel box (tiffin carrier), securing the lid tightly. Place the sealed box inside a large pot or steamer containing boiling water, ensuring the water level is below the box's lid. Steam the shutki for 30 to 45 minutes over a medium-high flame until the fish is completely tender and the oil separates, indicating it is fully cooked. Serve the intensely aromatic steamed shutki directly from the box with hot plain rice for an authentic regional experience.

To prepare Shutki Steamed, a pungent and flavorful tribal delicacy often featuring the flavor of bamboo shoot, begin by taking 1 cup of boiled and sliced bamboo shoot and 1 half cup of dried shrimp or small dried fish, and thoroughly wash the dried fish in warm water 3–4 times to remove all grit and sand. In a bowl, combine the washed dried fish and bamboo shoot with 1 cup of chopped onion, 2 tablespoons of crushed garlic, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of salt, 1 half cup of chopped coriander leaves, and 2 tablespoons of mustard oil, mixing all the ingredients well by hand. Transfer the mixture to a steel tiffin box or a similar sealed container and secure the lid tightly. Place the sealed container inside a steamer or a large pot of boiling water and steam on medium-high heat for 30 to 45 minutes until the fish is tender and the bamboo shoot is soft. Once done, remove from the steamer and serve hot with plain steamed rice.

To prepare a traditional Barisal-style Shutki Bhorta, which serves as a spicy, flavorful filling, begin with 100g of churi shutki (dried ribbon fish). Wash the shutki thoroughly under running water to remove any sand and soak it in warm water for about 10 minutes to soften. In a frying pan, dry roast a few whole dry red chilies and a few cloves of garlic until they become fragrant. Set these aside. In the same pan, heat a small amount of mustard oil and lightly fry the soaked shutki pieces until they are slightly crisp. In a mortar and pestle or on a grinding stone, first mash the fried dry chilies and roasted garlic with a little salt. Then add the fried shutki pieces and continue to mash until you get a coarse paste. Finally, add finely chopped onions and fresh coriander leaves, and mash them gently into the mixture, finishing with a drizzle of fresh mustard oil. This spicy and tangy bhorta is not typically used as a stuffing in a formal sense, but it is often served as a dense, packed ball or "stuffed" inside a side dish like a chili or brinjal. This bhorta is best served with hot rice.

To prepare Shutki Stuffed in the Chattogram style, a spicy and aromatic dried fish delicacy, start by soaking 250 g of dried shutki (dry fish) in warm water for 30 minutes to soften and reduce saltiness. Drain and finely chop the fish.

In a pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil until hot. Add 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, and salt to taste. Cook for 2–3 minutes until fragrant.

Add the chopped shutki and 1 chopped green chili, mixing thoroughly with the masala. Cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes until the flavors are well absorbed. Meanwhile, prepare small slits in 2–3 medium-sized eggplants or bell peppers (as preferred) to stuff with the cooked shutki mixture. Carefully fill each vegetable with the shutki masala.

Heat a little oil in a separate pan and place the stuffed vegetables, covering and cooking on low heat for 10–12 minutes until the vegetables are tender and slightly roasted. Garnish with chopped fresh coriander leaves before serving.

To prepare Shutki Stuffed in the Dhaka style, a richly spiced and aromatic dried fish dish, start by soaking 250 g of dried shutki (dry fish) in warm water for 20–30 minutes to soften and remove excess salt. Drain and finely chop the fish.

In a pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard or soybean oil until hot. Add 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, cooking until fragrant. Add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Cook the masala for 2–3 minutes until aromatic.

Add the chopped shutki and 2 chopped green chilies, mixing thoroughly with the masala. Cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes until the flavors are well absorbed. Meanwhile, prepare 2–3 medium-sized eggplants or bell peppers by making slits for stuffing. Carefully stuff each vegetable with the cooked shutki mixture.

Heat a little oil in another pan and place the stuffed vegetables, cover, and cook on low heat for 10–12 minutes until the vegetables are tender and slightly roasted. Garnish with fresh coriander leaves before serving.

To prepare Shutki Stuffed in the Mymensingh style, a spicy and aromatic dried fish delicacy, start by soaking 250 g of dried shutki (dry fish) in warm water for 20–30 minutes to soften and reduce saltiness. Drain and finely chop the fish.

In a pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard or soybean oil until hot. Add 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, cooking until fragrant. Add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of coriander powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Cook the masala for 2–3 minutes until aromatic.

Add the chopped shutki and 2 chopped green chilies, mixing thoroughly with the masala. Cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes until the flavors are absorbed. Meanwhile, prepare 2–3 medium-sized eggplants or bell peppers by making slits for stuffing. Carefully stuff each vegetable with the cooked shutki mixture.

Heat a little oil in another pan and place the stuffed vegetables, cover, and cook on low heat for 10–12 minutes until the vegetables are tender and slightly roasted. Garnish with fresh coriander leaves before serving.

To prepare traditional Rajshahi-style Shutki Stuffed, begin by washing 200 grams of medium-sized dried fish (usually rupchanda shutki, chanda shutki, or punti shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to reduce excess smell. Soak for 10 minutes, drain well, and gently open each fish from the belly without breaking it. Keep aside.

For the stuffing, heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan and add 1 small finely chopped onion, sautéing until light golden. Add 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 1.5 teaspoons red chili powder, salt to taste, and 1 teaspoon crushed mustard seeds. Stir well on low heat for 2–3 minutes, then add 2 tablespoons mashed boiled potato and 1 tablespoon chopped coriander leaves. Cook briefly until the mixture becomes dry and aromatic. Remove from heat and allow it to cool slightly.

Carefully stuff this spice mixture into the prepared shutki fish. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a shallow pan until lightly smoking, then gently place the stuffed fish into the oil. Fry on low to medium heat, turning carefully, until both sides become golden brown and crisp. This process takes about 6–8 minutes. Once cooked, remove and place on absorbent paper. Optionally, drizzle a few drops of raw mustard oil on top for authentic Rajshahi aroma before serving.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice, mashed potatoes (aloo bhorta), and green chilies for a complete traditional Rajshahi meal.

To prepare traditional Rangpur-style Shutki Stuffed, begin by washing 200 grams of medium-sized dried fish (commonly punti shutki or mola shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to reduce excess odor. Soak for about 10 minutes, then drain well. Carefully slit each fish lengthwise from the belly and remove any hard bones if needed, keeping the fish intact. Set aside.

For the stuffing, heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan and add 1 medium onion finely chopped, sautéing until soft and lightly golden. Add 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons red chili powder (Rangpur-style is slightly spicier), salt to taste, and 1 teaspoon crushed cumin seeds. Stir on low heat for 2–3 minutes. Add 1 tablespoon mashed boiled potato and 1 tablespoon finely chopped coriander leaves, mixing until the stuffing becomes dry and fragrant. Remove from heat and let it cool slightly.

Gently fill each prepared shutki fish with the spice mixture. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a shallow pan until lightly smoking, then reduce the heat and carefully place the stuffed fish into the oil. Fry on low to medium heat, turning carefully, until both sides are evenly golden and crisp, about 7–9 minutes in total. Finish by adding 2–3 slit green chilies into the pan for aroma during the last minute of frying.

Serve hot with plain steamed rice, aloo bhorta, and raw onion slices, which is typical of Rangpur cuisine.

To prepare traditional Tribal-style Shutki Stuffed, commonly found among indigenous communities of the Chittagong Hill Tracts and northern tribal regions of Bangladesh, begin by washing 200 grams of small to medium dried fish (such as punti shutki, mola shutki, or chapila shutki) thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times. Soak for about 10 minutes to reduce excess salt and odor, then drain well. Carefully slit the fish lengthwise, keeping them intact.

For the stuffing, place the soaked shutki in a bowl and lightly mash them using your fingers or a mortar. Add 2 tablespoons chopped fresh green chilies, 1 tablespoon crushed garlic, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, salt to taste, and 1–2 tablespoons chopped wild herbs or coriander leaves (tribal versions often use local leafy herbs). Mix everything well into a coarse paste. Unlike regional Bengali versions, no onion or garam masala is traditionally used, keeping the flavors raw, earthy, and rustic.

Stuff this mixture back into the slit fish. Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan until lightly smoking, then gently place the stuffed fish into the oil. Fry on low heat, turning carefully, until both sides are crisp and deeply aromatic, about 6–8 minutes. Optionally, a few crushed dried red chilies or bamboo shoot slivers may be added to the oil during frying for an authentic tribal aroma.

Serve hot with plain boiled rice or jum rice, along with mashed vegetables or simple boiled greens, as traditionally eaten in tribal households.

To prepare traditional Chattogram-style Shutki Tok, start by washing 150–200 grams of dried fish (shutki), such as loitta or chingri shutki, thoroughly in warm water 3–4 times to reduce excess odor, then soak it for about 10 minutes and drain well. In a pan, heat 3 tablespoons of mustard oil until slightly smoking, then add the soaked shutki and lightly fry for 3–4 minutes until crisp on the outside. Remove and keep aside.

In the same pan, add a little more mustard oil if needed, then add 1 medium onion thinly sliced and sauté until lightly golden. Add 1 tablespoon garlic paste, 1 teaspoon ginger paste, 1 teaspoon turmeric powder, and 1 teaspoon red chili powder, stirring well on low heat for 1–2 minutes. Add 2 medium tomatoes chopped and cook until they soften and release oil. Now add 2 tablespoons of tamarind pulp (or adjust to taste for sourness), salt to taste, and 1.5 cups of water, mixing everything well.

Once the gravy starts to simmer, add the fried shutki back into the pan along with 3–4 slit green chilies. Let it cook on medium-low heat for about 10–12 minutes so the flavors blend and the gravy slightly thickens with a balanced sour-spicy taste. Finish by drizzling 1 teaspoon of mustard oil on top for authentic aroma. Serve hot with plain steamed rice for the best traditional experience.

To prepare Shutki Tok in the Khulna style, a tangy and spicy dried fish dish with a hint of mustard aroma, start by soaking 200 g of dried shutki (dry fish) in warm water for 20–30 minutes to soften and reduce saltiness. Drain and cut into small pieces.

Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard or soybean oil in a pan until hot. Add 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, cooking until fragrant.

Add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Fry the spices for 2–3 minutes until aromatic. Add the soaked shutki pieces and mix well to coat them evenly with the spices.

Add 2–3 tablespoons of tamarind juice (adjust to desired sourness) and 2 slit green chilies. Cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes until the flavors are well absorbed and the dish becomes slightly dry with a tangy, spicy coating.

Garnish with chopped fresh coriander leaves and serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Shutki Tok in the Mymensingh style, a tangy and spicy dried fish dish, start by soaking 200 g of dried shutki (dry fish) in warm water for 20–30 minutes to soften and reduce saltiness. Drain and cut into small pieces.

Heat 3 tablespoons of mustard or soybean oil in a pan until hot. Add 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add 1 large chopped onion and sauté until golden brown. Stir in 1 teaspoon of garlic paste and 1 teaspoon of ginger paste, cooking until fragrant.

Add 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of cumin powder, and salt to taste. Fry the spices for 2–3 minutes until aromatic. Add the soaked shutki pieces and stir to coat them evenly with the spices.

Add 2–3 tablespoons of tamarind juice (or adjust to desired sourness) and 2 slit green chilies. Cook on low heat for 5–7 minutes until the flavors are well absorbed and the dish becomes slightly dry with a tangy and spicy coating.

Garnish with chopped fresh coriander leaves and serve hot with plain rice.

To prepare a traditional Rangpur-style Shutki Tok, start with 100g of dried fish (e.g., Loitta or Churi Shutki). Wash the dried fish thoroughly with hot water several times to remove any sand and impurities. Cut the fish into small pieces and set them aside. Heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil in a pan and add 1 large sliced onion, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, and 2-3 green chilies. Fry until the onion becomes soft and translucent. Add ½ teaspoon turmeric powder, ½ teaspoon cumin powder, ½ teaspoon red chili powder, and salt to taste. Stir for a minute, adding a splash of water to prevent the spices from burning. Now, add the cleaned dried fish pieces and 1-2 pieces of dried mango (amshi) or tamarind paste for the 'tok' (sour) flavor. Pour in about 1 cup of water and bring the mixture to a boil. Reduce the heat and let it simmer for 15-20 minutes, or until the fish is tender and the gravy has thickened to your desired consistency. Finish with chopped fresh coriander leaves. Serve hot with steamed rice.

To prepare Shutki Tok, a traditional sour and spicy dried fish curry from the Sylhet region, often called Shutki Shira which is usually cooked without oil, begin by soaking 5 to 6 pieces of dry shrimp or preferred shutki (dried fish) in warm water for 30 minutes, then rinse thoroughly to clean and set aside. In a deep saucepan, combine 1 chopped medium onion, 4 to 5 cloves of minced garlic, 1 teaspoon of red chili powder, 1 half teaspoon of turmeric powder, and salt to taste with about 1 cup of water, and bring the mixture to a boil over high heat, cooking for 5 to 7 minutes. Add the cleaned shutki, 1 chopped potato, and any other seasonal vegetables like pumpkin or eggplant, and add 2 more cups of water; cover and cook for 10 minutes until the vegetables are tender. To achieve the Tok (sour) flavor, add 2 tablespoons of tamarind pulp or 1 half cup of chopped tomatoes, along with 3 to 4 whole green chilies or a small slit Naga chili for a distinct flavor, and simmer for a final 5 to 7 minutes until the gravy is slightly reduced. Serve the sour and fragrant stew hot with rice.

To prepare Shutki Tok (sour dried fish curry) in the style of the Indigenous communities of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, such as the Chakma or Marma, which is commonly known as Pachon or Hutki Shira, begin by taking 4 to 5 pieces of dry fish and boiling them in 1 cup of water with a pinch of salt and 1 half teaspoon of turmeric powder for 5 minutes, then strain, reserving the water, and shred the fish. In a large pot, add the reserved dried fish water along with 3 cups of clean water, 1 large chopped onion, 5 to 6 cloves of minced garlic, 1 tablespoon of red chili powder, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, and salt to taste, bringing the liquid to a rolling boil. Add 1 half cup of chopped pumpkin, 1 half cup of sliced eggplant, 1 half cup of chopped potatoes, and other seasonal vegetables like yard long beans or bamboo shoots, and cook on high heat for 10 minutes until the vegetables begin to soften. Stir in the shredded dry fish, 3 to 4 whole green chilies, and the essential souring agent, which is 3 tablespoons of shredded unripe mango or 2 tablespoons of dried mango (amshi) for the authentic 'tok' flavor, and let it simmer for a final 5 to 7 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the sour broth is flavorful. Serve this thin, spicy, and sour stew hot with steamed rice.

To make traditional Bangladeshi Tehari, begin by washing and soaking 2 cups of kalijira or basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside. In a large heavy-bottomed pot, heat 4 tablespoons of mustard oil until it reaches smoking point to eliminate its rawness, then lower the heat and add 2 thinly sliced medium onions, frying until they turn golden brown. Add 500 grams of bone-in beef pieces, preferably small cuts from the shank or shoulder, along with 1 tablespoon of ginger paste, 1 tablespoon of garlic paste, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, 2 teaspoons of red chili powder, 1.5 teaspoons of salt, and 1 teaspoon of garam masala powder, then sauté everything for about 10–12 minutes until the meat browns and releases its juices. Add half a cup of plain yogurt and cook for another 5–7 minutes until the oil separates and the beef is coated in a rich, thick gravy. Pour in 2.5 cups of hot water, cover the pot, and let the beef simmer on low heat for about 45 minutes or until tender. Once the meat is soft and about 1.5 to 2 cups of liquid remain in the pot, add the soaked rice and gently stir to distribute it evenly. Let it cook uncovered over medium heat until most of the liquid is absorbed, then reduce the heat to low, cover the pot tightly, and steam the tehari for another 15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and fluffy. Before serving, fluff the rice with a fork and garnish with a few green chilies or a sprinkle of fried onions for added aroma.
